What to ask before the repair
How much diagnosis costs and what it includes: just reading codes, or also checking circuits and live data.
A preliminary price for the repair. Agree that any extra work is done only after they call you.
Timing: when you’ll hear the diagnosis and when the car will be ready if a part has to be ordered.
Warranty: on the labor, the parts or both, for how long, and what to keep for it — the receipt, the work order.
Whose parts — the shop’s or yours. If you buy them yourself, go by the catalog for your car.
Ask in advance for the removed parts to be handed back, or at least shown to you.
Which report to ask for

Ask for a printout or photo of the scan before the repair — codes in all modules and the freeze frame — and after it: no codes, car checked on a test drive. Add a work order listing the work and parts. That shows exactly what was found and what was done, and if the problem comes back you’ll have something to compare with.

Signs of unnecessary part replacement
A part is replaced based on the trouble code alone, with no measurements. A code points to a system or circuit, not a part.
They suggest replacing several parts at once “just in case” and can’t explain why each one is faulty.
The codes were cleared without being written down — and a day later the light came back on.
They say “the control unit needs replacing” right away, without checking its power and ground.
The price went up without your consent, and the removed parts weren’t shown.

A good mechanic goes from simple and cheap to complex — here are two cases from Oleg’s blog. A 2022 Omoda with misfires: there were no codes, and the misfires were found in live data. The spark plugs fitted earlier weren’t from the catalog — so first the right plugs and a recheck, not expensive coils right away. A 2025 Toyota Grand Highlander with codes in the EVAP fuel vapor system: the pump and valves turned out fine, and the car had been in a collision. The working pump wasn’t replaced — a leak check of the system was recommended instead.

If a red oil pressure, overheating or brake warning light is on, don’t drive the car to the shop — as in the lesson on dashboard warning lights. Describe everything over the phone and call a tow truck.
Before the visit, write down what happens, when and after what it started, under what conditions, what the dash shows and what has been replaced.
Before the repair, agree on the diagnosis price, a preliminary price, timing, warranty and a call before any extra work.
Ask for a scan report from before and after the repair and a work order listing the work and parts.
Replacing parts on a code alone without measurements, or several parts at once “just in case”, are signs of wasted money.

Which description will help the mechanic most?
“Something electrical, take a look”
“Stalls only when the engine is warm, started after a fill-up, I have a photo of the dash”
“My neighbor says it’s a sensor”
It has the conditions, when the problem started and a photo: the mechanic knows at once which system to start with. Guesses about parts and vague words don’t help.
A mechanic suggests replacing three parts at once based on a single trouble code, without measuring anything. What should you do?
Agree — the code showed everything
Clear the code and keep driving
Ask them to test the circuit and explain why each part is faulty
A code points to a system or circuit, not a part. Replacing parts without measurements, “just in case”, is a sign of wasted money.
Which report should you ask for after the repair?
A scan report from before and after the repair and a work order listing the work and parts
Just a verbal “it’s done”
A photo of the engine
The before-and-after report shows what was found and what was fixed, and the work order and receipt are needed for the warranty.
Why didn’t replacing the turn signal relay help the Lexus ES300 from the blog?
The relay was defective
The turn signal bulb had burned out
The wrong fuse was fitted
Leftover wiring from a removed alarm was shorting the turn signal circuit to the body

A hybrid has a regular engine, an electric motor and a traction battery; an EV has only the battery and the electric motor. There are more of them in Kazakhstan: according to Interior Ministry data cited by Kazinform on August 23, 2025, 17,976 EVs were registered, up from more than 12,000 in February 2025. Drivers don’t need to service the high-voltage system, but a few rules are worth knowing.

Orange wires and connectors carry high voltage that can kill, even when the car is switched off. Don’t touch or disconnect them, and don’t remove protective covers or the service disconnect: only a trained technician works on the high-voltage system, following the manufacturer’s instructions. More in the lesson on safety.
Charging at home
Charge with the cable that came with the car or a home charging station suitable for your model — following the manufacturer’s instructions.
No extension cords, power strips or adapters: charging draws high current for hours, and a weak connection heats up.
Before charging at home, have an electrician check that the wiring can handle it and install a dedicated circuit for charging. That’s the advice of NFPA, the US National Fire Protection Association.
Before charging, inspect the cable and plug: if there are cracks, melting or signs of overheating, don’t charge.
If the plug or outlet is hot or there’s a burning smell, stop charging from the car or the app and call an electrician.
Protect an outdoor outlet or station from water and snow, and don’t leave the cable in a puddle.
Dedicated circuit
Outlet or charging station
The car’s own cable
Charging
No extension cords or power strips
At home: a dedicated circuit from the panel and the car’s own cable, no extension cords or power strips.
Charging at a station
The station’s connector has to match your car’s charge port. Which connector your car uses is in the manual; which ones the station has is in its app.
Don’t charge from a station with a damaged cable or connector — report it to the operator.
In winter, clear snow and ice from the port beforehand; don’t yank a frozen connector out by force.
End the session with the button in the car, on the station or in the app, and only then unplug the connector.
The small 12 V battery

Hybrids and EVs also have an ordinary 12 V battery. It doesn’t crank an engine; it “wakes up” the control modules and the relays that connect the traction battery. If it’s flat, the car won’t go into READY mode and the dash flickers or goes dark, even though the traction battery is charged. Test it as in the lesson on the battery, charge it in the mode for its type — often AGM — and jump-start only from the points shown in the manual. If the car sits for a long time, the small battery runs down just as it does in a regular car.
12 V battery charged
Modules and relays
System is on
12 V battery flat
Car won’t switch on
The 12 V system switches on the traction battery: if the small battery is flat, there’s no READY.
Check the fuses first. If a hybrid or EV won’t wake up but the 12 V battery is charged, look at the 12 V system fuses before you think about expensive repairs.
Winter and range

In freezing weather range drops noticeably: energy goes into heating the cabin and the battery. In a test by the American Automobile Association, AAA (February 7, 2019), at 20 °F (−7 °C) with the heater on, range fell by 41% on average.
Preheat the cabin while the car is still plugged in, as AAA advises: the heat comes from the grid, not the battery.
A cold battery charges more slowly. Charge right after a drive while it’s still warm, and don’t leave the car in the cold for long with an almost empty battery.
In the cold a hybrid starts its engine more often to warm up and heat the cabin — that’s normal.
Before a long winter trip, check the forecast and plan charging stations along the way.
Towing

When the wheels turn, the electric motor turns with them and generates current. That’s why many manufacturers require a hybrid or EV to be carried on a flatbed tow truck. For example, the Tesla Model 3 manual says to transport it with all four wheels off the ground, or there may be serious damage and overheating. How to transport your car is in the towing section of its manual. Tell the tow company in advance that the car is a hybrid or an EV.

A hybrid has a regular engine, so Check Engine comes on just as in any car. An example from Oleg’s blog: on an almost new 2025 Toyota Grand Highlander HEV the cause was the fuel vapor system canister, damaged, presumably, during loading or shipping. One more thing: if a car was imported unofficially, the manufacturer’s recall may not cover it, and it has no warranty or dealer support — the blog covers this using the Zeekr 001 recall as an example.
Don’t touch the orange wires or the service disconnect: only a trained technician works on the high-voltage system.
At home: the car’s own cable and a dedicated circuit checked by an electrician, no extension cords or power strips; a hot plug means stop.
If the car won’t go into READY, check the 12 V battery and its fuses first.
Range is shorter in winter: preheat from the grid and charge after a drive. Transport such a car as the manual says, usually on a flatbed.

A driver can fix many small problems in a few minutes. The key is knowing where the line is: what you can do yourself and when it’s better to call a mechanic. Before any work under the hood, switch off the engine and take out the key.
Wiper blades
It’s time to replace a blade if it leaves streaks and smears, misses spots, squeaks or chatters. The rubber usually lasts 6–12 months, depending on driving and weather.
The driver’s and passenger’s blades are often different lengths: check the manual or the catalog for your model.
Lift the arm off the glass, press the latch and slide the blade off along the arm. Push the new one on until it clicks. Mounts vary — how to remove yours is usually shown on the new blade’s package.
While the blade is off, hold the arm: if it snaps back against the glass, it can chip or crack it.
In winter, don’t turn on the wipers if the blades are frozen to the glass: the motor strains for nothing and the rubber tears. Thaw the glass first.

A blade takes a minute to change; hold the arm so it doesn’t hit the glass.
Washer won’t spray
Is there fluid in the reservoir? Summer washer fluid in summer, winter fluid rated for the weather in winter. Don’t use plain water: in winter it freezes and can split the reservoir, hoses and pump.

Can you hear the pump when you hit the washer? If it hums but doesn’t spray, the nozzles are clogged, a hose has come off or the fluid has frozen. A clogged nozzle can be carefully cleared with a fine needle.
If the pump is silent — first the fuse, then the pump connector at the reservoir.
If the fluid has frozen, don’t keep holding the washer button: the pump runs dry and can burn out.
Check the fuses first. If just one thing stops working — the washer, the window defroster, the rear wiper — the first thing I check is that circuit’s fuse, using the diagram on the fuse box cover.
Rear window and mirror defrosters

The rear defroster is a set of thin conductive lines on the glass, with terminals at the sides. If the whole window stays cold, the problem is the power supply: the fuse, relay, switch, side terminals or the wires in the trunk lid rubber boot, where they often break. If it clears in stripes, individual lines are broken.

Whole window cold — look at the power supply; stripes — broken lines.

Finding a break: switch on the defroster and wait a few minutes — the stripe that hasn’t cleared is the broken line. For precision, use a multimeter: black probe on ground, then carefully run the red probe along the line. On an intact line the voltage falls smoothly from the positive edge to the negative edge; at a break it changes abruptly.
A line is repaired with the conductive compound from a repair kit: clean, degrease, apply and let it dry — the drying time is in the compound’s instructions.
Don’t scrub the inside of the glass across the lines with a scraper or a hard sponge, and peel off stickers carefully — that’s exactly how lines get broken.

On many cars the mirror heaters come on with the same button as the rear window. After 10–20 minutes the defroster usually switches itself off — that’s not a fault. If both mirrors stay cold, check the fuse; if just one, check its connector or the heater in the mirror.
Alternator belt and the charging light
What a worn belt looks like — cracks, glazing, squeal — is covered in the checklist lesson. Here’s what to do about it. The belt drives the alternator and, on many cars, the water pump as well.

If the battery light comes on while driving, stop somewhere safe and check the belt. If it’s broken and the engine temperature is rising, don’t drive on: without the water pump the engine will overheat.
If the belt is intact but the light stays on, the alternator isn’t charging. You can reach a shop on the battery’s reserve with extra loads switched off — but not far.
You can check charging with a multimeter, as in the multimeter lesson: 13.5–14.5 V at the battery with the engine running, including with the headlights, heater and rear defroster on.

Replacing the belt is a job for a mechanic or an experienced driver working from the manual: many engines need a tensioner tool and the routing diagram. Don’t set the tension by eye: an overtightened belt loads the bearings, and a loose one squeals and slips.

Inspect the belt and pulleys only with the engine off and the key out. The radiator fan can switch on by itself even with the engine off. Keep sleeves, scarves and long hair away from the belt.
Replace blades when they streak or squeak; hold the arm while the blade is off, and don’t run frozen wipers.

A “won’t start” or “start-stop doesn’t work” complaint often begins with the battery. Resting voltage, parasitic draw and cranking were covered in the lessons “Charging system”, “Parasitic draw” and “Starter motor”. Here is what a pro needs beyond that: how to prove a battery is worn, how not to get its type wrong, what the sensor on the negative terminal does and why a new battery must be registered.
Load test: charge first
Start with resting voltage: the car has sat, everything off. About 12.6 V or more — charged; 12.4 V — about 75 %; 12.2 V — about half. AGM rests a little higher.
Load-test only a charged battery — no lower than 12.4 V. Charge a flat one first, or you’ll mistake a good battery for a worn one.
After charging or a drive there’s a surface charge on the terminals, so the voltage reads high. Let the battery sit a few hours or remove it with a brief load.
The classic test: a load of half the CCA rating on the label for 15 seconds. At about 70 °F (21 °C) the voltage under load must not drop below 9.6 V.
In the cold the limit is lower: about 9.1 V at 30 °F (−1 °C) and 8.5 V at 0 °F (−18 °C). In winter it’s better to bring the battery inside and test it once it has warmed up.

Under a ½ CCA load a good battery stays above 9.6 V; a worn one drops below it.

A conductance tester doesn’t put a big load on the battery: it sends a small AC signal and from the response estimates internal resistance and, through it, the ability to crank the starter. It needs the battery type (standard, EFB or AGM) and the CCA from the label, and it gives the result in words: “good”, “charge and retest” or “replace”. Such a tester is safe, quick and checks even a flat battery — it simply asks you to charge it. Cars with a battery sensor estimate wear (SOH) themselves and on many a scan tool shows it, but that’s the module’s calculation, not a measurement: when in doubt, use a tester.
Standard, EFB and AGM
Standard flooded (calcium, Ca/Ca) — for cars without start-stop.
EFB — an enhanced flooded battery: it handles frequent starts and is fitted to cars with basic start-stop.
AGM — the electrolyte is soaked into glass-mat separators. For start-stop with energy recovery and a heavy electrical load. It’s sensitive to overcharging: charge it only in AGM mode.
Replace like with like: AGM only with AGM, EFB with EFB or AGM. Never fit a standard battery to a start-stop car (as battery maker Banner puts it).
Size, polarity, capacity and CCA — same as the original. A small capacity difference is usually fine, but register the battery that’s actually fitted.
The battery sensor on the negative terminal

Cars with start-stop and managed charging often have a battery sensor (IBS) on the negative terminal. All negative current flows through it: the sensor measures current from a tiny voltage drop across a shunt — a measuring resistor of very low resistance — plus voltage and temperature. From these it works out state of charge (SOC), state of health (SOH) and cranking ability and sends them to a module over the LIN bus. Using this data the module sets the alternator voltage (as in the lesson “Charging system”), allows or blocks start-stop and, when charge is low, switches off some comfort loads. Hence the rule: ground add-on equipment and the jump-start negative only to the ground point in the manual, never to the terminal — otherwise the sensor won’t see that current.

works out charge and wear

Allows start-stop
Add-on equipment

current unseen
✓ to the body:
the sensor sees it
Current for every factory load passes the sensor’s shunt — the drop across it is millivolts.
All negative current runs through the sensor’s shunt; a ground that bypasses it is current the module can’t see.
Registering a new battery

The energy management module remembers which battery is fitted and how worn it is. When you fit a new one, you have to tell it: register the battery with a scan tool. According to Banner, BMW requires registration on start-stop cars with a battery sensor from 2008 on — without it the new battery may be overcharged; on a Porsche start-stop won’t work until the battery is registered; on VAG cars (Audi, Seat, Skoda, Volkswagen) and Mini it’s recommended, and on a Mini it’s required if the battery type changes; some newer Mercedes from model year 2016 need it too, and Hyundai and Kia start-stop models need battery initialization. In the scan tool you enter the type (AGM or EFB), the capacity and sometimes the maker and serial number. On VAG you normally enter the BEM code from the original battery; an aftermarket battery has none, so scan tools let you pick the parameters from a menu.
Register batteries with a proper scan tool. I recommend Launch — it’s proven equipment. Cheap ELM327 adapters sometimes “brick” the car.
Replacing a battery without losses
Make sure the battery is the problem: charge and test it, check for parasitic draw and charging.
Choose a battery of the same technology, size and polarity; note the type and capacity for registration.
Connect a memory saver — a power supply or jump pack to the jump-start points per the manual — so settings and learned values aren’t lost.
Switch off the ignition and everything else, wait the time in the manual for the modules to sleep, and remove the negative — by the clamp, not by the sensor or its wire. Then the positive.
With a memory saver connected the cables stay live: insulate the positive clamp so it can’t touch the body.
Fit and secure the battery, connect the positive, then the negative with the sensor; torque the clamps to the manual’s spec.
Register the battery with a scan tool, read codes in all modules and run the relearns the manual calls for — as in the lesson “Adaptations and resets” of the course “Scan tool diagnostics”.

Batteries give off hydrogen: no flames, no sparks. Connect a load tester’s clamps before switching the load on and remove them after switching it off. Never disconnect the battery with the engine running. Don’t charge an AGM on a standard high-voltage setting, and never charge a frozen battery — let it thaw first.
Load-test only a charged battery (at least 12.4 V): ½ CCA for 15 seconds, no lower than 9.6 V at 70 °F; the limit is lower in the cold.
A conductance tester estimates internal resistance without a heavy load; it needs the battery type and the CCA.
AGM is replaced only with AGM, EFB with EFB or AGM; a standard battery never goes into a start-stop car.
The sensor on the negative sees only the current through it: ground add-ons to the body. Register a new battery with a scan tool.

The SRS — airbags and seat belt pretensioners — fires once, in a fraction of a second. A technician’s mistake here is costly: an accidental deployment injures, and a warning light “switched off” without a repair leaves people unprotected. What drivers must not touch is in the lesson “Safety” of the course “For drivers”, scan tool functions are in the course “Scan tool diagnostics”. Here: how the system is built, its codes and the work procedure for an auto electrician.
What makes up the SRS
The SRS module sits near the middle of the car, under the console or dash. Inside are acceleration sensors, a processor and an energy reserve so it can fire even if a crash cuts battery power.
Crash sensors are at the front and sides, in the pillars or doors. They confirm the impact, and the module decides what to fire and when.

Airbags: the driver’s in the wheel, the passenger’s in the dash, side airbags in the seats, curtains above the doors, knee airbags on some cars. Each has a squib and a gas generator; the bag fills in tens of milliseconds.
Belt pretensioners are pyrotechnic too: in a crash they take up belt slack. The buckles have “belt fastened” switches.
The passenger seat occupant sensor tells the module whether to arm the passenger airbag. There’s an “airbag off” indicator, and some cars have a key switch to disable it for a child seat.
The clock spring is a ribbon with tracks in the steering column assembly: it connects the turning wheel to the wiring — airbag, buttons and horn.

Crash sensors tell the module about the impact, and the module sends a pulse to the airbag and pretensioner squibs.
How the module watches its circuits

After the ignition is switched on, the SRS light stays on for a few seconds and goes out — the module has checked itself and its circuits. It measures each squib circuit’s resistance itself with a safe small current and compares it with limits; on many cars the result shows in the scan tool’s live data in manufacturer mode. SRS connectors are usually yellow, and the squib-side half has a shorting bar: while the connector is apart it shorts the squib pins together, protecting it from static and stray voltage.

In resistance mode a multimeter pushes current from its own battery — how much depends on the meter and range. A squib is designed to fire from a short current pulse, and manufacturers explicitly forbid connecting an ohmmeter, test light, probe or any power source to it. Only the SRS module tests the circuit; the auto electrician reads its codes and live data and follows the manufacturer’s procedure.

SRS codes and common causes
Circuit resistance too high — an open or poor contact: the clock spring, connectors under the seats, the pretensioner connector.
Resistance too low — a short between the circuit’s wires; a short to ground or to battery voltage — damaged wiring, water in a connector.
No communication with a crash sensor, a faulty occupant sensor, low module supply voltage — check the battery, grounds and the module’s fuse first.
The clock spring is a frequent culprit: the ribbon tears from wear or if the wheel was turned with the column apart. Signs: the SRS light, a driver airbag circuit code, dead wheel buttons and horn.
A crash is recorded — after a deployment the module, deployed airbags, pretensioners and sensors are replaced as the manufacturer directs.

Working safely, step by step
Read and save the SRS codes with a scan tool — before disconnecting the battery.
Switch the ignition off and remove the key, disconnect the negative battery cable and insulate it.
Wait the time in the manual: the module stores reserve energy. For example, Toyota specifies at least 90 seconds and Honda at least 3 minutes (per I-CAR).
Only then unplug SRS connectors. Carry a removed airbag module with the cover facing away from you and set it down cover up.
When removing the wheel, lock the clock spring centered and don’t turn it. Welding nearby only after removing SRS parts from the repair area, as the manufacturer requires.
Reassembly: ignition off, every connector in place and latched, battery negative last. When switching the ignition on, keep out of the airbags’ path; the light must come on and go out.
Read the codes again and clear them only once the cause is fixed.

Never measure squibs with an ohmmeter and never connect test lights, probes or power sources to them. Don’t work on SRS connectors with the ignition on or without waiting after disconnecting the battery. Deployed airbags, pretensioners and the module are never repaired — only replaced as the manufacturer directs.

What we don’t do: we don’t fit resistor “defeat devices” in place of airbags, and we don’t “reset” crash data while leaving deployed parts in the car. The light goes out, but in the next crash the airbag won’t deploy. If a customer asks to “just turn the light off”, explain why not and note in the work order that they were warned.
Check the fuses first. If the SRS light is on and the scan tool can’t see the airbag module, the first thing I check is its fuse and power supply, and only then do I look into the airbag circuits.
The SRS is a module with an energy reserve, crash sensors, airbags with squibs, pretensioners, an occupant sensor and the clock spring.
Only the module measures squib circuits, with a small current; no ohmmeter, test light or probe ever goes on a squib.
Before work: codes with a scan tool, ignition off, negative removed and insulated, wait per the manual.
Deployed parts — replace only; no defeat devices and no crash resets without replacement.

In resistance mode the meter supplies its own current, which may be enough to fire it. The SRS module checks the squib circuit itself — look at its codes and live data.

Codes and module data first — that’s the manufacturer’s procedure. Connectors are touched only after the battery is off and the wait time has passed.

Almost everything an auto electrician measures passes through semiconductors: the alternator’s diode bridge, a relay’s suppression diode, the transistor switches in the ECU and body module. Soldering them on the board belongs to the course “ECU repair”, but everyone needs to understand how they work: then the multimeter numbers and the oscilloscope picture make sense.
Diode: current one way
A diode passes current from anode to cathode and blocks it the other way. A conducting silicon diode drops about 0.6–0.7 V, a Schottky diode about 0.2–0.4 V.
To test, use diode-test mode: forward the meter reads about 0.5–0.7 V, reverse it reads OL. Near 0 both ways — shorted; OL both ways — open.
In the car: the alternator’s diode bridge rectifies the stator’s AC (lesson “Charging system”); a shorted bridge diode causes ripple and can drain the battery while parked (lesson “Parasitic draw”).
Also the reverse-polarity protection diode at module power inputs and the diode in a relay (lesson “Relays and control circuits”).
An LED is a diode too: it drops 1.8–3.3 V depending on color, and it needs a current limiter — a resistor or a driver.
Zener and TVS diodes: limiting voltage

Forward, a Zener diode behaves like an ordinary diode; in reverse it starts to conduct once the voltage reaches its rating — say 5.1 V — and then holds it nearly constant. It’s used to limit voltage: to protect module inputs and absorb coil spikes. A TVS diode, or suppressor, is its relative for short, powerful spikes. Some alternators use avalanche diodes in the rectifier: they rectify like ordinary ones and clamp the spike during a load dump (as described in SAE paper 872002, 1987). A multimeter only tests a Zener as a diode; its clamping voltage is measured on the bench — feed it through a resistor and measure the voltage across it.

The transistor as a switch
A bipolar transistor (NPN or PNP): a small base current controls a large collector current. Switched on, it loses tenths of a volt between collector and emitter.

A MOSFET is controlled by gate voltage, with almost no current. Its on-resistance is milliohms, so a switched-on MOSFET drops hundredths of a volt. It has a built-in body diode between drain and source.
Low-side switch: the load gets positive through a relay or fuse, and the module switches its negative. That’s how injectors, valves and relays are driven (lesson “Actuators and PWM”).
High-side switch: the module feeds positive to the load. Body modules often drive lamps and motors this way; such switches often have protection and open-load detection.
An ignition transistor (IGBT) is a special switch for coils: it withstands spikes of hundreds of volts.

Reading a measurement at a module output
Low-side switch off: the module pin shows supply voltage that came through the load. That’s normal, not “positive from the module”.
Switch on: the pin is near 0 V. More than a few tenths of a volt — the switch isn’t fully on or the module ground is poor (lesson “Fuel injection, ECU power and grounds”).
The command is there, per the scan tool or scope, yet the pin still shows supply — the switch won’t turn on: it failed open or isn’t being driven.
The load runs without a command and won’t switch off — the switch has shorted or the wire from the load to the module is shorted to ground.
Switch off and 0 V at the pin — the load has no supply or the load itself is open.
Inductive spike and the suppression diode

While current flows through a relay or valve coil, energy is stored in it. When the switch turns off, the current is cut abruptly and the coil throws a spike: the drain voltage jumps to tens or hundreds of volts. A diode across the coil, cathode to positive, lets the current circulate back through the coil itself, so the drain sits at supply plus about 0.7 V. In an ECU this protection is built into the driver; in a home-made switch it’s added separately. A diode suits a relay; where the current must collapse quickly, as with injectors, use a Zener or TVS (details in the course “ECU repair”).

The diode loops the coil current back through the coil: no spike, the relay just drops out a little later.
Without a diode the coil spikes at turn-off; with one, the drain stays at about supply plus 0.7 V.

Never short a module output to positive or feed 12 V to a module pin “to test it”: short-circuit current will flow through the switched-on transistor and it will burn out faster than any fuse. Check ECU outputs with an LED test light or a scope, not a high-power bulb. Probes are never connected to direct-injection injector outputs, piezo injectors or the ignition secondary.
Check the fuses first. Before blaming a transistor in the module, I check the load’s fuse and supply: with no positive at the load the switch “doesn’t work”, even when it’s fine.

A coil spikes at turn-off; a suppression diode keeps the drain at supply plus 0.7 V.

That’s exactly how a good silicon diode behaves: about 0.5–0.7 V forward and OL in reverse.
An ECU drives a relay with a low-side switch. No command. What does a voltmeter read at the module pin if all is well?
An off switch doesn’t connect the pin to ground, so supply appears on it through the coil. With the command on it drops almost to 0 V.

Why is a diode fitted across a relay coil?
At turn-off the coil throws a spike of tens or hundreds of volts. The diode loops the current through the coil, so the switch sees only supply plus about 0.7 V.
So the relay pulls in faster
To absorb the inductive spike at turn-off
To protect the battery from reverse polarity
How does a MOSFET differ from a bipolar transistor?
A MOSFET turns on with gate voltage, needs almost no drive current and its on-resistance is milliohms. That’s why MOSFETs are the main switches in modern modules.
It’s controlled by base current
It isn’t used in vehicle modules
It’s always on the positive side

Here it is on real cars. All the cases come from Oleg’s blog at avtoelektrik-pro.kz: the car, the complaint, the codes and the findings are given exactly as in the article, with links at the end of the lesson. If an article skips a step, we don’t make it up, and general rules are marked “Takeaway.”

Case 1. Lexus GS300: the starter cranks, but the dash stays dark
Complaint: with the ignition on, the dash doesn’t light up; the starter cranks, but the engine won’t start.

Checks: already over the phone the owner was advised to look at the fuses — they were fine. On site they were checked again, then whether the alarm was blocking the start, and the ignition switch contact group.
Cause: a faulty ignition switch contact group. Power wasn’t reaching some of the electronic systems, while the starter control circuit still worked — that’s why the starter cranked.
Repair and check: the contact group was replaced on site, no tow truck needed. The dash came on and the engine started.
Takeaway: “cranks but won’t start” isn’t always fuel or the starter. A dark dash while the starter cranks points you to the power feed after the ignition switch.
More in the blog: “Lexus GS300 — the starter cranks the engine, but it won’t start”.
Cases 2 and 3. Won’t start: the fuel pump isn’t running

Toyota Hiace 2018. Complaint: it stopped starting. Over the phone the owner warned that the diesel had earlier been swapped for a 3.0 L gasoline engine, and the van had run fine for a long time after that.

Checks: the scan tool showed P1200 — per the scan tool’s description, the fuel pump control circuit or its relay. The code was recorded and cleared — it didn’t come back, but the engine still wouldn’t start. Lightly tapping the bottom of the tank didn’t help. Power was checked through the service hatch: voltage reaches the pump.
Cause: after a light knock on the fuel module cover, the pump started running and the engine started. Most likely the pump itself is worn or a contact inside the module is unreliable.

Recommendation: replace the pump, check the module’s connectors and contacts, and after the repair check fuel pressure and that it starts every time. Choose the pump to suit the fuel system actually installed — the engine was swapped, after all.

Takeaway: a cleared code that doesn’t return is not yet a repair. A similar case is the Kia Soul 2009: after clearing, six codes didn’t return, yet the engine wouldn’t start; the pump was getting power but didn’t run. The pump and fuel filter were replaced, and the car started.
More in the blog: “Toyota Hiace 2018 won’t start — code P1200, fuel pump diagnosis” and “Kia Soul 2009 won’t start — codes P0343, P0336 and a fuel pump replacement”.

When a fuel pump is silent, the first thing I ask is to tap the bottom of the tank — not hard, but firmly. If the pump starts, it’s worn and needs replacing soon, even if the car drives off. On the Hiace, tapping the bottom of the tank didn’t help, but the pump came back after a light knock on the module cover under the hatch — same conclusion: the pump must be replaced and the module contacts checked.
Nissan Patrol 2015. Complaint: won’t start, and the fuel pump can’t be heard running.
Checks: the FUEL PUMP fuse, the pump relay and a possible alarm lockout of the pump were all fine. The rear seat was removed to reach the fuel pump module: voltage gets that far.
Cause: the positive contact inside the module had burned and the mating connector on the wiring was scorched — the pump wasn’t getting power.

Repair: the module was removed, a new power wire was run around the burned connection and its exit point was sealed. The article stresses that inside a fuel pump module you use only wires and connections rated for contact with fuel, and then check for leaks.

Check: the pump got its power back and the engine started — all done on site. Takeaway: work along the circuit from the fuse to the load; “voltage reaches the plug” doesn’t yet mean it reaches the pump.
More in the blog: “Nissan Patrol 2015 won’t start — a burned contact”.

Remove a fuel pump module only with the car cooled down, the battery negative disconnected, no flames or sparks, and good ventilation; wipe up any spilled fuel right away. After working inside the tank, check for leaks: there must be no fuel smell in the cabin.
Case 4. Volkswagen Polo 2021: the cooling fan runs nonstop
Complaint: the cooling fan runs all the time. Mileage: 273,075 km.

Checks: the engine module had P0116 (coolant temperature sensor signal implausible, active) and P3052 (terminal 50 feedback circuit, intermittent); other modules held more than a dozen codes, but none were tied to the complaint. The codes were recorded and cleared — the fan immediately went back to normal, and the sensor’s live data was fine. Instead of replacing the sensor, they inspected its connector.
Cause: corroded contacts in the temperature sensor connector. The contact kept dropping out, P0116 set, and the module ran the fan in protective mode.
Repair and check: the contacts were cleaned, the connector treated and the fan checked — it works normally. The sensor didn’t need replacing.
Takeaway: from a long list of codes, pick the one that explains the complaint and write the rest down for a separate check. Before replacing a sensor, look at its connector.
More in the blog: “Volkswagen Polo 2021 — code P0116, the cooling fan runs nonstop”.
Case 5. Cadillac CTS Coupe 2011: cranks but won’t start, code U0100
Complaint: the starter cranks, but the 3.6 V6 won’t start.

Checks: memory held U0100, lost communication with the engine control module. They checked ECU power, the fuses, the system relay and the ECU power relay, did continuity tests on the circuits and inspected the wiring and connectors.
Cause: corrosion in the wiring was disrupting the ECU’s power and data exchange.

Repair and check: the damaged section was restored, the contacts cleaned and the circuits checked. The engine started, communication with the module came back, U0100 didn’t return, and a repeat scan showed no codes.

Takeaway: “no communication with the ECU” is not a death sentence for the module. Check fuses, relays, power, grounds and wiring first — more on this in the “ECU repair” course, lesson “A module that won’t communicate.”
More in the blog: “Cadillac CTS Coupe 2011 won’t start”.
Case 6. Nissan X-Trail 2021: no crank when cold
Complaint: on cold mornings the starter won’t crank; after about 30 minutes of attempts the car starts, and then everything is fine all day.
Checks, in order: fuses, connectors, grounds, and the starting and starter control circuits.
Cause: the starter relay. It sits in an awkward spot — under the left headlight, near the bumper.
Repair and check: the relay was replaced; the car was kept in use and watched — the fault never came back, including after cold nights.

Takeaway: you confirm an intermittent fault by watching the car after the repair. A similar case in reverse is an Iveco motorhome: with a hot engine the starter wouldn’t crank until it cooled down. The battery, ignition switch and starter were fine, but the starter relay stopped working once it got hot — it was replaced.
More in the blog: “Nissan X-Trail 2021 won’t crank when cold” and “Iveco motorhome won’t start when hot”.
A case goes in five steps: complaint, checks, cause, repair, final check — and the customer report follows the same order.
A code points to a direction, not a part to replace: behind U0100 was wiring, behind P0116 a corroded connector.
A cleared code that doesn’t return is not yet a repair: check that the part actually works.
Work along the circuit from the fuse to the load and remember the conditions of the failure: cold, heat, vibration.

Six typical complaints and where to look on the board. The highlight steps through the rows.
No communication, engine won’t start

Car first: fuses, power, grounds and the bus at the module connector — the order is in the lesson “A module that won’t communicate.” From the blog: on a Cadillac CTS Coupe 2011 with U0100 the culprit was corroded power wiring, and on a Kia Cerato 2016 the modules communicated on the bench — a CAN bus wire was duplicated.

Power on the board: the input protection diode, the power supply chip, the 5 V regulator. Check the bench current with a current limit and 5 V at the regulator output. Automotive regulators often have a reset output for the processor: until 5 V is in range it holds the processor in reset and won’t let it start — that’s how the Texas Instruments TLE4275-Q1 is described, for example.

The CAN transceiver is an eight-pin chip near the connector. Per NXP’s data sheet for the common TJA1050: pin 3 is the 5 V supply, 2 is ground, 7 and 6 are CAN-H and CAN-L, 1 and 4 are transmit and receive to the processor. Check 5 V at the supply pin and the line-to-ground resistance with the module unpowered, as in the lesson “A module that won’t communicate.”

Soldering under a BGA processor: the pins are balls under the package, so a crack can’t be seen. From the blog: a DAF 106 2018 wouldn’t communicate or start — the solder joints under the processor had lost contact, and reballing fixed it. The whole repair is in the lesson “One repair start to finish: a module from intake to handover.”
Water: on a Nissan Juke after an engine wash, corrosion damaged traces and vias — they were restored and the module was sealed.
Misfire, no spark, coils burning out

The section: the ignition driver, the transistor that switches the coil. Check it with a scope on the output and a load simulator, as in the lesson “Output stages.” A driver that has failed shorted keeps the coil energized all the time: the output sits near 0 V and the coil overheats and burns out.

From the blog: a Hyundai Accent misfired and kept burning out coils — the coil control transistor in the ECU had failed. The module was repaired, its housing re-glued and sealed, and the misfire was gone.

From the blog: a Honda CR-V 1998 had no spark because of the ignition module. The owner replaced it himself but mounted it on the distributor incorrectly — and the control signal from the ECU disappeared: the output transistor was damaged. The ECU was restored and the module properly mounted, and the spark came back.

The cause is often outside. The article on Kia and Hyundai modules lists cheap non-original coils, worn spark plugs and wiring shorts among the causes: until they’re fixed, a new driver will burn out the same way.

A healthy driver produces pulses; a shorted one keeps the coil energized all the time, so it overheats and burns out.

I advise Kia and Hyundai owners to fit good-quality or original coils and change spark plugs on time: a worn plug and a poor coil overload the ignition circuit, and down the chain it’s the control module itself that suffers.
Cuts out over bumps, failed after a wash

The section: solder joints on heavy parts, the connector and the BGA, plus traces near the connector. Check with light tapping and gentle heating on the bench and inspection under magnification, as in the lessons “Moisture, corrosion and vibration” and “Testing after repair and handing over to the customer.”

From the blog on the DAF 105 and 106: the module sits on rubber damping rings; when they dry out, vibration goes straight into the board — microcracks appear, parts come unsoldered and contact with the sensors is lost. The blog notes the same rings on diesel Hyundai, Kia and Mercedes CDI.

Water: an engine wash, heavy rain, deep puddles, a leaky housing. From the blog: after an engine wash a Hyundai wouldn’t start — water had got into the ECU connector, the contacts corroded and some traces rotted away; once the board was restored, the car started.
After welding, a jump start or an alarm install

The section: the power input (protection diode, power supply chip, regulator) and the power drivers. Check the bench current: if it hits the limit right away, there’s a short on the supply; then the protection diode in diode test mode and the voltage at the regulator output.

From the blog: after the sills were welded with the battery still connected and the welding ground clamped far from the work, the car stopped starting and wouldn’t communicate — the power components in the module had burned out. On another car, a cheap alarm install burned out a power circuit in the ECU.

For the DAF 105 and 106 the blog singles out jump starting: wrongly connected clamps, voltage spikes and powerful booster packs burn through traces and power components. Sometimes the protection trips before the module does: on a Lexus LX 470 2005, after a jump start, probably with reversed polarity, three fuses blew — once they were replaced the car started, and no other faults were found.

Before welding on the body or frame, disconnect the battery terminals, unplug the ECU if possible and clamp the welder’s ground as close to the weld as you can — that’s Oleg’s advice in his blog. Jump-start only with the correct polarity; the 24 V rules are in the lesson “Truck and heavy equipment modules.”

Not every fault can be fixed with a soldering iron. From the blog: when the ECU of a Toyota Corolla 2012 was opened, the power section was fine but the fault was in the processor section. The module was replaced with an equivalent one with matching factory numbers and paired with the factory immobilizer using dedicated equipment — the procedure took about 35 minutes, and the car started. What has to match, and why pairing is done only with the vehicle’s documents, is in the lesson “Replacing a module with another one.”
Go from complaint to section: no communication — power, 5 V, crystal, transceiver, BGA solder; coils burning out — the ignition driver; vibration — cracked solder; water — connector and traces.
Car first: the module may be fine — on the Cadillac CTS the wiring was to blame, on the Kia Cerato a CAN bus wire.
A burned-out driver is a consequence: check the coils, plugs and wiring before repairing the module, or it will burn out again.
Take component pin functions from open data sheets, and vehicle pinouts only from trusted sources.

Case facts and general practice, stage by stage. The bench stage isn’t in the article, so there is only general practice.
In this case: a 2018 DAF 106; the engine control module wouldn’t communicate with the scan tool and the engine wouldn’t start.

Usual practice: record the complaint in the customer’s words, the VIN, the module and software numbers and what has already been done to the vehicle; photograph the housing, connector and mounting before removal. Give the time and price after diagnosis. What to record for yourself is in the lesson “Testing after repair and handing over to the customer.”
Vehicle first, then the module

In this case: the article states it plainly — no communication with a module doesn’t always mean a faulty processor: power, ground and wiring problems look the same, and the cause has to be found by testing.

Usual practice: the module’s fuses and relays, the battery isolator switch, +30, +15 and grounds at the connector under load, the CAN bus, a look at the connector — the order is in the lesson “A module that won’t communicate,” and the 24 V specifics in “Truck and heavy equipment modules.” The module comes off only once the vehicle checks out.
In this case: the article doesn’t describe any bench measurements — it only says the module was taken apart.

Usual practice: connect the module to a current-limited power supply using a verified diagram — 24 V for the DAF — and check the current, 5 V, the crystal and the transceiver, as in the lessons “Connecting a module on the bench” and “A module that won’t communicate.”
Usual practice: before heating the processor, save a full memory backup if it can be read — see the lesson “Module memory and backups.”
The board and the repair

In this case: the fault was lost contact in the solder joints under the processor. The processor is in a BGA package: its pins connect to the board through solder balls. When those joints are damaged the module can stop working and communicating, and the processor itself doesn’t have to shift — cracks and lost contact in the solder are enough. The module sits on anti-vibration mounts, which lose their elasticity over time and damp vibration less well. Another blog article, on the DAF 105 and 106, names vibration and worn mounts as one of the most common reasons these modules fail.
Why communication was lost and what reballing restored
BGA processor
Hardened mounts: vibration hits the board
Cracked solder balls: no contact
Before: the module won’t communicate
After reballing: new solder balls
Contact restored
The processor itself may not move — cracks in the solder are enough
Hardened mounts damp vibration poorly, and vibration can damage the ball joints under the BGA; reballing restores the contact.

In this case: the module was taken apart, the processor removed from the board and reballed — its ball contacts restored — then put back and soldered; the module was reassembled and fitted to the truck.

Usual practice: BGA work needs proper equipment and experience, as the lesson “Soldering and replacing components” says: bottom preheating of the board, a stencil and balls of the right size, flux, then cleaning and inspection under magnification; neighboring parts are shielded from heat.

Never leave a BGA station or hot-air tool unattended, and work under fume extraction: flux fumes are harmful. Don’t heat the processor until you’ve saved a memory backup, if it can be read, and don’t overheat the board — the settings are chosen for the specific board.

When I repair a module that has suffered from vibration, I look not only at the board but at the mounting too. If the anti-vibration mounts have hardened or are damaged, they damp vibration poorly, and the repaired module will take the same punishment. So I always take the mounts into account.
Testing and handover
In this case: the ECU communicated with the scan tool again, the engine started, and the module was saved without a full replacement.
Usual practice on the bench: current, communication and part numbers, memory compared with the backup, an extended run, light tapping and gentle heating — a must after any solder repair.
Usual practice in the vehicle: codes in all modules before and after a drive, starting, live data, a drive in the conditions where the fault appeared; hardened mounting bushings are replaced.

Usual practice: a report for the customer — the complaint, what was found (lost contact in the solder under the processor), what was done (reballing), the outside cause (vibration, the state of the mounts), photos of the board, the warranty and its terms. More in the lesson “Testing after repair and handing over to the customer.”

The engine module isn’t the only “computer” in a car. The ABS module, the body control module (BCM), the automatic transmission module and the instrument cluster are built the same way: power supply and regulator, processor, inputs, output stages, bus transceivers — as in the lesson “What’s inside an ECU”. But each has its own operating conditions, its own typical failures and its own limits: what can be repaired on the board and what can’t.

First make sure the module really is at fault. The blog has a write-up on a 2019 Volkswagen Polo: the ABS light was on, the turn signals, hazard lights and brake lights didn’t work, and the ABS module wouldn’t communicate — code U012100 was stored in several modules at once. The fuses were checked with a test light, then the power at the ABS module: one of the two power feeds had no voltage. When power was applied to that circuit as a diagnostic check, the module came online. So there’s no need to remove the module — the next step is checking the wiring against the diagram.
Check the fuses first. A fuse that looks intact proves nothing yet, so I check it with a test light: that shows whether the circuit has voltage under a small load.

Each module has its own operating conditions and its own typical hardware failures.

An ABS unit usually has two parts: a hydraulic unit with valves and a pump, and an electronic module. The valve coils sit in the module and slide over the valve stems, and the pump motor is connected to the module by power terminals.

Typical hardware failures: cracked solder joints and corrosion on the coil and pump motor terminals, an open coil winding, a burnt valve or pump motor driver, and the power feed and connector — water and road salt get there.

Signs: codes for the valves, the pump, supply voltage or an internal module fault. Wheel speed sensor codes mean the sensor, connector and wiring first, as in the lesson “Other systems and scan tool service functions”.

An example from the blog: on a Toyota Prado 150, after suspension repairs, the ABS light came on now and then with code C1414 — the front left wheel speed sensor circuit. The sensor and connector were checked, the sensor was removed and cleaned of dirt, and the owner was advised to come back for diagnostics if the code returned. The ABS module itself wasn’t touched.

On many units the electronic module comes off the hydraulic unit without opening the brake system. If the brake system was opened, bleed it following the manufacturer’s procedure, often with a scan tool.

The valve coils are in the electronic module; the weak spots are the solder joints on their pins and on the pump motor pins.

ABS and ESP are safety systems. On the board, restore only the factory circuit: the same part or a direct equivalent per the datasheet. A homemade transistor replacement for a channel, as in the lesson “A burnt-out driver: building a replacement from transistors”, is not done here. After the repair: codes in all modules, wheel speeds in live data, bleeding if the brakes were opened, and a braking check at low speed in a safe area. The car goes back with a firm pedal and no ABS codes.
The body control module switches the lights, turn signals, brake lights, locks, wipers and heaters — through relays on the board and power transistors. It’s often combined with the fuse box.

Water is the main enemy: through a leaking glass seal, a clogged drain, the sunroof or the A/C. That brings corrosion, eaten-away traces and shorts, as in the lesson “Moisture, corrosion and vibration”. Until the leak is found, the board repair isn’t finished.

Relays on the board: burnt or welded contacts. Power transistors: they burn out after a short in the turn signal, brake light or parking light wiring. A new transistor goes in only after the short is found, otherwise it will burn out the same way, as in the lesson “Output stages: why they burn out and how to test them”.

The body control module often stores immobilizer and key data and the equipment coding. Before the repair, make a memory backup, as in the lesson “Module memory and backups”. We don’t touch immobilizer and key data: if pairing is needed after the repair, it’s done at a dealer or by the manufacturer’s procedure, and only with the vehicle documents.
Automatic transmission module
A transmission module can be separate — in the cabin or under the hood — or built into the gearbox together with the valve body. A built-in one takes the heat of the oil and the vibration.

Hardware failures: cracked solder joints, the power supply and regulator, solenoid outputs, the connector and ribbon cables, water in a separate module. Clutch packs, the valve body and the mechanicals are for a transmission specialist.

Before opening it up: codes, live data and a check of what the transmission receives — the brake signal, selector position, power. The blog has a Range Rover Evoque whose rotary gear selector didn’t work: the cause turned out to be the transport mode lock, and no module repair was needed.
After repairing or replacing the module: reset the adaptations and run the transmission relearn by the manufacturer’s procedure, as in the lesson “Adaptations and resets”.
The needles are driven by stepper motors. A needle that sticks, jumps or doesn’t return to zero means a worn stepper motor or a cracked solder joint on its pins.
Part of the dial is dark — a backlight LED, its resistor or its transistor. The cluster goes dark over bumps — cracked solder at the connector pins or a power problem.
As with other modules, the fuse, connectors, ground and power come first, then the board — the blog article “Instrument cluster not working” covers this.

Our cluster repair is hardware only: motors, backlight, soldering, power, display. We don’t read, write or transfer the memory that holds the mileage. The odometer is photographed at intake and at handover — the readings must match.

The line is simple: we take hardware repairs and restore the factory circuit. We don’t take airbag (SRS) modules after a crash: after deployment the module stores crash data, and it’s replaced together with the deployed parts by the manufacturer’s procedure, as in the lesson “Other systems and scan tool service functions”. We also don’t take work on the mileage memory, immobilizer and key data, or modified software — as in the lesson “Module memory and backups”.

A stepper motor is a hardware repair, so we take it. We don’t touch the mileage memory: changing the mileage deceives the next buyer.

Sometimes a fault is fixed not with a soldering iron or a new part but with a new version of the module software. The manufacturer finds a bug in the software — say, harsh transmission shifts or a false code — and releases an update along with a service bulletin. What each type of equipment can do was covered in the lesson “Scan tools and adapters: what to choose and how to connect”. Here: how to write an update officially without damaging the module.
When an update is a repair
There’s a manufacturer service bulletin or recall that matches the customer’s complaint and applies to this VIN. The software number in the module is older than the one in the bulletin.
The module was replaced with a new one: it often arrives with no software or a base version, and the software is written by the manufacturer’s procedure.
Don’t update “just in case”. New software with no complaint and no bulletin fixes nothing, and afterward adaptations may be needed.
Software won’t fix a broken wire, a poor ground or a faulty sensor. Normal diagnostics come first: codes, live data, measurements, as in the lesson “The scan tool diagnostic procedure”.
The official route: J2534 and the manufacturer’s portal

J2534 is an SAE recommended practice for a “pass-through” adapter, PassThru. It only connects the computer to the car; the software, files and access rights come from the manufacturer — through its service portal on a subscription (for a day, several days or a year) or through dealer equipment. The manufacturer’s software also checks the right to program: in a 2020 Toyota bulletin, the module requires a digital signature during the update, which the software gets from the manufacturer’s portal. In Kazakhstan, portal access depends on the make — check with the official distributor. Gray-market imports may have no manufacturer support: the blog has an article on this using the Zeekr 001 as an example.
Manufacturer’s portal
software, files, signature
Manufacturer’s software
The manufacturer supplies the software and files, the J2534 adapter just passes them to the module, and the power supply holds the voltage.
Power and communication while programming

Connect a power supply that holds a steady voltage under load — not an ordinary battery charger and not a jump from another car. The voltage follows the manufacturer’s requirements: in the same Toyota bulletin, 13.5 V from the power supply and no lower than 11.8 V during programming; other makes have their own figures.
Switch off everything you don’t need: headlights, climate control, heaters, the radio. Doors, hood and key position as the procedure requires.
Laptop on its charger, sleep mode and automatic updates off, a stable internet connection. The adapter cable isn’t pulled tight and can’t get underfoot.

While programming, don’t switch off the ignition, unplug the adapter or start other programs. Lights on the dash may flash: other modules briefly lose contact with the one being programmed — that’s no reason to stop.

A voltage drop or a dropout mid-write can leave the module without working software, and it will stop communicating. The blog article “Why Kia and Hyundai ECUs fail” lists attempts to “flash it on the spot” and cheap equipment among the causes.

With a power supply: a steady 13.5 V
Battery only: the voltage sags

Without a power supply the voltage sags under load and programming can abort; with a power supply it stays steady.

Don’t unplug anything in a hurry: check the power, the adapter connection and the internet.
Repeat the programming with the same manufacturer software, following its prompts: many programs can retry the write or recover the module.
If that doesn’t work, contact the manufacturer’s support or a dealer.
Don’t write some “random” file from the internet: it may be for a different module version and carry another car’s data, as in the lesson “Module memory and backups” in the ECU Repair course.
Secure gateway

Many newer cars have a secure gateway, SGW, between the diagnostic connector and the modules — the same gateway as in the lesson “No communication: the scan tool can’t see the modules”, only protected. Without authorization a scan tool reads codes and live data, while clearing codes, active tests and, depending on the make, coding and programming are locked. On some Jeep, Chrysler, Dodge and Fiat vehicles from about the 2017–2018 model years, access is opened by registering the shop and the scan tool with AutoAuth. On Volkswagen and Audi the similar protection is called SFD: it’s unlocked through a manufacturer account or purchased access. Some Nissan and Mercedes-Benz models also require authorization.

Without authorization the gateway lets only reading through; after official registration the service functions open up.

What we don’t do: modified software — chip tuning and “emissions-off” software that disables EGR, the DPF, AdBlue/SCR or the catalytic converter; mileage changes; disabling the immobilizer, including “via a flash”; bypassing a secure gateway and working through someone else’s account. We write only the manufacturer’s official software for this VIN, or our own verified file for the same module from a backup. Such changes break the law, and whoever made them is responsible — as in the lesson “Adaptations and resets”.
It’s better to get a Launch scan tool — it’s proven equipment. Cheap ELM327 adapters sometimes “knock out” the car, and in the middle of programming such a dropout can cost you the module.

ADAS means driver assistance systems: automatic emergency braking, adaptive cruise control, lane keeping, blind-spot monitoring, surround-view cameras. They’ve long been more than a luxury-car feature: Jetour, Chery, Haval, Changan and Geely were all in the top ten for new-car sales in Kazakhstan in January–October 2025, and these systems now come on mass-market models too. An auto electrician’s job is to recognize when calibration is needed, check what’s within reach — power, connectors, communication — and send the car for calibration by the manufacturer’s procedure, not set sensors “by eye”.
Where the sensors are
The front camera is on the windshield behind the mirror: lane markings, signs, vehicles and pedestrians.
The front radar is behind the badge, the grille or in the bumper: the distance and speed of the car ahead for cruise control and braking.
Corner radars are in the rear and sometimes the front bumper: blind spots and backing out.
Surround-view cameras are in the mirrors, grille and liftgate; ultrasonic parking sensors are in the bumpers.
The systems also need data from other modules: wheel speeds from ABS, steering angle, turn signal status. So an ADAS code can be the result of a fault in a completely different system.

The camera looks through the windshield and the radars through the bumper and badge: any repair near them can knock their angle out.
What the scan tool shows
Calibration codes: “camera not calibrated”, “radar not aligned”, “alignment out of range”. On some cars, live data shows the calibration status and the sensor’s mounting angles.
Temporary blocking: “radar blocked”, “camera view restricted”. Causes: snow, ice, dirt, a sticker, a fogged windshield, bright sun. Clean the sensor and check on a drive: no calibration needed here.

Power and communication: lost communication with the camera or radar, low voltage. This is ordinary electrics — power, ground, connector, bus, as in the lesson “No communication: the scan tool can’t see the modules”.

Secondary codes. The blog has a 2023 Haval after an off-road trip: codes in almost every module, including ESP, automatic braking and the front camera. After clearing and rechecking, only codes for lost communication with the AWD coupling remained, and the cause was a broken latch on its connector. Once the connector was repaired, the codes were gone.

Another example from the blog is a 2025 Subaru Outback: driver-assist warnings and many stored codes, including EyeSight. After clearing, one code stayed active — B2D04, front camera circuit or harness. The cause was a broken latch on the camera connector; the connector was repaired and the system started working.

Check the fuses first. And when codes light up for AWD, ESP, cameras and driver assists all at once after off-roading, I don’t rush to replace modules: I check the connectors, wiring, signs of moisture and physical damage first.
When calibration is needed

Replacing or removing the windshield on a car with a front camera, replacing the camera or its bracket. GM has required camera calibration after windshield replacement on all models since 2017; so does Honda, and the windshield must be genuine.

Removing, repairing or replacing the bumper, grille or badge near the radar, or a bent radar bracket after a minor impact. Honda, for example, requires radar aiming after a bumper cover repair within 300 mm of the radar.

Wheel alignment, suspension and steering repairs. Here the makes differ: the 2016 Subaru Legacy requires EyeSight camera calibration after an alignment and suspension work, while Honda doesn’t need it after an alignment unless the service information says so. The steering angle sensor is calibrated as in the lesson “Other systems and scan tool service functions”.
After a collision, an airbag deployment or replacement of the sensor itself. The exact list is in the manufacturer’s service information for that car: it outranks any general rules.

Why not “by eye”: in IIHS tests published in 2018, a Honda Civic camera that was 0.6° off misjudged the distance to the lane line by up to 69 cm (27 in). In an automatic braking test from about 40 km/h (25 mph), the car with that camera started braking later and hit the target at about 32 km/h (20 mph). A level and a tape measure can’t reach that precision — it takes the equipment and the manufacturer’s procedure.
Static and dynamic calibration

Static, in the bay: targets are set at the distance and height given in the procedure, square to the car’s centerline. You need a level floor, glare-free lighting, tire pressures per the placard, fuel and load as required, an empty cabin and trunk, and sound suspension.

Dynamic, on the road: the scan tool puts the system into calibration mode, and the car is driven at a set speed on a road with clear markings and moderate traffic. In snow, rain or on worn markings it may not complete.
Some makes require both in turn — static first, then dynamic; others let you choose one.

You need a scan tool or software that supports this make and its calibration function, plus a battery maintainer during the procedure, as in the lesson “Scan tools and adapters: what to choose and how to connect”.

Don’t clear calibration codes to turn off a warning light, and don’t set sensors “by eye”. An uncalibrated system may brake for no reason, fail to brake for an obstacle or steer the car out of its lane. If you don’t have the equipment, tell the customer honestly, send them to a dealer or a specialist calibration shop, and note in the report which system needs calibration and why.

Emission system codes are the P04xx group, as in the lesson “Trouble codes: statuses, freeze frame and root cause”: catalytic converter, evaporative emissions (EVAP), exhaust gas recirculation (EGR), secondary air. With these codes the car usually still drives, and the customer asks you to “just clear it” or “delete” it. But behind every code there is a cause you can find with a scan tool and a meter: misfires, mixture, a leak, carbon, a weak pump. Readiness monitors are covered in the lesson “The scan tool diagnostic procedure”, oxygen sensors and trims in “Fuel trims and oxygen sensors”, and valve control in “Actuator tests”. Here — how to take an emissions code all the way to a repair.
Mode 06: how far from a code

Readiness monitors only say “tested” or “not yet”. The results of the tests themselves are stored in Mode 06, found in the scan tool’s generic OBD-II section. For each test it shows a value, a minimum and maximum limit, and a “passed” or “failed” mark.
A code sets when the value goes past the limit. Mode 06 shows how much margin is left: the test passed, but the value is right at the edge — a reason to warn the customer before the light comes on.

Compare the value with its own limits, not with another car: units and scaling differ between makes. On CAN vehicles the tests are labeled to a standard — catalyst, EGR, EVAP, secondary air, O2 sensors, misfires by cylinder; on older cars the test names come from the manufacturer’s data. Not every car supports Mode 06.
The module keeps the result of the latest test even after the ignition is switched off, but clearing the codes erases the Mode 06 results too. So look at them before you clear anything.
After the repair, let the car complete a drive cycle and compare again: the value should move away from the limit. That way the repair is proven with a number, not just a light that went out.

Catalytic converter: P0420 is a consequence, not a diagnosis

The module judges the converter by the downstream O2 sensor: a healthy converter stores oxygen and the downstream sensor stays steady, while a worn one lets the upstream sensor’s swings through — see the lesson “Fuel trims and oxygen sensors”. Many modules also test actively: they briefly richen and lean the mixture and see how long the downstream sensor takes to respond. P0420 and P0430 mean catalyst efficiency below threshold, bank 1 and bank 2; P0421 and P0431 are the same for the warm-up converter closest to the engine. The catalyst monitor only runs under its own conditions, so “the code didn’t come back after clearing” proves nothing. On a 2007 Mitsubishi Outlander with P0421 and P0431, the codes didn’t return for 20 minutes after clearing; the oxygen sensors weren’t replaced on the strength of these codes, and the owner was sent to have the converters and exhaust checked (details on the blog: “Mitsubishi Outlander 2007 — Check Engine, codes P0421 and P0431”).
Save the codes, freeze frame and Mode 06, and scan all modules.

Fix whatever is killing the converter: misfires, a mixture that’s too rich or too lean, oil or coolant consumption. P0420 next to P0300 or P0171 is a consequence. On a 2005 Toyota RAV4, P0171 was set along with P0420, and the advice was to find the cause of the lean mixture first (details on the blog: “Toyota RAV4 2005 code P0125”).
Check the exhaust upstream of the downstream sensor: a leak through a burnt-out spot or a gasket feeds the sensor extra oxygen and spoils the test.
Check the sensors themselves on a warm engine: a lazy or stuck downstream sensor means repairing the sensor, not the converter.
Compare the banks in Mode 06: the worn converter’s test is closer to the limit.

If everything else is fine, it’s the converter: melted, clogged or “poisoned”. A clogged one also chokes the engine; exhaust back pressure is checked by an exhaust specialist. After the repair — a drive cycle and Mode 06 again.
EVAP: leaks and purge

EVAP keeps gasoline vapor out of the air: it goes from the tank into the canister — a container of charcoal — and while driving the module opens the purge valve so the engine draws the vapor into the intake and burns it. The vent valve connects the canister to the atmosphere; to test for leaks the module closes it and watches the tank pressure.

Codes: P0455 — large leak, P0442 — small, P0456 — very small; P0441 — incorrect purge flow, P0443 — purge valve circuit, P0446 — vent valve performance. US rules require on-board diagnostics to find a leak about 0.5 mm (0.020 inch) across — too small to see by eye.

Start with the simple things: the fuel cap and its seal, the filler neck, the valve connectors and hoses. On a 2022 Hyundai Tucson with a very small leak code, the first recommendation was to replace the fuel cap (details on the blog: “Hyundai Tucson 2022 — code P04567A”).

Then the scan tool: test the purge and vent valves and watch the tank pressure in live data — a single click from the valve isn’t enough. A purge valve stuck open is a vacuum leak into the intake: the idle hunts and the engine is hard to start after refueling.

If the valves and sensors are fine, look for the leak with a smoke machine. A 2025 Toyota Grand Highlander had large-leak codes after a collision, but the pump and valves passed their tests — the owner was advised to have the lines and connections checked for leaks (details on the blog: “Toyota Grand Highlander 2025 — diagnostics”).

Gasoline vapor burns and explodes. Feed smoke into EVAP only with a smoke machine made for this system, at the low pressure its instructions specify; compressed shop air is never fed into the tank. No flames or smoking nearby, a ventilated area, engine off.
EGR and secondary air

EGR returns part of the exhaust to the intake to lower combustion temperature and nitrogen oxide emissions. P0401 — not enough flow: most often carbon in the valve and passages. P0402 — too much flow: the valve doesn’t close, the idle is rough and the engine stalls.

Modules check the flow in different ways: by the jump in intake pressure when they open the valve during engine braking, or with a temperature or differential pressure sensor — it depends on the car. Compare the commanded and actual valve position as in the lesson “Actuator tests”: if the valve moves but there’s a flow code, it’s most likely carbon in the passages.

Secondary air only works after a cold start: a pump blows air into the exhaust to warm up the converter faster. The module checks the system with the upstream O2 sensor — it should read “lean” — or with the system’s pressure sensor. Codes: P0410 — system, P0411 — incorrect flow, P0418 — pump relay circuit.

The pump is switched through its own relay and fuse — check those first. Common failures: the pump seized from moisture, or the valve won’t open. Test it with the scan tool on a cold engine: you hear the pump, and the upstream sensor goes “lean”.
The customer asks to “delete” it

Requests to “cut out the converter”, “block off the EGR” or “disable” a system in software are common. We don’t do this, and we explain to the customer why. A code is a signal about a cause: misfires, mixture, carbon, a leak. “Deleting” the system doesn’t cure the cause, it hides it: the misfires or rich mixture remain and the carbon keeps building up. The car no longer meets its emissions class, emissions go up, and at inspection the exhaust is checked with a gas analyzer — a 2011 Toyota Tundra failed it on CO (details on the blog: “Toyota Tundra 2011 fails inspection on CO”). The law and the technician’s liability are covered in the lesson “Adaptations and resets”. Offer an honest repair: find the cause, clean or replace the valve, fit a suitable new converter and prove the result with the monitors and Mode 06.

With P0420 I don’t replace the converter on the strength of the code alone. First I look at misfires, fuel trims and the exhaust before the downstream sensor: if you don’t remove the cause, a new converter will be ruined the same way.
Mode 06 shows each test’s value and limits: a test on the edge is visible before a code sets. Check it before clearing.

In a Common Rail system the high-pressure pump feeds fuel into a common rail at high pressure, and the ECU opens the injectors with electrical pulses. Many diesels — especially Euro 4 and newer trucks — also have SCR in the exhaust: AdBlue is injected into the exhaust, and the catalyst turns nitrogen oxides into nitrogen and water. Both systems are electronic, and the scan tool sees inside them. J1939 codes are covered in the lesson “Trucks and heavy equipment: a 24 V scan tool”, injector codes and DPF regeneration in “Other systems and scan tool service functions”, and per-cylinder corrections in “Engine tests with a scan tool: compression, balance, misfires, timing”. Here — how to find the cause from live data and where the electrician’s job ends.
Common Rail: what to check in live data

Rail pressure — target and actual. The ECU sets the pressure from rpm and load, the rail sensor reports how much there really is, and the actual should follow the target: in a healthy system the difference is usually up to 30–50 bar. Typical guidelines: at least 200 bar while cranking to start, from 250 bar at warm idle, more than 1,000 bar under load; modern systems go up to 2,700 bar. Guidelines are on the “Sensors” tab, exact figures in the manufacturer’s data. The scan tool may show MPa: 1 MPa = 10 bar.

The metering valve on the high-pressure pump and the pressure regulator on the rail are how the ECU holds pressure; some systems have one of them, others both. The scan tool shows their current or duty cycle. Compare with the manufacturer’s data or a healthy vehicle with the same engine: if the valve is at its limit and the pressure won’t build, the ECU is short of fuel.

The rail pressure sensor is usually a three-wire sensor with a 5 V supply: with no pressure the signal is about 0.5 V, and it rises with pressure. With the engine off and the pressure bled away, the scan tool should read close to zero; hundreds of bar on a stopped engine means the sensor or its circuit.

Injector corrections per cylinder: if one is at its limit, check that injector and the cylinder’s compression. Injector codes are entered with the scan tool after replacement — see the lesson “Other systems and scan tool service functions”.
Boost and airflow: black smoke and loss of power can come from the air side too, not just the fuel.
