What’s withheld from pay and what the IP pays on top

Payroll payments fall into two groups. Some the IP withholds from the gross pay and remits for the employee; others the IP pays out of pocket, on top of the salary. Rates for 2026 per Kaspi Guide and clarifications from the ENPF and GFSS:

Withheld from pay: OPV (mandatory pension contributions), 10% (on up to 50 minimum wages); VOSMS (health insurance contributions), 2% (on up to 20 minimum wages); IPN (individual income tax), 10% after deductions, or 15% on annual income over 8,500 MCI (₸36,762,500).

The IP pays on top: OPVR (employer pension contributions), 3.5% (on 1 to 50 minimum wages); SO (social contributions), 5% of pay minus OPV (base of 1 to 7 minimum wages); OOSMS (employer health insurance contributions), 3% (on up to 40 minimum wages).
No OPVR is paid for employees born before January 1, 1975, pensioners, or people with a permanent group I–II disability (ENPF).
No social tax is paid on the simplified regime (KGD clarification).

Example: a ₸200,000 salary, employee born in 1975 or later. Withheld from the salary: OPV ₸20,000 and VOSMS ₸4,000, plus IPN. On top the IP pays OPVR ₸7,000, SO ₸9,000 ((200,000 − 20,000) × 5%), and OOSMS ₸6,000, for ₸22,000 in all. The employee’s full cost to the IP is ₸222,000 a month. IPN is withheld after deductions: check with the KGD on the 2026 basic deduction amount and the terms of the single payroll payment for small businesses.

Withholdings and payroll payments are remitted every month, by the 25th of the following month (KGD tax calendar for 2026). Once a quarter you file Form 200.00, by the 15th of the second month after the quarter: May 15, 2026, Aug. 15, 2026, Nov. 15, 2026, and Feb. 15, 2027. If a deadline falls on a weekend, check the KGD calendar. The IP’s payments for themselves don’t go on 200.00; they’re on 910.00. If you work with an individual under a civil-law (GPH) contract, you file 200.00 too; check GPH rates for 2026 with the KGD.
Employee calendar: 2026–2027
Every month, payments by the 25th; every quarter, Form 200.00 by the 15th of the second month.
Workplace safety and insurance
The employer’s workplace safety duties are in Article 182 of the Labor Code (check the 2026 version on adilet.zan.kz). The main points for a shop:
Before work starts: a workplace safety briefing and a fire safety briefing (fire safety is in the next lesson).
Workplace safety training and knowledge testing are at the employer’s expense; the manager and responsible staff take it at least once every 3 years.
Work clothes, safety footwear, and personal protective equipment per the norms; medical checkups if the work is hazardous or heavy.
Mandatory insurance of the employee against accidents on the job: a contract with an insurance company.
Workplace accident: report it to the labor inspectorate within a day; a commission is set up within 24 hours, and the investigation takes 10 working days.
Employment contract before work starts, details into ESUTD within 5 working days; working off the books risks fines.
Withheld from pay: OPV 10%, VOSMS 2%, and IPN; on top the IP pays OPVR 3.5%, SO 5%, and OOSMS 3%; there’s no social tax on the simplified regime.
At a ₸200,000 salary the employee costs the IP ₸222,000 a month; payments by the 25th, Form 200.00 once a quarter.
A briefing before work; accident insurance, work clothes, and PPE are the employer’s duties.

You don’t need a separate license for repair, diagnostics, auto electrics, tire service, or car washing: these aren’t on the permits and notifications list (Law No. 202-V, in the version checked), as in the OKED lesson. But the premises themselves have sanitary, fire, and environmental requirements. Here are the main points from the rule texts.
Sanitary rules

Shop requirements are in the sanitary rules “Sanitary and Epidemiological Requirements for Vehicle and Passenger Service Facilities” (Ministry of Health Order No. KR DSM-98 of Sept. 23, 2021). For example, a shop is placed downwind of residential buildings (item 8); industrial and storm runoff is treated, and with no sewer, local treatment facilities are installed (item 78). Check the size of the sanitary buffer zone for your shop with the sanitary and epidemiological authorities before you lease or build.
Fire safety
The key document is the Fire Safety Rules (Ministry of Emergency Situations Order No. 55 of Feb. 21, 2022). For a shop, these points matter most:
Fire safety instructions for the premises (item 5).
The person responsible for firefighting equipment is named by order (item 9).
Staff may work only after fire safety training and a briefing (item 8).
Oily rags go in noncombustible lidded bins and are taken out at the end of the shift (item 29).
Oil-soaked work clothes are kept in metal lockers (item 30).
Flammable and combustible liquids may not be stored in basements or utility rooms (item 24(1)).
Shop bay: fire safety checks
Fire safety instructions for the premises (item 5)
Extinguisher and a person responsible, named by order (item 9)
Oily rags in a noncombustible lidded bin (item 29)
Oily work clothes in a metal locker (item 30)
Flammable liquids: not in a basement or utility room (item 24)
A bay per the Fire Safety Rules: instructions, an extinguisher with a responsible person, rags in a lidded bin, work clothes in a metal locker.
How many extinguishers and what kind is set in Appendix 3 to the Rules; choose by your premises. Whether a shop needs a fire safety audit, check with the emergency services authorities.
Environment: site category

Under the Environmental Code (No. 400-VI of Jan. 2, 2021), sites fall into four categories. Only Category I and II sites need an environmental permit; Category III files an environmental impact declaration with the local executive body; Category IV needs neither. Per a bank’s explanation in public sources (alataucitybank.kz), a shop is usually Category IV but moves to III if it accumulates more than 1,001 kg of oily rags or used tires. Check your shop’s category with the local executive body.

Used oil, old batteries, and oil filters are hazardous waste. Hand them only to organizations allowed to handle such waste (with a license or notification).
Don’t pour oil down the drain or on the ground: under the sanitary rules, shop wastewater is treated.
Don’t stockpile rags or old tires: the site category depends on how much there is, and under the Fire Safety Rules rags go out at the end of each shift.

Tax control starts with your reporting. The KGD checks your returns against other data, and if it finds a discrepancy, it writes to your taxpayer account. Let’s see how this works, what to do with a notice, what happens if a return or tax payment is late, and which fines are worth knowing. Amounts are for 2026 (MCI ₸4,325).
Desk audit (cameral control)

A desk audit is a check without visiting you: the KGD reviews your reporting and compares it with the data it has. If it finds a discrepancy, a notice arrives. According to accounting websites (mybuh.kz, 2026), since 2026 desk audits have been preventive in nature and work together with the tax risk management system (SUNR). Where a repair shop’s discrepancies come from: income from receipts and transfers didn’t match Form 910.00, no ESF was issued to a company (lesson 9), or repair money went to a personal card — since 2026 banks report such transfers to the KGD when certain criteria are met (lesson 7).

Desk audit: the KGD checks your reporting against other data; if there’s a discrepancy, a notice arrives in your account.
A notice arrived: what to do
Open it in your ISNA taxpayer account; you sign in with your EDS (lesson 2).
Read it: which period, what the discrepancy is, and the reply deadline.
Check it against your records: KKM receipts, acts, ESFs, and the IP bank statement.
If the mistake is confirmed, file an amended return for the same period and pay the extra tax with interest.
If there’s no mistake, reply by the notice deadline with an explanation and documents; ask your local tax office how to format the reply.

If Form 910.00 isn’t filed on time, per the KGD the ISNA system files a zero return itself. A zero return with real income is a mistake: after it, the correct figures go on an amended return (per clarifications in public sources, with the actual figures for the same period).
Interest and measures for tax debt

If tax isn’t paid on time, late-payment interest accrues for every day late, from the day after the deadline through the payment day. According to clarifications in public sources (mybuh.kz, 2026), its annual rate is 1.25 times the National Bank base rate, and ISNA accrues it automatically every day. At a 16.25% base rate (as mybuh.kz reported on Oct. 21, 2026), that’s 20.3125% a year. Example: the Form 910.00 tax for the first half of 2026 is ₸270,000, due Aug. 25, 2026, paid Sept. 24, 2026. That’s 30 days late, and the interest is 270,000 × 20.3125% ÷ 365 × 30 ≈ ₸4,508. The base rate changes, so check the current one with the KGD or the National Bank.

Interest accrues every day, and the measures get tougher as the debt grows, per accounting websites.

A debt won’t go away on its own. According to accounting websites (mybuh.kz, March 18, 2026), with a tax debt of up to 20 MCI (₸86,500) you get a notification; from 20 to 45 MCI (up to ₸194,625), a notice, suspension of debit transactions on the account, and a collection order; over 45 MCI, an account freeze and inventory of property. The ₸270,000 tax in the example is over 62 MCI.
How far back an audit can go

Per the text of Art. 65 of the Tax Code (a copy of the code in public sources), the statute of limitations for taxes is 3 years after the end of the tax period, and 5 years for large taxpayers and some others. During all that time the KGD can audit the return and assess additional tax, so keep your documents for those years. If you find an old mistake yourself, fix it with an amended return: the sooner, the less interest.

Your IP information and tax regime aren’t chosen forever. You moved to a different bay, added a type of work, changed your last name, outgrew the simplified regime, or a big customer on OUR cares about your regime: you notify the tax authority of each such change. Let’s go over what to file, where, and by when.
The regime notice: moving to the 2026 code

Anyone who was on the simplified regime, the retail tax, or the fixed deduction in 2025 and wanted to stay on the simplified regime had to file a notice of the applied tax regime between January 1 and March 1, 2026. Per the KGD, those who filed on time use the simplified regime from Jan. 1, 2026, and those who didn’t were moved to OUR retroactively, also from January 1, 2026. Former patent payers who didn’t file the notice were automatically deregistered as IPs on March 1, 2026, effective January 1. Check your regime in the taxpayer account: your returns and deadlines depend on it.

Per finance.kz and the Kaspi Guide (2026), it’s free and due within 10 business days of the change. Moving to OUR by choice

You can move from the simplified regime to OUR voluntarily, for example if fleets on OUR care about deductions (lesson 9) or you want to work with VAT: on the simplified regime you don’t register for VAT (lesson 4). Per clarifications in public sources (mybuh.kz, Apr. 24, 2026), the notice is filed before the 1st of the month you’re switching from. Per the Kaspi Guide, if you change regimes in Kaspi Pay after Mar. 1, 2026, the new regime applies from the 1st of the following month, data in the state database updates within 24 hours, and an IP registered in 2026 can change regimes only after Mar. 1, 2026. Run the numbers first: OUR has different taxes and the Form 220.00 return (lesson 4).
Mandatory switch and VAT

If you exceed the simplified-regime limit of 600,000 MCI a year (₸2,595,000,000 in 2026) or start an activity on the banned list (lesson 3), per clarifications in public sources (mybuh.kz, 2026) you file a notice of moving to OUR within 5 business days. From what date OUR applies when income exceeds the limit hasn’t been officially confirmed, so check with your local tax office. For a banned activity, per accounting websites, OUR applies from the 1st of the month of the violation, and one act under such a code is enough.

On OUR, watch your turnover: past 10,000 MCI a year (₸43,250,000 in 2026), the VAT registration application is due within 5 business days of crossing the threshold (KGD statement). Per mybuh.kz (Nov. 28, 2025), late registration carries a fine of 50 MCI (₸216,250), and turnover during the time you should have been registered but weren’t is charged 15% of that turnover; the KGD has also mentioned the 15%. If you move back from OUR to the simplified regime, that’s grounds to deregister you for VAT: there’s no VAT on the simplified regime (KGD clarification).

A car alarm isn’t one box but a system. The control unit receives signals from the fob, pin switches, sensors and the ignition switch, decides what to do, and controls the siren, turn signals, locks and engine kill. An installer needs to know what each part is for: then they’ll wire it correctly and later find faults fast. How a driver sees the alarm is covered in the drivers’ lesson on car alarms; here we look at it as installers.
The control unit

The control unit is the “brain” of the system. It’s hidden in the cabin, usually behind a panel, and connected to the car by a wiring harness. The unit remembers its mode — disarmed, armed or alarm — and when armed it keeps watching its inputs. If something changes on an input, it triggers the alarm through its outputs. Which harness wire does what and what signal it expects — positive or negative — is in the manual for your system.

The unit “hears” its inputs and controls its outputs; power comes through a separate wire from the battery.
Inputs: what the unit “hears”
Antenna/transceiver — fob commands over the radio: arm, disarm, open the trunk. It’s a separate module on a cable, stuck to the glass.
Pin switches — door, hood and trunk switches: they tell the unit something was opened. On the doors the factory switches are usually used; a separate one is often fitted for the hood.
Shock, tilt and interior motion sensors — the car was hit, jacked up, or someone is inside.
Ignition — a wire that goes positive when the key is turned to ON. It tells the unit the car is being started or driven.
Service button — often called Valet. It’s used for programming, valet (service) mode and emergency disarming with a personal PIN code if the fob is lost or broken.
Outputs: what the unit controls
Siren — a loud sound during an alarm and short chirps when arming and disarming. It goes under the hood, in a protected spot.
Turn signals — flash when arming, disarming and during an alarm: visible from a distance.
Central locking — the unit locks and unlocks the doors on a fob command.
Kill relay — opens a circuit the engine can’t start without, such as the fuel pump or starter circuit. The kill must never activate while driving.
LED in the cabin — shows the mode: it flashes when armed, so from outside you can see the car is protected.
Key fob: one-way and two-way

A one-way fob only sends commands. Whether a command worked, or whether the car is going off, the owner knows only if they can see or hear it. A two-way fob — with feedback — also receives a reply: it shows on its screen, with a sound or vibration, that the command is done, and reports an alarm — what was triggered: a door, the hood, the shock sensor. The range is given in the system manual, but in practice it’s shorter: it’s reduced by the antenna location, interference, weather and a weak fob battery. More in the lesson on the siren, antenna and GSM.
One-way fob
Transmit only: the fob can’t tell if the command arrived
Two-way fob
Reply and alarms
Transmits and receives: the screen shows the command was done
A one-way fob only transmits; a two-way fob also gets a reply from the car.
Shock, tilt and interior motion sensors
The shock sensor reacts to a hit on the body or glass. It usually has two zones: a light hit gives a warning with short siren chirps, a hard hit sets off the alarm.
The tilt sensor notices that the car has been jacked up to take the wheels, or is being lifted onto a tow truck.
The interior motion sensor watches the space inside the cabin and goes off on movement inside — for example, if someone reaches through a broken window for a bag on the seat.
Sensitivity is set during installation: a sensor that’s too sensitive gives false alarms from wind and passing trucks. How to set it is in the lesson on sensors.
The shock sensor
A hit to the body or glass
Light hit — warning,
hard hit — alarm
Tilt sensor
The car is jacked up
or loaded onto a tow truck
Motion sensor
Movement in the cabin
e.g. a hand through the glass
Each sensor catches its own thing: a hit, the car tilting, or movement in the cabin.
GSM and telematics

A GSM module is a SIM card inside the alarm. It reports alarms to the owner’s phone — by call, text or in an app — and from the app the car can be armed or disarmed, the battery voltage and temperature checked, and with GPS its location seen on a map. Distance doesn’t matter as long as the car and the phone have cellular coverage. The SIM card needs credit or a suitable plan with the carrier, and in an underground garage or out of town the signal can drop. And the module draws current all the time: when armed, a system with GSM draws more than one without — the figures are in your system’s manual.
Check the fuses first. If the alarm is dead but the battery is charged, the first thing I look at is the alarm’s own fuse on its power wire.
The control unit listens to its inputs — antenna, pin switches, sensors, ignition — and controls its outputs: siren, turn signals, locks, kill relay, LED.
A one-way fob only sends commands; a two-way fob also shows the car’s reply and alarms.
Shock sensor — a hit to the body; tilt sensor — a jack or tow truck; interior motion sensor — movement in the cabin.
GSM module — alarms and control on your phone while there’s cellular coverage; it needs a SIM card with credit, and the armed current is higher.
Which of these is an input of the control unit, not an output?
Door pin switch
LED in the cabin
The pin switch tells the unit a door was opened — that’s an input. The siren, kill relay and LED are outputs: the unit controls them.
How is a two-way fob different from a one-way fob?
It works without a battery
It reaches any distance
It receives a reply: it shows the command was done and what was triggered in an alarm
A one-way fob only sends commands. A two-way fob also receives a reply from the car — about the completed command and about alarms.
Which sensor will notice that the car has been jacked up to take the wheels?
The hood pin switch
The tilt sensor reacts to a change in the body’s angle — a jack or loading onto a tow truck.
What does a GSM module need to report an alarm to a phone?
A two-way fob near the car
Only an interior motion sensor
A second siren
A SIM card with credit or a plan, and cellular coverage at the car
A GSM module works over the cellular network: with no coverage or no credit, the message won’t go out. The distance to the car doesn’t matter.

An alarm is chosen not by advertising but for the car and the owner’s needs. One customer is fine with a simple system and a fob; another wants phone control, winter warm-up and a CAN connection. The installer’s job is to ask the right questions, check the car against the maker’s list and explain what the customer is paying for. Brands in this lesson are only examples.
Analog hookup

In an analog hookup every signal has its own wire: from the door, hood and trunk pin switches, from the ignition, to the turn signals, to the central locking control. For that, the factory wiring is tapped — every wire you need. This way you can connect almost any car, including old ones with no data bus. The downside is more work and more taps, which means more places where a bad connection can appear over the years.
CAN connection

On modern cars the modules exchange data over the CAN bus, as in the lesson on data buses. The CAN module — built into the alarm or separate — connects to the CAN-H and CAN-L wire pair. It “reads” from the bus what an analog hookup takes through separate wires: doors, hood, trunk, ignition, parking brake, speed. On many models it also sends commands: lock and unlock, flash the turn signals, close the windows. Fewer taps, neater work.
Doors
Tap into a factory wire
CAN module
Power, ground and kill relay — wired
Two taps into the bus instead of many
Analog means a wire for every signal; over CAN the unit takes data from the bus, while power, ground and the kill relay stay wired.

What the CAN module can do on a particular car depends on the make, model, year and even trim. Check this before buying, against the alarm maker’s compatibility list: for StarLine it’s the can.starline.ru service, for Pandora the “Table of commands and statuses” on alarmtrade.ru. The system is set up in the maker’s software, following its manual.
If a function isn’t on the list, it’s wired analog. A common example is the hood: many cars have no factory hood switch, so a separate one is fitted.
Power, ground and usually the kill relay are wired either way.

Before installing, read the codes in all modules with a scan tool and save the report: if codes appear after you connect to the bus, you’ll have something to compare with. How to connect to the bus and check it is in the lesson on the CAN bus during installation.
GSM and remote start

A GSM module is needed if the owner wants to know about an alarm and control the car from a phone at any distance, not just within fob range. It’s handy when the car sleeps in the yard and the apartment windows face the other way, or when it’s in a paid parking lot. The customer pays for it: the system costs more, it needs a SIM card with credit from a cellular carrier, and the armed current is higher.

Remote start fires up the engine on a command from the fob or phone, on a timer or by temperature — in our frosts it’s requested a lot. Many systems, including StarLine and Pandora, can do it over the CAN bus, but only on models the alarm maker supports. So first comes the compatibility list: is the model there, and is remote start supported for it? If so, and the transmission is automatic, remote start is usually enabled through setup per the maker’s manual: the car model and the needed functions are selected in the software or app. The system will start the engine only with the selector in P.

With a manual transmission, besides setup you need “software neutral” — a procedure done when arming, described in the system manual. Without it the system won’t allow remote start: that way the car can’t drive off if it was left in gear. Show the owner this procedure when you hand the car over.

Bypassing the factory immobilizer is not covered in this course. If the model isn’t on the compatibility list or remote start isn’t supported for it, we don’t do remote start: no homemade solutions, no key copies, no disabling the factory security. Tell the customer honestly that this system has no reliable solution for their car; the alarm can be installed without remote start. And warn them: frequent remote starts in winter without driving drain the battery — as in the drivers’ lesson on car alarms.
What to ask the customer
The car: make, model, year, trim, transmission — is it on the compatibility list, and what is supported over CAN.
Where the car sleeps and whether the siren can be heard from there — is a two-way fob or GSM needed.
Is winter warm-up needed — and is remote start supported for this model.
Does the car often sit for a long time without driving — GSM and remote start use up battery charge.
What the budget is — so you offer a system that covers the needs, not the most expensive one.
What the customer gets for the extra cost
Basic system
security, siren, sensor, kill relay
+ two-way fob
reply and alarms on the fob screen
+ CAN module
fewer taps, data from the bus
+ GSM and app
alarms and control from the phone
+ remote start
only if supported for the model
Each price step is a new capability you can explain to the customer.

When explaining the price, talk about needs, not brands: “for this extra you’ll know about an alarm without leaving the apartment,” “with the phone you see the car from anywhere,” “over CAN there are fewer taps into the factory wiring.” A CAN connection can cost more not because of the wires but because it needs a compatible module, a check against the list and careful work on the bus.
Analog — a wire and a tap for every signal, fits any car; CAN — data from the bus and fewer taps, if the model is on the list.
What the system can do over CAN depends on the make, model, year and trim: check the maker’s compatibility list before buying.
Remote start only where the maker supports it for the model: on an automatic — setup per the manual, on a manual — plus software neutral; model not listed — we don’t do it.
Explain the price through the customer’s needs: knowing about an alarm from afar — a two-way fob or GSM; sparing the wiring — CAN.
What does a CAN module connection give compared with an analog hookup?
The alarm works without power
Fewer taps: the unit reads doors, ignition and more from the bus, and on many models also controls the locks
No car ever needs a hood pin switch
There’s no need to check the car against the list
The CAN module takes from the bus what an analog hookup gets through separate wires, and on many models it sends commands itself. But exactly what it can do depends on the model.
Where do you find out what an alarm can do over CAN on a particular car?
By the color of the bus wires
Connect it and see what works
In the alarm maker’s compatibility list — by make, model, year and trim
CAN functions depend on the make, model, year and even trim. Check this before buying — for StarLine on can.starline.ru, for Pandora in the “Table of commands and statuses.”
The model is on the list, remote start is supported for it, and it has a manual transmission. What else is needed?
Software neutral per the system manual — so the car can’t drive off in gear
Nothing, same as an automatic
A second fob
With a manual, the system allows remote start only after software neutral is done when arming — so the car won’t move if it was left in gear.
The customer’s model isn’t on the compatibility list, but they want remote start. What do you do?
Rig up a homemade solution
Install it without checking — it might work
Refuse to install the alarm at all
Don’t do it: look for the model in other makers’ lists, and if there’s no solution, explain honestly to the customer
Remote start is done only with a solution the maker supports for that model. Not on the list — we don’t do it, and the alarm can be installed without remote start.

An alarm goes into someone else’s car, often a new one, and the customer will judge not only how the system works but also the state the interior is returned in. Half of success is preparation: the right tools at hand, the car protected, dangerous circuits left alone. The general auto electrician’s kit is covered in the lesson on the profession; here is what you need specifically for installation.
The installer’s tools
Multimeter — for finding wires: voltage at the pin switch with the door open, at a turn signal, on the ignition wire; continuity and resistance. How to use it is in the lesson on the multimeter.

Logic probe or LED test light — to quickly see positive, negative and pulses while barely loading the circuit. Don’t hunt for wires with an incandescent test lamp: it draws hundreds of milliamps and can damage a module input or output.
Soldering iron with a stand, solder and rosin flux — for soldered joints, as in the lesson on wiring repair.
Heat shrink in different sizes and a heat gun — to insulate every joint.
Tape: cloth tape for wrapping harnesses in the cabin so they don’t squeak or rattle, like factory ones; PVC where moisture resistance is needed. Neither replaces heat shrink on the joint itself.
Split loom — to protect wires where they run near metal edges and moving parts.
Plastic trim tools — to remove panels without scratches. Don’t pry plastic with a screwdriver.
Zip ties, spare clips, a flashlight, covers — and a scan tool to read codes before and after the job.
Installer’s kit
find the wire by measuring
Logic probe
positive, negative, pulses
Soldering iron
soldering joints
Heat shrink

Tape

protects wires from chafing
Trim tools
panels without scratches
codes before and after the job
An installation kit: measure, solder, insulate, route — and don’t scratch anything.
Preparing the car
With the customer present, check that everything factory works: locks, power windows, lights, turn signals, instrument cluster, starting. Read the codes with a scan tool and save the report.
Take “before” photos: the cluster with the mileage and warning lights, the panels you’ll remove, any existing scratches and chips.
Covers on the seat, steering wheel and shifter, a mat on the floor, a fender cover if you work under the hood. Tools go on an organizer mat, not on the seat or the dash.
Remove only the trim you need, using trim tools. Clips and screws go in a separate box.
Find the wires you need with a multimeter and a probe — the battery has to be connected for these measurements.
Before cutting wires, soldering and connecting the unit’s power, disconnect the battery negative terminal.

“Before” photos and the scan report protect both you and the customer. If after installation the customer says a scratch or a code appeared at your shop, it will be clear what was there before the job. If something factory didn’t work before you started, say so right away and write it on the work order, as in the lesson on the profession.
The battery terminal

A disconnected negative terminal protects against an accidental short: a screwdriver slips, a bare wire end touches the body — with the battery connected, a fuse blows, and if the wire isn’t fused, the wiring melts. Disconnect the terminal with the ignition off and move it aside so it can’t touch the post by accident. Never disconnect the battery with the engine running.
Terminal connected
Spark — the fuse blows
Terminal off
No current — nothing burns
With the battery connected, an accidental short blows the fuse; with the terminal off, there’s no current.

Warn the customer in advance: after the battery is disconnected the clock, radio and power-window settings may reset, and on some cars an initialization per the owner’s manual is needed after reconnecting. After the job, restore everything that was reset.
Leave the airbags alone

Airbag and seat-belt pretensioner harnesses and connectors are usually yellow. Leave them alone: don’t unplug, pierce or tap into them, don’t measure anything in them, don’t take power from them, and don’t run your wires tight next to them. An accidental airbag deployment is dangerous for anyone nearby, and an SRS code after installation will be on you. If the job requires removing a panel with an airbag — on the steering wheel, a pillar or by a seat — that’s work done per the car’s service manual; this course doesn’t cover it.
Yellow connectors — hands off
Airbags and their harnesses — hands off
Work here: under the dash, by the driver’s feet
Under the dash by the driver’s feet is the work zone; the steering wheel, pillars, passenger dash and yellow connectors are off-limits.
Look after the interior

How to dress and how to cover the car is covered in the lesson on service culture. For an installer the main thing is the plastic: remove panels with trim tools, don’t break clips, don’t lose screws. Replace a broken clip with a new one: a rattling panel is a common complaint after an alarm install. Put removed panels on something soft, face up, away from your feet.
Covers on the seat and a separate one on the steering wheel show you care about the customer’s car. That’s exactly what sets you apart from a backyard repair shop.
The installer’s kit: multimeter, logic probe, soldering iron, heat shrink, cloth tape, split loom, trim tools, scan tool.
Prep: check factory functions and codes, “before” photos, covers, trim tools; wires are found with the battery connected.
Cut, solder and connect the unit’s power only with the negative terminal off; never disconnect the battery with the engine running.
Yellow connectors and airbag harnesses are left alone, and nothing is connected to them.
Why disconnect the negative terminal before soldering and connecting the unit’s power?
So the soldering iron heats up faster
So the alarm learns the fob
So an accidental short with a tool or wire doesn’t blow a fuse or burn the wiring
With the terminal off there’s no current in the circuit: a slipping screwdriver or a bare wire touching the body won’t burn anything.
Why look for wires with a logic probe or LED test light rather than an incandescent test lamp?
The probe barely loads the circuit, while the lamp draws hundreds of milliamps and can damage a module input or output
The lamp can’t be seen in daylight
The lamp only shows negative
An LED test light draws a few milliamps. A lamp is a load: on module circuits it can burn an output or cause a malfunction.
What do you do with yellow connectors and airbag harnesses during installation?
Take power from them
Unplug them for the installation
Check them with a multimeter
Leave them alone: don’t unplug, pierce or connect anything to them
Airbag circuits are not for the alarm installer. Any interference can cause a deployment or an SRS code.
Why take “before” photos and a scan report before installation?
For social media ads
To show the car’s condition before the job: scratches, warning lights, codes
The alarm requires it
The scan tool is needed to pair the fob
Photos and the report settle disputes: what was there before you is clear at once. A fault found before the job goes on the work order.

Many alarm “quirks” — false alarms, lost settings, a unit that ignores the fob — start with power and ground. The unit needs three circuits: constant positive, ignition positive and ground. Getting them right isn’t hard, but a mistake here takes hours to track down later.
Constant +12 V
Positive is taken with a separate wire from a reliable source: the battery positive terminal or a constant-positive (+30) power wire that is always live — with the key out and while starting.
The fuse goes at the source — right at the connection point, not at the unit. It protects the wire: if the wire shorts to the body anywhere, the fuse blows, not the wiring.
The rating is per your system’s manual. Power outputs — turn signals, locks — draw more current than the unit itself, so the harness often has several fuses.
Insert the fuse last, once everything is connected and insulated.
Fuse at the source
Constant +12 V — its own wire
Ignition switch
+15: live in ON and while starting
Alarm unit
Unit ground — on cleaned bare metal
If the wire shorts to the body, the fuse blows — not the wiring
Its own wire from the battery, a fuse at the source, ground to the body.

Why not “from the cigarette lighter”? On many cars the lighter and radio run off the ACC circuit (terminal 75): positive disappears with the key out and during starting — and the alarm shuts off with it. Even if the socket is on constant positive, it’s someone else’s circuit: its fuse is shared with the phone charger and other loads. If it blows, the car is left unprotected and nobody notices.

Never connect power without a fuse or fit a fuse larger than the rating: an unprotected wire shorted to the body gets red-hot in seconds, melts nearby harnesses and can set the car on fire. Before soldering and connecting, disconnect the battery negative terminal, as in the lesson on tools and safety.
Ignition positive: check by measuring

The ignition input tells the unit that the key is turned or the engine is running. The wire is found by measuring, not by color: multimeter on DC volts, black lead on ground, red lead on the wire at the ignition switch or module connector, from the terminal side, without piercing the insulation.
Key out — 0 V.
Key in ON — about 12 V, same as the battery.
Cranking — positive stays. The voltage dips to about 10 V — that’s normal.
Key back to OFF — 0 V.
If positive drops out during starting, it’s ACC or an auxiliary ignition circuit: not suitable for the alarm. Same with push-button start: check in ignition mode and while cranking.
Key position
lighter, radio
+15: live in ON and while cranking — for the ignition input
ACC: 0 V while cranking — not suitable for the alarm
Only a wire that’s live both in ON and while cranking will do.

The unit’s ground goes to the body: a factory ground point or a separate bolt into body metal. Paint and primer under the terminal are cleaned down to shiny metal, the terminal is a crimped ring terminal, the nut is tightened with a washer, and the spot is coated with corrosion protection afterward. Keep the ground wire as short as possible.
Don’t ground to painted brackets or bolts on plastic parts: contact with the body there is hit-or-miss.
Don’t tap into thin ground wires of other modules: the alarm gets its own ground to the body.

Test under load — turn on the turn signals or the siren: the voltage drop between the unit’s ground and the battery negative should be hundredths of a volt. Over 0.1 V — redo the connection, as in the lesson on troubleshooting method.
A bad ground is a common cause of resets and false alarms: every flash of the turn signals makes the unit’s voltage sag.
Turn signals on
paint under the terminal
metal cleaned to a shine
Battery negative
Voltmeter
Unit ground
Bolt on paint: 1.20 V — bad ground, redo it
Metal cleaned: 0.03 V — good
Under load, normal is hundredths of a volt; over 0.1 V — redo it
Load reveals what you can’t see at rest: paint under the terminal costs more than a volt.
Wire sizes and connections
When extending a wire, use one no thinner than the original wire in the alarm harness.
Unit power and ground — usually 1–1.5 mm²; wires that carry heavy current go thicker, sized for the current. Signal inputs — pin switches, buttons — are fine with 0.35–0.5 mm².
Connections — solder and heat shrink, not a twist under electrical tape; details in the lesson on wire routing and mounting.
Run the power wire along factory harnesses and through rubber grommets, not over sharp metal edges: a positive wire chafed against the body is a short.
Check the fuses first. If the unit doesn’t respond or keeps resetting, the first thing I look at is the fuse at the source and its holder: is the fuse intact and seated firmly.
Constant positive — a separate wire from the battery or a +30 power feed, fuse at the source; not from the cigarette lighter.
The ignition positive is found by measuring: live in ON and while cranking, 0 V with the key out.
Ground — to cleaned body metal; under load the drop is hundredths of a volt, over 0.1 V — redo it.
Wire size — no thinner than the original; connections — solder and heat shrink.
Where does the fuse for the constant-positive wire go?
At the alarm unit, so it’s handy
At the source — right at the point where it connects to positive
Wherever is convenient, as long as there is one
The fuse protects the wire. At the source, it blows on a short anywhere along the wire; at the unit, the section before it is left unprotected.
Which wire is right for the “+ignition” input?
One that’s live all the time, even with the key out
One that’s live only in ON and drops out while cranking
The cigarette lighter wire
One that’s live in ON and while cranking, and 0 V with the key out
That’s how a true ignition positive behaves. One that drops out during starting is ACC or an auxiliary circuit; one that’s always live is constant +30.
Why isn’t the alarm powered from the cigarette lighter?
It’s someone else’s circuit: it often drops out with the key out and during starting, and its fuse is shared with other loads
The lighter supplies too high a voltage
It’s fine if the socket is in good shape
The alarm should depend only on its own wire and its own fuse at the source.
The turn signals are flashing, and right then there’s 0.8 V between the unit’s ground and the battery negative. What does that mean?
Normal: that’s how it should be under load
The alarm unit is faulty
Poor ground contact — clean the metal and redo the connection
Normal is hundredths of a volt. 0.8 V on the ground is a poor contact: on every flash the unit is short of voltage — hence the resets and false alarms.

A pin switch is a switch that reports whether a door, the hood or the trunk is open. Through the pin switches the alarm won’t arm with a door open and sounds the alarm when a door is opened. Connect to them so the factory functions — interior lights, the “door open” icon on the dash — keep working as before.
Ground-side and positive-side
A ground-side pin switch — on most cars. Door opened — the switch connects the wire to ground and the dome lamp comes on. On the wire: door closed — about 12 V, open — about 0.
A positive-side pin switch is less common. Door opened — the switch puts positive on the wire. On the wire: closed — 0, open — about 12 V.
A pin switch may be a plunger in the door opening or built into the door latch — then its wire runs through the rubber boot between the door and the body.

On many modern cars the body control module reads the pin switches and turns on the dome lamp itself, as in the lesson on body electrics. The pin switch wire still changes voltage when the door opens — that’s what you look for.
Ground-side pin switch
Dome lamp
wire to the alarm
Positive-side pin switch
less common
Door closed: switch open
Door open: switch closed
Look for the wire whose voltage changes when the door opens
The pin switch type is told by what happens on the wire when the door opens.
How to find the wire
Find the harness with the door wires: at the body control module, in the pillar or under the sill.
Multimeter on DC volts, black lead on ground. Check the wires with the red lead from the terminal side of the connector.
Open and close the door. Your wire is the one whose voltage changes: from 12 V to 0 or the other way around. A logic probe shows it right away — “positive” or “ground”.
Check every door: on many cars they share one wire, but the driver’s door is often separate.
Write down which wire is which — it’ll come in handy at handover and for repairs.

In the pillars and under the sills, side airbag and curtain airbag harnesses often run next to the door wires — yellow connectors and sleeving. Don’t touch them, don’t pierce them and don’t connect anything to them.
Check the fuses first. If the pin switch wire doesn’t change from any door and the dome lamp won’t come on, the first thing I look at is the dome lamp and body module fuses.
Hood and trunk
Trunk: many cars have their own pin switch or a switch in the lid latch; its wire is found the same way — by the voltage change when it opens.

Hood: there’s often no factory pin switch, so a separate one is fitted — it usually comes in the alarm kit. Location — rigid metal where water doesn’t run and dirt doesn’t fly; with the hood closed, the plunger must be pressed with travel to spare.

The hood pin switch goes to its own alarm input — usually a ground-trigger input: when opened, it connects the input to ground. Route the wire away from hot and rotating parts, as in the lesson on wire routing.
Check: hood closed — plunger pressed; lift the hood a few centimeters — the alarm should see it open.
Rigid body metal
Plunger — travel to spare
Hood input (ground)
Hood closed: plunger pressed
Hood ajar: input grounded
Location: rigid metal, dry, away from dirt and heat
Hood opened slightly — the plunger came out and grounded the input
A plunger with travel to spare: the switch trips as soon as the hood is opened slightly.
Isolation diodes

If the alarm has one door input but the car’s doors are on separate wires — often the driver’s door is separate — the wires can’t be joined directly. Open one door, and the body control module will “see” the others open too: it may turn on the wrong light or show the wrong door on the dash. Each wire goes to the input through its own diode. Do the same if you have to bring the trunk pin switch onto the door input.
Dome lamp, body module
“doors” input
stripe — cathode
Driver’s door
Other doors
Driver’s door open: the other wire stayed at 12.6 V
Another door open: the driver’s wire stayed at 12.6 V
Ground-side switches: the diode stripe goes to the switch wire
Each diode passes the signal only to its own switch: the door wires don’t connect to each other.
For ground-side switches, the diode goes cathode — the striped end — to the switch wire and anode to the alarm input. For positive-side switches, the other way around.
The current here is tiny — an ordinary rectifier diode such as a 1N4007 will do.
Diodes — soldered, with heat shrink on each lead; mounted somewhere dry with no strain on the wires.
After connecting, check each door separately: the alarm sees it open, and the factory lights and dash icons work as before.
A pin switch is ground-side (more common) or positive-side: when the door opens, the wire changes from 12 V to 0 or the other way around.
The wire is found by measuring at the connector or module; each door is checked separately.
The hood usually needs its own pin switch: on rigid, dry metal, with plunger travel to spare.
Doors on separate wires go to one input through diodes: for ground-side switches, stripe toward the switch.
Door closed — 12 V on the wire, open — 0 V. What kind of pin switch is it?
When opened, a ground-side switch connects the wire to ground — the voltage drops to zero.
What’s the most reliable way to find the pin switch wire?
Measure at the connector: the wire whose voltage changes when the door opens
By wire color — it’s the same on every car
Pierce the wires in the door boot one by one
Colors differ from car to car, and piercings in the boot, where the wire flexes constantly, soon break. The reliable way is measuring at the connector or module.

Twist the wires together and run them to the input
Connect only the driver’s door

Through a resistor
The diodes keep the wires from connecting to each other: the alarm sees every door, and the body module sees only the one that’s open.

On the plastic cowl grille by the windshield
Next to the exhaust manifold

A hood pin switch has to be pressed reliably and survive water, dirt and heat: plastic flexes, and near the manifold the switch and wire overheat.

The alarm flashes the turn signals when the car is armed and disarmed, and together with the siren during an alarm. The lights can be connected in different ways, but one rule holds: the factory turn signals and hazards work as before, and the alarm output isn’t overloaded.
Three ways
To the bulb wires — left and right side. The alarm output feeds positive straight to the bulbs; you need diode isolation or a separate channel for each side.

To the hazard button. On many cars the hazard button sends a signal to the body control module, and the module does the flashing; the alarm “presses” that button through a relay. Exactly how — by holding it or with short pulses — depends on the car and the alarm settings: see your system’s manual.
Over CAN. The CAN module tells the body control module to flash, if the alarm maker supports it for your model; details in the lesson on the CAN bus during installation.
Bulb wires: how to find them

The side wires are found by measuring at the body control module, the flasher relay or the lamps. Multimeter or probe to ground, turn on the left signal: the wire where positive comes and goes in time with the flashing feeds the left-side bulbs. Then the same on the right. Turn on the hazards — both wires you found should flash. A wire whose signal stays steady while the turn signal is on is the command from the stalk to the module; bulbs aren’t connected to it.
Diode isolation

Many alarms have a single light-flash output. Wire it straight to both sides, and the sides get connected to each other: turn on the left signal, and the right one flashes too, like the hazards. So the output goes to each side through its own diode: the alarm’s positive reaches the bulbs, but one side’s positive can’t reach the other.

The diodes must handle the side’s current with margin. Amps flow through them: a small 1 A 1N4007, fine for pin switches, will overheat and fail here; you need a 5–6 A diode or bigger.
About 0.7–1 V is lost across the diode — the bulbs are a little dimmer when the alarm flashes them, and that’s normal.

The alarm must lock and unlock the doors just like the factory switch or key fob. To do that, its outputs are connected to the central locking control circuit. The wiring depends on how the lock gets its command in this particular car, so first you identify the control type by measuring, and only then reach for wires and relays.
Five control types

Negative pulses. The body control module or door lock unit gets the command over separate “lock” and “unlock” wires. At rest the wire sits at pull-up voltage — usually about 12 V, sometimes 5 V — and during the command the switch grounds it.
Positive pulses. The opposite: 0 on the wire at rest, and +12 V arrives during the command.

Two-wire reversing actuator. The actuator motor is driven by reversing polarity: to lock, one wire gets positive and the other ground; to unlock, the other way around. At rest the factory unit usually holds both wires at ground. These wires carry motor current — several amps.
Pneumatic. On older Mercedes-Benz and some Audi and Volkswagen models, a central locking pump pushes air through tubes to the actuators. It needs a long pulse — several seconds.

CAN. The body control module receives the lock or unlock command over the data bus. Then the alarm’s CAN module sends it — only if the alarm manufacturer supports that model. More on this in the lesson on the CAN bus during installation.
Negative control — the wire “drops” to zero; positive — it “rises” to 12 V; with a reversing actuator the positive moves from one wire to the other.
What the wire shows on command
Negative control: the “lock” wire
Positive control: the “lock” wire
Reversing actuator: two wires to the motor
Wire 1
Wire 2
Identifying the control type by measuring

Look for the control wires where they are common to all doors: at the body control module or door lock unit, or in the driver’s door harness on the cabin side. Wire functions come from your car’s wiring diagram: pin numbers differ from model to model, and this course doesn’t give them.

Set the multimeter to DC volts, black lead on body ground, red lead back-probing the terminal from the rear of the connector without piercing the insulation. A logic probe is handy too: its light shows positive or negative and it barely loads the circuit.
Lock and unlock the doors with the factory switch or the key and watch what the wire showed at rest and what it shows during the command.

12 V at rest and 0 on command — negative control; 0 at rest and 12 V on command — positive. On a pair of wires, positive appears on one and then the other — reversing actuator. A pump runs for a few seconds and the locks close with a hiss of air — pneumatic; the pump’s command wire is found the same way, by measuring.
The doors lock, but none of the wires you found changes — the command most likely travels over the bus. Check the alarm manufacturer’s compatibility list.

Don’t check body control module or door lock unit wires with a test light: its current can damage the module output. Use only a multimeter or logic probe. Don’t cut or solder the wires in the rubber boot between the door and the body — they flex there constantly. Leave the yellow airbag connectors in the pillars and under the seats alone.
Connecting through relays

Alarm central locking outputs vary: some systems have low-current transistor outputs rated for a fraction of an amp, others have built-in relays. Check your system’s manual to see which you have. The rule is simple: a low-current input of the body control module or door lock unit may be connected straight to the alarm output if the manual allows it. A wire that carries actuator motor current goes only through a relay.
A reversing actuator is wired by cutting into both wires with two changeover relays with terminals 30, 87 and 87a, as in the lesson on relays.
Cut the wire: the actuator side goes to 30, the factory-unit side to 87a, and 87 gets positive through its own fuse at the source.
At rest the relays are de-energized: the actuator is connected to the factory unit through 87a, and the door switch works as before.

On command the alarm energizes one relay: the actuator wire is disconnected from the unit and gets positive. Current flows through the motor and returns over the second wire through the other relay and the factory unit to ground.
This works when the factory unit holds both wires at ground at rest. If the car is built differently, wire it according to your system’s manual.
At rest the relays pass the factory unit’s command; on the alarm’s command one of them feeds positive to the actuator.

Pulse length
Electric actuators usually need only a short pulse — about a second.
Pneumatics need a long one — several seconds, until the pump has locked all the doors.
Too short a pulse — not all locks operate, or they don’t go all the way, especially in the cold, when the grease in the actuators thickens.
Too long on an electric actuator — the motor sits stalled at the end of travel under current and heats up.

On some cars the first pulse unlocks only the driver’s door and the second unlocks the rest; for them alarms often offer a double unlock pulse. Pulse length and such functions are chosen in the settings — according to your system’s manual.

When the central locking stops working, I check the fuses first — both the factory lock fuse and the one on the relay’s positive feed. Only then do I take the trim panel off and look for a wiring mistake.

Check the factory switch in the cabin, the key in the door and the factory key fob, if there is one: they must work as they did before the installation.
Repeat several times in a row — the locks must not miss commands.
In winter, check on a cold car: actuators need more time in the cold.

Measure with a multimeter or logic probe, not a test light.
Actuator motor current goes only through relays; a reversing actuator is cut in with two changeover relays, positive through its own fuse.
Pulse: about a second for electric actuators, several seconds for pneumatics; check every door, including in the cold.

A CAN module is the part of the alarm that connects to the car’s data bus with two wires. Instead of a dozen wires to the pin switches, locks and turn signals, it reads and sends bus messages. Installation becomes faster and neater, but a wiring mistake can take the bus down: warnings light up on the dash, modules lose communication, the engine may not start. How the bus works is covered in the lesson on CAN, LIN and K-line — here is only what you need for installation.
What a CAN module gives you
Reads: doors, hood and trunk, ignition, engine running, speed, brake pedal, factory key fob buttons — the set depends on the model.
Controls: central locking, turn signals, and on some cars — closing the windows, opening the trunk and the factory alarm.

What the module can do on a particular car is listed in the alarm manufacturer’s compatibility list for that model and model year. Whatever isn’t on the list is wired, as in the lessons on pin switches, turn signals and central locking.
The module is connected with a short tap to the pair at the body control module; the bus isn’t cut, and there are still two resistors at its ends.

Where to look for the pair
The connection point for the model is usually given in the alarm manufacturer’s instructions: most often it’s the pair at the body control module, the instrument cluster or the ignition switch.
CAN-H and CAN-L run as a twisted pair. Wire colors differ between makes, so the pair is confirmed by measuring, not by color.

The OBD connector is for checking only. On many cars its pins 6 and 14 are separated from the other buses by a gateway, and there are no body messages there until a scan tool asks for them. Besides, wires at the OBD connector are quickly found by anyone looking for the alarm.
A car can have several buses — engine, body, multimedia. You need the one specified for this model in your system’s manual.
Checking the pair by measuring
Ignition on, the bus is active. Multimeter on DC volts, black lead on body ground.
Red lead — back-probe each wire of the pair at the connector. CAN-H will read about 2.6–2.7 V, CAN-L about 2.3–2.4 V, about 5 V combined: the meter averages the signal around the 2.5 V rest level.
Turn the ignition off and disconnect the battery negative. Resistance between the wires of the pair is about 60 Ω: that’s the two 120 Ω resistors at the ends of the bus.
About 120 Ω or close to zero — the bus is already faulty. Don’t connect the module to such a bus: find the cause first, as in the lesson on buses.
On a live bus the multimeter reads about 2.6–2.7 V on CAN-H and 2.3–2.4 V on CAN-L; with the car powered down, about 60 Ω between the wires.

That’s what high-speed CAN looks like. A fault-tolerant low-speed comfort bus has different voltage levels and no 60 Ω — as in the lesson on buses. Which bus is at the connection point, check in your system’s manual.
Connecting without cutting the bus
Disconnect the battery negative: a soldering iron near a live bus risks a short.
Don’t cut the bus wire. Strip about 1 cm of insulation without nicking the strands.

Wrap the stripped section with the module wire and solder it with rosin flux, as in the lesson on wiring repair. Twisted splices and piercing connectors are no good on the bus: contact is lost over time and the bus starts to glitch.

Insulate each joint separately — several layers of good PVC electrical tape overlapping onto the intact insulation. Offset the CAN-H and CAN-L joints by a few centimeters along the length so they can’t touch each other.
Keep the wires from the module to the bus short and twist them together, like the pair in the car. Module CAN-H to the car’s CAN-H, CAN-L to CAN-L.
If the module or other equipment has its own 120 Ω resistor, it is not enabled on the car’s bus: a third resistor gives about 40 Ω.
The bus isn’t cut: strip a section, wrap it with the module wire, solder it and insulate each joint separately.

Cut the bus wire and twist it together with the module wire
With a piercing connector

The bus isn’t cut, and the joint is reliable and vibration-proof. Twisted splices and piercing connectors lose contact over time, and the bus glitches.
Engine kill

An engine kill prevents starting the car while it’s armed: the alarm uses a relay to interrupt a circuit the engine can’t start without. Done badly, it can stall the engine while driving or leave the owner stranded. That’s why the relay, the circuit and the location are chosen by the rules. The factory immobilizer is left alone: the kill is added on top of it.
Normally closed and normally open relays
The upside of an NC kill: if the alarm fails or loses power, the car starts and drives. The downside: cut the alarm’s power and the kill is gone too.
Normally open — NO, contacts 30 and 87. The circuit is closed only while the alarm keeps the coil energized — that is, the whole drive.

The upside of an NO kill: without the alarm the engine won’t start. The downside: if the relay, its power feed or the alarm output fails, the car stops. The coil is energized all the time and the relay warms up, so you need a quality relay and a reliable power feed.
Which scheme to choose and which alarm output to use for it — follow your system’s manual.
When the alarm energizes the coil, an NC relay opens the pump circuit and an NO relay closes it.
Normally closed (NC)
Contacts 30–87a
Pump stopped
Without the alarm the car drives
Normally open (NO)
Contacts 30–87
Without the alarm the engine won’t start
Coil off: the alarm is idle or has no power
The alarm has energized the coil
What to interrupt
The fuel pump circuit — the pump’s power wire. The current is a few amps. Without the pump the engine won’t start, and if the kill triggers while driving, it stalls.

The starter circuit — the control wire, terminal 50. The starter is needed only for starting, so this kind of kill can’t stall the engine while driving. During cranking the wire on terminal 50 carries the solenoid current — up to tens of amps.

Find the right wire from the car’s wiring diagram and confirm it by measuring. On many cars the pump wire gets positive for a couple of seconds when the ignition is switched on and keeps it while the engine runs; terminal 50 gets it only while the starter is cranking.
The main rule: never while driving

The kill must never trigger while the engine is running and the car is moving. An engine that dies in traffic or on the highway means steering and brakes that suddenly get heavy — a direct road to a crash.
The kill engages only when armed; with the engine running and the car moving — never.

The kill must not stall a moving engine on any command

Don’t enable functions that can stall the engine while driving.
A normally closed contact carries the pump current the whole drive. A corroded or weak contact will stall the engine on the road just like a triggered kill.
Check on a parked car: start the engine, press the fob buttons, open and close the doors — the engine keeps running. When armed the car doesn’t start; after disarming it starts on the first try.

A kill that can stall the engine while driving is unacceptable — even if the customer asks for it. And never cut into the airbag circuits with yellow connectors, ABS, power steering, brake lights or the factory immobilizer wiring.
Circuit current and the relay
Before installing, find out the circuit current: measure it with a clamp meter while the pump runs or during cranking. The rating of the circuit’s factory fuse also tells you the ballpark.
Choose a relay with margin: its contacts must be rated for at least the current of the circuit’s factory fuse.
Wires to the relay contacts — the same gauge as the factory wire you cut, or heavier.
The alarm output drives only the relay coil. Never run pump or starter current through the alarm output: it is usually rated for a fraction of an amp and will burn out.
The pump wire is cut and routed through contacts 30 and 87a; the alarm output drives only the coil.

Don’t put the relay next to the alarm unit or in plain sight: that’s where it will be looked for first.

The relay must not dangle: secure it to the harness with a zip tie. All connections — soldered and insulated, no twisted splices.
Record the relay location and the circuit in your own archive along with photos of the installation: a year later it will save hours of searching.

Pump current flows through the normally closed contact the whole drive. A bad contact weakens or stops the pump, and the engine dies. That’s why the relay must be good quality and the joints soldered.

Normally closed — NC, contacts 30 and 87a. At rest the circuit is closed and the car works as if there were no alarm. To kill, the alarm energizes the coil and the contact opens. A regular relay coil draws about 0.1–0.15 A, so it is not kept energized for the whole time the car is parked: the kill output is set to switch on only when someone tries to start the car while it is armed — the system's manual says how.

Pin switches only notice that a door, the hood or the trunk was opened — that’s covered in the lesson on pin switches. Sensors guard the car when everything is closed. The shock sensor hears a hit to the body or glass, the tilt sensor — jacking or loading onto a tow truck, the interior motion sensor — movement in the cabin. Where the sensors go and how they are set decides whether the alarm protects the car or wakes up the neighborhood at night.
Shock sensor: two zones

Inside the sensor is a sensing element: a piezo element, a magnet over a coil or, in newer systems, an accelerometer chip. A hit becomes an electrical signal, and the sensor compares it with two thresholds. A light hit crosses only the warning-zone threshold: the siren gives a short chirp and the turn signals flash. A hard hit crosses the alarm-zone threshold too: a full alarm, and on systems with GSM a message to the phone as well. A separate sensor has its own output for each zone, usually a negative one: at rest the zone wire carries a voltage held by the control unit, and when the sensor trips it briefly pulls the wire to ground, so the unit sees a pulse.
A light hit crosses only the warning threshold; a hard hit crosses the alarm threshold too.

Warning threshold

Where to mount the sensor
On a rigid part of the body or a sturdy factory bracket under the dash, close to the middle of the car: that way the sensor hears hits from both sides equally.
Screw the housing down or strap it tight to the bracket. A sensor hanging on its wires sometimes misses a hit and sometimes trips by itself when it swings.
Not on thin plastic and not next to anything that shakes — small motors, the heater blower: the sensor will take their vibration for a hit.
The sensitivity knob should stay reachable for adjustment, but out of sight.
If the shock and tilt sensor is built into the control unit, as in many modern systems, all of these rules apply to where the unit itself goes.

Airbag harnesses run under the dash — they have yellow connectors and often a yellow sleeve. Don’t fasten sensors or their wires to them, don’t splice anything into them, and don’t put sensors where an airbag deploys.
Setting the sensitivity
Start with low sensitivity. The knob is on the sensor housing; built-in sensors are set from the fob, in the app or with software — per your system’s manual.
Arm the car and wait for the sensors to come on: many systems have a delay after arming.
Test it: a light slap with your palm on a body pillar or a tire should give a warning, a harder one an alarm. Don’t hit the glass, and don’t kick the car.
Raise the sensitivity a little at a time and test after every step — on both sides of the car, front and rear.
If the sensor has a separate knob for each zone, the alarm zone must stay noticeably less sensitive than the warning zone.
A good setting: a truck driving past doesn’t trigger an alarm, but the sensor hears a light palm slap.
Tilt and interior motion sensors

The tilt sensor remembers the car’s position when it’s armed and raises the alarm if the position changes: the car is jacked up or loaded onto a tow truck. It ignores slow changes — snow on the roof, tires that have cooled down. It’s mounted rigidly to the body, in the orientation the manual requires.

A microwave interior motion sensor “sees” movement in the cabin and a little around the car — through the glass. It has two zones too: the outer one — someone walked right up — gives a warning, the inner one — a hand inside the cabin — an alarm. It goes near the center of the cabin, for example in the tunnel between the seats, away from metal.

An ultrasonic interior sensor — a transmitter and receiver pair up by the headliner, usually near the dome light — watches the air in the closed cabin. It only works with the windows and sunroof closed.
The motion sensor’s outer zone gives a warning, the inner zone an alarm.

False alarms
Wind and vibration: gusts rock the car, trucks or a streetcar go by, construction is going on nearby. A less sensitive setting helps, especially on tall vehicles and cars with a roof rack.
The sensor is loosely mounted or hangs on its wires — it swings.

A “floating” ground: the sensor or unit ground is on a painted or rusty bolt, or there’s a poor contact in a connector. The unit takes the noise on its input for a trigger. Clean the spot and tighten the ground, as in the lesson on unit power and ground.
A chafed zone wire touches the body — to the unit that’s the same “to ground” signal as the sensor tripping.

For the motion sensor — anything that moves in the closed cabin: a toy or air freshener on the mirror, sunshades, insects, airflow from the heater or a parking heater. For the ultrasonic one — also a window or sunroof left slightly open.
Sometimes false alarms show up only in freezing weather or only in the heat: then recheck the setting in that season.
When to bypass the sensors

Sometimes the car needs to be locked with the sensors bypassed for a while: a dog or cat stays in the cabin, a parking heater or the heater blower is running, the sunroof is open, the car is carried on a tow truck or a ferry. For this, systems let you bypass the sensors or individual zones from the fob or the app — exactly how is in your system’s manual. The pin switches and the engine kill keep working. If the system has remote start, many systems bypass the shock sensor on their own while the engine is running. Explain all this to the customer when you hand the car over.
If the alarm suddenly stops hearing hits or goes completely silent, I check the fuses first — both in the alarm wiring and the factory ones — and only then take panels off and turn knobs.
The shock sensor works in two zones: a light hit gives a warning, a hard one an alarm; a separate sensor’s zone outputs are usually negative.
Mount the sensor rigidly to the body near the middle of the car, not on plastic and not next to anything that shakes; set it starting from low sensitivity, testing after every step.
Tilt means a jack or a tow truck, motion means movement in the cabin; false alarms come from wind, poor mounting, a “floating” ground, a chafed wire and things moving in the cabin.
A pet, a running heater, an open sunroof — bypass the sensors from the fob or app per the manual; the pin switches and the kill relay stay active.
A light palm slap on a tire gave a short siren chirp, and a harder one a full alarm. What does that mean?
A light hit crosses only the warning-zone threshold, a hard one the alarm-zone threshold too. That’s exactly how it should be.

The siren, antenna and GSM module are how the alarm talks to the world: the siren to the street, the antenna to the fob, GSM to the owner’s phone. Where they go decides whether the siren is still heard after a few winters, whether the fob reaches the car from the parking lot, and whether alarm messages arrive on time.
Siren: where to mount it
Under the hood, in a protected spot — for example behind the headlight or by the fender, on a sturdy bracket: so the siren is hard to reach from above or below.
Horn facing down: water and dirt drain out instead of collecting inside. A siren with the horn up fills with water, and in winter with ice, and goes quiet.
Away from hot parts — the exhaust manifold, the turbo — and from anything that spins: the radiator fan, belts.

The wire runs in split loom along the factory harnesses and into the cabin through the factory firewall grommet. If you had to drill, fit a rubber grommet and sealant, as in the lesson on routing wires.
The siren ground goes to the body, on a cleaned spot, like the unit ground.
Horn down, in a protected spot, wire in split loom — that’s how a siren lasts.

The siren connects to the siren output of the control unit. The current that output is rated for is in your system’s manual. If you fit a more powerful siren or two sirens, connect them through a relay, as in the lesson on relays. A siren with its own backup battery keeps wailing even if its wires are cut; it’s shut off with a key or a code — also per the manual.
Fob antenna
The antenna module — the transceiver — is usually stuck to the inside of the windshield, near the top: from there it “sees” the farthest.
Away from metal — the body frame, metal parts and wiring — at the distance given in the manual. Metal nearby “eats” the range.

Not on metallized tint film and not on an athermal windshield with a coating: the radio signal gets through them poorly. Coated windshields often have an uncoated area, usually by the mirror — check where it is on the actual car.
Not right next to a dash cam or radar detector: their electronics cause interference.
Degrease the glass and stick it on in the warm: tape holds poorly on cold glass. In winter, warm up the cabin first.

The antenna wire runs under the pillar trim along the factory harness. Many cars have curtain airbags in the pillars and above the doors: don’t lay the wire over the curtain, fasten it so it can’t keep the curtain from deploying, and don’t touch its yellow connectors. Remove and refit the pillar trim as described in the car’s service manual.

The range on the box is for ideal conditions, in an open field. In the city it’s noticeably shorter.

A customer never notices good installation work. Bad work shows up months later: a twisted splice corrodes and the kill relay or central locking fails, a wire chafes through and blows a fuse, the unit knocks under the dash on every bump. The rules in this lesson save you from those comebacks.
Connections: solder, not twists

A twisted splice under tape corrodes over time: resistance grows, the joint heats up, voltage is lost — the lesson on wiring repair covers this in detail. An alarm install has a lot of connections, and each one is soldered or properly crimped. Use neutral flux, such as rosin: acid flux eats copper. Use a soldering iron powerful enough for the solder to flow, not sit in a blob.
Find the wire by measuring, as in the lessons on pin switches and central locking, and check it once more right before you splice in.
Strip a 1–1.5 cm window in the insulation without cutting the strands.
Spread the strands, push the stripped end of the new wire through the gap and wrap it around.
Solder it so the solder flows in between the strands, and let it cool without moving the wire.
Insulate: several layers of tape overlapping the insulation, cloth tape on top. Where heat shrink can be slipped on, use heat shrink.
Strap the tap wire to the factory wire with a zip tie so vibration doesn’t crack the solder joint.
Splicing in without a cut: window, strands, solder, insulation — and the tap wire on a zip tie.

Run the alarm wires along the factory harnesses and zip-tie them at short intervals — the harness must not sag.

Keep clear of everything that moves: pedals, the steering shaft and its U-joint under the dash, seat tracks and mechanisms, door, hood and trunk hinges. Wires go into a door only through the factory boot.
Under the hood keep clear of hot parts — the exhaust manifold and turbo — and don’t lay wires on the engine.
Don’t fasten wires to brake or fuel lines or to an adjustable steering column.
Through metal only via a rubber grommet or a factory seal: a sharp edge will cut through the insulation.
Under the hood the wires go in split loom: it protects them from rubbing, dirt and dust.
Leave a little slack at connectors so they can be unplugged, but no dangling loops.

A wire rubbing on the steering shaft, a pedal or a metal edge will sooner or later wear through to the copper. A positive wire on the body is a short circuit: without a fuse it can catch fire, and with a fuse the car is left without the alarm, sometimes without starting. So not a single positive wire without a fuse at the source — as in the lesson on unit power and ground.
The unit: hidden and secure
Hide the control unit deep under the dash and not in the most obvious place: behind the glovebox and under the steering column are where people look first.
The spot must be dry: not on the floor, where meltwater from snowy boots gets in, and not under the windshield, where it may leak.
Zip-tie the unit to a sturdy harness or bracket, and wrap it in cloth tape where it could knock on metal. If the unit has a built-in shock sensor, mount it rigidly, as in the lesson on sensors.
Wrap the wires from the unit the same way as the factory harness next to them — cloth tape or split loom — so they blend in.
Mount the kill relay separately from the unit, somewhere else along the harness, as in the lesson on engine immobilization.
Reassembly order
Reconnect the battery terminal and test all functions while the panels are off: that way a mistake is easy to fix.
Clear the cabin of wire, insulation and zip-tie offcuts.
Plug back in every factory connector you unplugged: switches, lights, sensors.
Refit the panels in reverse order and make sure no wires get caught under clips or screws. Replace broken clips.
Check the factory functions: power windows, lights, the instrument cluster, locks, the horn.
Drive over a rough road and listen: nothing should knock or rattle.

If something rattles after reassembly, look among the things you touched: the unit or a relay touching metal, a loose harness, a panel not fully clipped in. Wrap the unit and relays in cloth tape, zip-tie the harness, replace the clips. In freezing weather plastic is brittle: remove and refit trim in a heated bay, or the clips break and the panels squeak later.

After reassembly I hook up a scan tool and check whether any new codes have appeared in the modules — especially if the alarm is connected over CAN. Go with a Launch scan tool: it’s proven equipment, while cheap ELM327 adapters sometimes “knock the car out”.

The harness runs along the factory one on zip ties, clear of pedals, the steering shaft, seats, hinges and heat; through metal only via a grommet or seal.
The unit sits in a dry hidden spot, secured and silent; the kill relay goes separately from the unit.
First test all functions with the panels off, then reassemble, check the factory functions and test-drive: nothing rattles.

The installation is finished, but don’t put the panels back yet: first the system is programmed and every function is tested — while everything is open, a mistake is easy to fix, as in the lesson on wire routing. Programming means learning the fobs and the owner’s phone, choosing the car model for the CAN module and setting the functions for the car and the customer. Menu names and button sequences differ from system to system, so everything is done per your system’s manual; here is the general order and what gets forgotten most often.
Fobs and phone
Fob learning mode is usually entered with the Valet button with the ignition on, then a button on the fob is pressed. The system confirms with a siren chirp or LED flashes.
Learn all the customer’s fobs in one session. On many systems, entering learning mode erases the old fobs from memory: learn one new fob and the rest stop working.
After learning, test each fob separately: arming, disarming and, on a two-way fob, the reply on the screen or by signal.

The owner’s phone is paired in the app or by command — per the manufacturer’s instructions, usually with the code from the owner’s card. Check that commands work and that the alarm notification arrives.
Learn all the customer’s fobs at once: on many systems a new session erases the old ones.
