That 36 V is being supplied — to have some headroom
What voltage the module is designed for: trucks are usually 24 V
Truck modules are designed for 24 V, passenger car modules for 12 V. The voltage is checked against the documentation before switching on.
The awake module’s current is normal, but the scan tool can’t see it over CAN. What should you check?
Replace the processor
Raise the voltage to 18 V
The CAN-H and CAN-L connections, the common ground with the adapter and the 120 Ω resistor
The module is working, so the problem is in the communication line: the bus wires, the adapter ground or the termination resistor.

“No communication with the module” is a common complaint and a common diagnostic mistake: the module gets removed and taken in for repair, but it’s fine — power or the bus just isn’t reaching it. So the order is: the car first, then the bench.
The car first

See which modules you have communication with. None at all — look for a common cause: power and ground at the OBD connector (16 is positive, 4 and 5 are ground), the bus as a whole, or a module that’s “jamming” the bus, as in the lesson on digital buses. No communication with just one — check that one.

Power and grounds at the module connector: +30, +15, power from the main relay and all grounds — from the wire side, under load, as in the lesson on ECU power and grounds. Which pin is which — only from a pinout from a trusted source.
Bus: with the car unpowered, about 60 Ω between CAN-H and CAN-L; with the ignition on, about 2.5 V on each wire at the module connector. K-line at rest — about battery voltage.
The module connector terminals: water, corrosion, spread or backed-out terminals — as in the lesson on wiring repair.
Everything is normal but there’s still no communication — the module is removed and tested on the bench.
Check the fuses first. If a module is silent, the first thing to look at is the fuses for its power feeds and for the main relay.
On the bench: from simple to complex

Connect the module using a verified diagram, as in the lesson on connecting on the bench. Each next step only makes sense if the previous one is normal: there’s no point measuring the crystal while the processor has no power.

Current draw. It doesn’t rise when +15 is switched on — the module hasn’t woken up. It hits the limit right away — a short in the power circuit: don’t power it up any further, look for the shorted component.
Power on the board. +30, +15 and power from the relay must get from the connector pins to the board — check after the protection components and at the regulator input.

5 V regulator. With +15 on, measure at its output or at the capacitors near the processor relative to board ground: it should be a steady 5 V. If the module has 3.3 V, check that too. No voltage, or it “wanders” — the power supply chip is faulty or something is loading its output.

Crystal. With an oscilloscope on its pins — a clean sine wave at a frequency that’s usually marked on the package. Set the probe to x10: an x1 probe loads the crystal more and can stop the oscillation. No oscillation — the crystal, the capacitors next to it or the processor.

CAN transceiver. On an awake module, CAN-H and CAN-L read about 2.5 V each. On an unpowered module, the resistance from each line to ground is high, not a few ohms. Almost zero — the transceiver or a protection component at the bus input is shorted.
Traces and vias. Do a continuity test from the connector pin to the component: power — to the regulator, CAN — to the transceiver, ground — to board ground.
Signs of moisture: white or green deposits, darkened areas, corroded pins, especially near the connector. What to do about them — in the lesson on moisture and corrosion.

Measurements on a powered board — only with fine probes and with your hand braced. A slipping probe will short 12 V onto a neighboring 5 V circuit — and you’ll lose the processor. The oscilloscope ground clip goes only to board ground. Don’t leave jumpers or loose wires on a powered board.
Symptoms and likely causes
Current almost zero with +15 on — power isn’t reaching the board: a broken trace, a protection component at the input, or the regulator won’t start.
Current hits the limit — a short in the power circuit: a protection diode, a capacitor, a driver, the power supply chip.

Current is normal, 5 V is present, the crystal is running, but there’s no communication — the transceiver, the bus traces, water near the connector, or a corrupted program in memory; more on that in the lesson on module memory.
Communication comes and goes — cracked solder joints, corrosion, a bad contact. Check how the module reacts to light tapping and to heating.
Module or wiring

The bench gives the final answer. If the module comes online on the bench with correct power — look in the car: power, grounds, bus, connector. If it won’t communicate on the bench, while power, grounds and the bus at the connector in the car are fine — the module is faulty. It also happens that the module works on the bench but not in the car — because of a spread terminal in the harness connector.

On trucks with Weichai and Cummins engines, the engine ECU is often mounted right on the engine. Vibration, heat, frost and pressure-washing the engine hit both the connector and the board, so on these trucks inspecting the connector is the first step.
The car first: fuses, power and grounds at the connector, the bus, the terminals — and only then does the module go on the bench.
On the bench, in order: current, power on the board, 5 V, crystal, transceiver, traces, signs of moisture.
The crystal is measured with an x10 probe; on a powered board, work with a fine probe and your hand braced.
Works on the bench but not in the car — look in the wiring and the harness connector.
The scan tool can’t see any module in the car. Where do you start?
Remove the engine ECU and take it to the bench
Replace the transceiver in the engine ECU
With what they all share: fuses, power and ground at the OBD connector, the bus as a whole
When all the modules are silent, the cause is a common one. A single module rarely explains losing communication with all of them.
On the bench the current is normal, 5 V is present, there’s a sine wave on the crystal, but no CAN communication. What do you check next?
The CAN transceiver and the traces from it to the connector
The current draw, once again
Raise the supply voltage to 24 V
Replace the crystal
Power and clock are fine, which means the processor is running. The next section on the way to the bus is the transceiver and its traces.
Why is the crystal checked with an oscilloscope probe set to x10?
It shows the current better
x1 mode is prohibited for boards
So the frequency reads 10 times higher
An x1 probe loads the crystal more and can stop the oscillation
An x10 probe has lower capacitance, so it barely affects the oscillator and doesn’t distort the picture.
The module communicates on the bench but not in the car. Where should you look?
In the car: power, grounds, the bus and the harness connector terminals
A module that works on the bench tells you it’s missing something in the car: power, ground, the bus or a contact in the connector.

An output stage, or driver, is a transistor or chip through which the module switches on a load: an injector, a coil, a relay, a flap motor. It’s rated for its load’s current with a small margin. With a short in the wiring, the current rises several times over, and the driver fails: modern drivers do have short-circuit protection, but it isn’t all-powerful. After the failure, the module can’t switch on the injector or relay, or sometimes, on the contrary, keeps them on all the time.
Why outputs burn out

The control wire shorted to positive. The driver switches the wire to ground, but the wire is already connected to positive — only the wiring limits the current. Typical cases: a chafed injector harness or a wire pinched against a positive wire.
A faulty load: shorted turns in an injector, a valve or a relay coil.
The wrong load: low-impedance injectors instead of high-impedance ones, a relay with a different coil, add-on equipment on the module output.
A broken-down ignition coil, or checking for spark “to ground” without a spark tester, as in the lesson on actuators.
Mistakes during work: reversed polarity when jump-starting, welding without disconnecting the module, a test lamp on the module pins.
On trucks, the harnesses are long and run along the frame — check the places where they touch the frame and brackets.

The main rule: first find and fix the cause in the car’s wiring. A new driver on the same wiring with the same short will burn out again — sometimes within the first seconds after starting. The customer pays twice, and you lose the part, your time and their trust.
Wiring and load first
Read the codes: on which outputs the module itself sees an open, a short to ground or a short to positive. You’ll find code descriptions in the “Error codes” tab.

Turn off the ignition, disconnect the battery negative and the module connector. From the harness side, measure the resistance of the load — injector, coil, relay. Spec — per the manual; compare identical circuits with each other.
Disconnect the load and check the control wire for a short to ground and to positive: the resistance should be high. Wiggle the harness — a chafed spot often shorts only when it moves.
Find the damage and repair the wiring, as in the lesson on wiring repair. Only after that — repair or install the module.
Check the fuses first. A blown fuse in the injector or coil circuit is a clue: there was a short somewhere, and it may be exactly what finished off the module output.
Testing with a load simulator

On the bench, a load simulator is connected to the output instead of an injector or relay. If the output switches the negative, the simulator’s positive is taken from contact 87 of the main relay or from the power supply, and its negative from the module output; if the output switches the positive, the simulator is connected between the output and ground. When the output switches on, the simulator lights up.
An LED with a resistor of about 1 kΩ for 12 V (about 2.2 kΩ for 24 V) draws about 10 mA: it’s safe for any output and shows the pulses by blinking.

A small bulb tests the output under load: a “tired” driver may light an LED but not hold a bulb. The bulb’s current must be no higher than this output’s factory load; a 21 W test lamp can burn out a weak output.
The most accurate simulator is the factory load itself: a real injector or relay.

To make the module switch an output on, you need an actuator test with the scan tool or a simulated crankshaft signal on the test bench: without a rotation signal, many modules won’t switch the injectors and coils on.
Oscilloscope on the output

Probe on the module output with the factory load connected, ground clip on module ground. On a good output that switches the negative: while it’s off — supply voltage, about 12–14 V; when it switches on — a drop almost to zero; on an injector, when it switches off — an inductive spike, as in the oscilloscope lesson.
Under the factory load, the drop isn’t almost to zero but noticeably higher — a volt or more: the driver is “tired”, it runs hot and will soon fail.
No pulses, supply voltage on the output all the time — the driver is open, or the module hasn’t received the command: no rotation signal, or the test isn’t running.
The output reads almost zero all the time, even when it should be off — the driver is shorted.
The spike on one channel is noticeably lower than on the neighboring ones — check the load winding and that driver’s protection circuit.

A burnt-out driver is replaced with an identical part or a full equivalent; if the output was part of a multi-channel chip, the chip is replaced. Check the neighboring components too: resistors, protection diodes, the trace — a short often damages them as well. Soldering is covered in the lesson on soldering and replacing components, testing after repair in the lesson on handing the unit back to the customer.

A module with a shorted injector output must not be installed on the car: the injector will pour fuel continuously — flooded spark plugs, oil washed off the cylinder walls and, with a large amount of fuel, hydrolock. Gasoline direct injection and Common Rail diesel injector outputs operate at voltages from tens to hundreds of volts: LEDs and bulbs are never connected to them; they’re tested only with equipment designed for this.
A driver burns out from a short in the wiring or the wrong load — first find and fix the cause in the car.
On the bench, an output is tested with an LED and a resistor of about 1 kΩ, a small bulb whose current matches the factory load, or the factory load itself.
Oscilloscope: a good output drops almost to zero, a “tired” one doesn’t, a shorted one is always near zero.
Direct injection and Common Rail mean high voltage: bulbs and LEDs are never connected to them.
After the injector driver was replaced, the module was installed on the car, and a minute later the output burned out again. What was the main mistake?
The driver was too powerful
The short in the car’s wiring wasn’t found and fixed
The codes weren’t cleared after the repair
The short was still there — and the new driver burned out just like the old one. Wiring first, then the module.
What can you safely use to test a module output on the bench?
A 21 W test lamp
Apply 12 V directly to the output
An LED with a resistor of about 1 kΩ from positive to the output
An ohmmeter with the module powered on
An LED with a resistor draws about 10 mA — that’s safe for any output and easy to see.
Under the factory load, when the output switches on, the voltage drops not almost to zero but to a few volts. What does that mean?
That’s normal for any output
The load has burned out
A good driver pulls the output almost to zero. A few volts left over is a sign of a worn transistor.
On the bench, a good module won’t switch the injectors on. Why does this happen?
Injectors never work on the bench
The power supply is too powerful
The antistatic wrist strap is interfering
Without a crankshaft rotation signal, many modules won’t switch the injectors on
The module only injects fuel when it sees rotation. On the bench you need a scan tool test or a simulated crankshaft signal.

Water and vibration are the most common reasons a once-healthy module ends up on the bench. Corrosion eats away a trace over years, and a cracked solder joint causes a fault only over bumps or in freezing weather. Such modules can be repaired if you find all the damage and eliminate the cause.
How water gets into a module
Through a dried-out or damaged housing or connector seal.
Along the wires: water runs into the harness and wicks along the strands under the insulation all the way to the connector.
From outside: a clogged drain under the windshield, a leak into the cabin, pressure-washing the engine, and on trucks, spray with salt and de-icing chemicals.
Condensation: in winter a frozen module goes into a warm service bay, and moist air gets in through a poorly sealed housing and settles on the cold board.

With power on, moisture between pins at different voltages acts as an electrolyte: metal dissolves, and corrosion and thin conductive “bridges” grow. That’s why you must never power up a wet module “to check it” — you’ll only speed up the damage.
Inspection, cleaning and drying
Photograph the board before you start work — for the customer report.

Inspect both sides under a magnifier or microscope: green or white deposits, darkened traces, rusty connector pins, bulging or leaking electrolytic capacitors — their electrolyte causes corrosion on its own. Look from the side under chip packages: corrosion often hides there.

Clean off the deposits with isopropyl alcohol of 99% purity or higher and a soft brush. Heavy corrosion is removed with a stiff brush or a fiberglass pen, without scraping off the solder mask — the protective layer over the traces.
Leaking capacitors and parts with eaten-away leads are replaced — that’s covered in the next lesson.

An ultrasonic cleaner gets under components better than a brush, but crystals, built-in pressure and acceleration sensors and parts with membranes can be damaged by it. Ordinary ultrasonic tanks aren’t designed for flammable liquids: don’t pour alcohol into them, only a fluid permitted by the cleaner’s manual. If in doubt, clean with a brush.

Drying is done slowly and gently: with warm air at about 50–60 °C for several hours, not with a hot-air station. Moisture leaves from under the chips slowly. Power up for the first time only when the board is dry, from a bench power supply with current limiting, as in the lesson on connecting on the bench.
Restoring traces
Find the break with a continuity test. Check the vias too — the plated holes that connect the board layers: corrosion eats them from the inside.
Scrape the solder mask off the ends of the trace with a scalpel down to clean copper and tin them — coat them with a thin layer of solder.

Solder in a jumper of thin insulated wire along the shortest path. In power circuits — power, grounds, injector and coil outputs — the wire’s cross-section must be no smaller than the trace’s, otherwise it will overheat.
Secure the jumper against vibration with a drop of glue or coating, and check it: it has continuity, and there’s no short to neighboring traces.
If a trace has rotted away near the connector and you can’t see where it went, don’t connect it “by eye” — check against the car’s wiring diagram and a good board.
Vibration and cracked solder joints

Heavy components — electrolytic capacitors, chokes, power transistors, on-board relays — and the connector pins rock from vibration for years, heating up and cooling down. A ring-shaped crack forms around the lead, and the contact comes and goes. This happens especially often on trucks — Shacman, Howo, KAMAZ.
Symptom: the fault appears over bumps, when cold or when hot, and goes away by itself.
Under a magnifier you can see a thin dark ring around the lead, and the solder joint looks dull.
On the bench, with the module powered on, tap the board lightly with a plastic stick while watching the current and communication; gentle heating or cooling of the area also helps.
The repair isn’t a drop of solder on top: the old solder is removed and the lead is resoldered with flux.
Conformal coating and the root cause

During repair, the factory conformal coating is removed only where you solder. After the repair, the board is cleaned of flux, dried and coated with PCB conformal coating, keeping it off the connector contacts, the programmer pads and the sensor openings. The module is installed once the coating has dried — per the coating’s instructions. But coating is no substitute for finding the cause: replace the seal, clear the drain, seal the connector and explain to the customer where the water came from. Otherwise the module will be back within a season.
A wet module is never powered up: corrosion progresses faster under voltage.
Cleaning — with alcohol and a brush; ultrasonic — with caveats and no flammable liquids; drying — slowly and gently.
A jumper in a power circuit must be no thinner than the trace; secure it and check it for shorts.
Vibration cracks are resoldered from scratch; after the repair — conformal coating and eliminating the source of moisture.
A module from a car with a flooded interior has been brought to the bench. What must you not do first?
Photograph the board
Apply power to see whether it’s alive
Inspect the board under a magnifier
Under voltage, moisture acts as an electrolyte, and corrosion progresses faster. Inspection, cleaning and drying come first.
What’s the danger of pouring isopropyl alcohol into an ordinary ultrasonic cleaner?
None, everyone does it
Alcohol is worse at removing corrosion
The cleaner isn’t designed for flammable liquids — a fire is possible
Alcohol dissolves the copper traces
Ordinary ultrasonic cleaners aren’t meant for flammable liquids. Only use what the cleaner’s manual permits.
A jumper is used to restore an output stage’s power trace. What wire should you use?
One with a cross-section no smaller than the trace’s
The thinnest one — it’s neater
Any wire, as long as it has continuity
A high current flows through a power circuit. A thin wire will overheat and burn through.
A truck module loses communication over bumps but works on the bench. What should you look for on the board?
A bug in the module’s program
A wrong software number
Corrosion on the housing label
Ring-shaped solder cracks at heavy components and connector pins
Vibration and temperature swings crack the solder around the leads. A magnifier and light tapping on the board on the bench help you find the crack.

Almost any module repair ends with soldering: a burnt-out driver, a leaking capacitor, a crack at a lead. You can ruin a board in seconds — overheat it, tear off a pad, blow away neighboring parts. Good soldering is preparation, the right flux and patience. We covered the tools in the lesson on the workbench.
What’s on the board

SMD parts are surface-mount devices; they’re soldered onto pads with no holes. Resistors often have numbers on them: “103” means 10 followed by three zeros, that is, 10 kΩ. Capacitors usually have no markings — their values are taken from an identical good board.

Transistors and drivers come in small three-lead packages (SOT-23) or in power packages with a wide heat-sinking pad underneath (DPAK). The pad is soldered to large copper areas, so these parts are the hardest to remove.
Chips: SOIC — leads on two sides at a 1.27 mm pitch; QFP — leads on all four sides at a finer pitch, often 0.5–0.8 mm.
Replace with the same part or a full equivalent in value, package, voltage, current and temperature. Better still — automotive grade, AEC-Q qualified.
Flux, solder, temperature
Flux cleans oxides off the metal and helps the solder flow. For boards — no-clean or rosin flux gel. Soldering acid and active fluxes are no good: their residue eats away the traces.
Factory solder is often lead-free and harder to melt. A little ordinary tin-lead solder helps melt it.
A soldering iron for ordinary solder is usually set to 300–350 °C; for lead-free solder and massive leads — higher, with a thick tip. The tip stays on the lead for seconds, not tens of seconds.
Hot-air station: choose the temperature and airflow according to the station’s manual and the size of the part, starting low. Strong airflow blows away small parts.
Desoldering braid — copper braid with flux — removes excess solder. Press it down with the tip and don’t rub: it’s easy to tear off a pad.
Removing and installing
Photograph the spot and note the chip’s pin 1 mark and the polarity of the capacitor and diode.
Shield the neighboring parts — plastic connectors, electrolytic capacitors, the crystal — with Kapton tape or a foil shield.

Small parts are removed with two soldering irons, hot tweezers or a hot-air station with a narrow nozzle. SOIC and QFP — with hot air, heating all the leads evenly, or with a low-melting alloy such as Rose’s metal: it keeps the leads molten longer. Lift the part only when all the leads have melted, otherwise you’ll tear off the pads.
Clean the pads with desoldering braid and flux. Remove the low-melting alloy completely — it makes the solder joint brittle.

New part: tin one pad, place the part with tweezers and tack one lead — on a chip, two opposite corners. Check that all the leads are on their pads, solder the rest, and remove any bridges with the braid.
Wash off the flux with alcohol and check under a magnifier: each lead has a smooth, shiny fillet — a smooth transition of solder onto the pad — with no bridges or solder balls.
This is especially true for soldering: a tip free of carbon buildup, a clean hot-air nozzle, fresh flux. You can’t solder well with a dirty tip, even on an expensive station.
How not to overheat the board
A multilayer board with thick copper soaks up heat. Bottom preheating — a heater under the board — evens out the temperature, so you need less heat from above.
Signs of overheating: a darkened or blistered board, lifted pads, shifted neighboring parts. Stop and let the board cool down.
A board that has been in water is dried first, as in the lesson on moisture: with sudden heating, moisture can delaminate the board and the components.
Don’t hold the hot air on one spot longer than necessary, and don’t heat a plastic connector — it will warp.
BGA is a separate story

On a BGA, the leads are solder balls under the chip package; you can’t see them or check them with a magnifier. Replacing one requires a station with bottom preheating and a thermal profile — a set heating and cooling curve — stencils for reballing, experience, and an X-ray for inspection. A BGA processor stores the program: after replacement it has to be programmed, and without a memory backup, which is covered in the next lesson, the module can’t be restored. Don’t take on BGA until you’re confidently replacing QFP chips, and don’t believe videos that make it look easy.

Flux fumes are harmful — work with fume extraction. After working with lead-containing solder, wash your hands and don’t eat at your workbench. Keep the soldering iron only in its stand, and don’t unplug the hot-air station right away: the station has to cool the handpiece down in cool-down mode.
For boards — no-clean or rosin flux; never acid.
A part is removed when all the leads have melted; pads are cleaned with braid, not rubbed.
Neighboring parts are shielded with Kapton or foil; bottom preheating reduces the heat needed from above.
BGA is a job for proper equipment and experience; the processor is programmed after replacement.
Which flux must never be used to solder a module board?
No-clean flux gel
Rosin flux
Soldering acid
Acid residue keeps eating away at the traces and leads. Boards need no-clean or rosin fluxes.
A QFP chip is being removed with hot air. When can you lift it with tweezers?
When all the leads have melted
Exactly 10 seconds after you start heating
When the flux starts smoking
When the leads on one side have melted
If some leads are still holding, the pads will tear off with them. Lift the chip only after everything has fully melted.
An SMD resistor is marked “103”. What is its value?
10 kΩ
The first two digits are the value, the third is the number of zeros: 10 and three zeros — 10,000 Ω.
Why is a BGA processor replaced only when you have the equipment and a backup?
BGA is soldered with an ordinary soldering iron, it just takes longer
A new processor already contains this car’s program
A backup is only needed for a used processor
The balls under the package can’t be seen — you need a station with preheating and experience, and after replacement the processor has to be programmed
BGA soldering can’t be checked by eye, and it needs precise heating. The program is stored in the processor, so without a memory backup the module can’t be restored.

A module’s memory holds not just the program but also data specific to this car: the VIN, the immobilizer pairing, adaptations. Lose them, and you turn a repaired module into one from somebody else’s car. So there’s one rule: before soldering, flashing or changing anything on the board, make a backup.
What is stored where

Flash is program memory. It holds the module’s program and calibrations — the tables it uses to control the engine: fuel delivery, ignition timing, sensor thresholds. It’s usually built into the processor, sometimes it’s a separate chip.
EEPROM is memory for data that changes: the VIN, immobilizer data, adaptations, fault codes, equipment coding, counters. Sometimes it’s a small separate chip, sometimes part of the processor.
The bootloader is a small service program that runs first and can accept a new program. Modules are flashed through it.
Backup first
Read all the memory areas your equipment supports: flash, EEPROM and the rest. The program alone isn’t enough — it’s the EEPROM that’s unique to the car.
Read it again and compare the files. If they match, the read is reliable.
Check the file: its size equals the memory capacity, and it isn’t all FF or 00 inside. A file like that means the memory wasn’t read or is empty.
Label the files — make, VIN, module numbers, date — and store them in two places. This is customer data; it isn’t shared with outsiders.
Only after that, start the repair.
How memory is read
Via diagnostics — through the diagnostic connector or the diagnostic line, without opening the module. Convenient, but not all modules and not all areas can be read this way.

On the bench via the bootloader — the module is connected to a bench power supply and to the adapter over CAN or K-line, as in the lesson on connecting on the bench. Sometimes entering the bootloader requires a service contact on the board. This usually gives a more complete read.

With a programmer on the board — to the processor’s debug interface (BDM, JTAG and the like) or directly to the memory chip: on the board contacts, with a clip, sometimes by removing the chip. The most complete method, but it requires a precise connection.
How to connect and what to press — per the manual for your programmer or tool. Power must be stable: from a bench power supply only, not from a battery charger or a run-down battery.
Checksums

A checksum is a number calculated from the memory contents and stored alongside them. At startup, the module recalculates it and compares. If it doesn’t match, the module considers the program corrupted: it won’t start, goes into limp mode or waits to be flashed. That’s why, after writing, you always verify what was written against the file — almost every programmer has a verify function. Write only your own verified file or an official update from the manufacturer. Someone else’s file from the internet may be from a different module version and contain another car’s data.
What we don’t do
We touch immobilizer data and the VIN only when there are documents for the car: the registration certificate and the owner’s ID or a power of attorney. And some jobs we always refuse.
Disabling the immobilizer, so-called “immo off”: it makes the car easier to steal.
Changing the mileage: it deceives the next buyer.
Software removal of EGR, the diesel particulate filter (DPF), AdBlue/SCR: the car emits more harmful substances, doesn’t meet environmental requirements and may fail its vehicle inspection.

Such modifications break the law and the requirements for the vehicle, and the person who made them is responsible for them. If the engine fails, there’s an accident or the car is stolen because a system was disabled, the questions will go to the technician. Refuse directly and offer to find and fix the real cause — a faulty sensor, valve or wiring.
Flash holds the program and calibrations, EEPROM holds this car’s data: the VIN, immobilizer, adaptations.
Before any repair — a backup of all areas, read twice and compared.
After writing — verify what was written; we write only our own file or an official update.
Immobilizer and VIN — only with documents; immo off, mileage changes, EGR, DPF, AdBlue removal — we don’t do these.
What is unique to a specific car and is most often stored in EEPROM?
The VIN, immobilizer data and adaptations
Fuel delivery tables
The bootloader
The program and calibrations are the same in modules of the same version. But the VIN, the immobilizer pairing and the adaptations are data specific to this car.
You read a module’s flash twice on the bench, and the files differ. What does that mean?
You can use either of the two files
You should write one of them back right away
The read is unreliable: check the connection and power and read it again
That always happens
The program in memory doesn’t change between reads. Different files point to a bad contact, a voltage sag or a communication glitch.
After writing, the module won’t start and is waiting to be flashed. What is most likely?
Old fault codes are still in the module
The checksum didn’t match or the write was interrupted
The memory was read for too long before writing
The module checks the checksum at startup. It won’t run a corrupted or incompletely written file.
A customer asks you to “remove AdBlue in software” so they don’t have to buy the fluid. What do you do?
Do it if there are documents for the car
Do it, but don’t put it on the work order
Disconnect only the level sensor
Refuse and offer to find and fix the fault in the system
Removing emissions systems in software breaks the law and the requirements for the vehicle, and the technician is responsible for it. We find and fix the cause.

Sometimes a module can’t be repaired: the board is burnt out, the processor is damaged, corrosion has eaten too much. Then it gets replaced. But a control module isn’t a light bulb: putting in another one and starting the car right away rarely works.
First make sure the module is faulty

Many “dead” modules are actually fine: they’re short of power, ground or communication. Check this at the connector, as in the lessons on ECU power and grounds and on a module that won’t communicate. And find out what killed the old module: if the cause is a short in the wiring, the new one will burn out the same way, as in the lesson on output stages.
New, remanufactured or used
New — from the manufacturer or a dealer. The most predictable and the most expensive. It often comes without a program or with a basic one, and needs flashing and pairing at the dealer.
Remanufactured — repaired by a specialist shop, with its own warranty. It’s important that it’s prepared for your car, not sent “as is”.
Used — from a salvage yard. The cheapest of all, but its history is unknown: it may have been flooded, overheated or already repaired. And it contains another car’s data.
What has to match
The module number — the hardware number on the housing label. Modules that look identical but have different numbers are different inside.
The software number and version. With the same hardware, the program may be for a different engine, power output, transmission or emissions class.
Equipment: manual or automatic, air conditioning, cruise control and other options the module has to “know” about.

Market. For right-hand-drive Japanese cars, a module from the same model for a different market may have a different program and immobilizer. On Shacman, Howo and FAW, a module from the same Weichai or Cummins engine but with a different power rating also has a different program.
What to transfer and adapt

If the old module still communicates, before replacing it record its coding and parameters with the scan tool and save a memory backup, as in the lesson on module memory. They make it easier to set up the new one.

Immobilizer pairing: the module has to recognize this car’s keys and immobilizer unit. It’s done at the dealer or following the manufacturer’s procedure, with the right equipment and only with the car’s documents; a PIN code and all the keys are often needed.
VIN and coding — writing the car’s data and its equipment into the module following the manufacturer’s procedure.

Adaptations — teaching the module to the car: throttle position, idle, and on some cars the crankshaft sensor. On Common Rail diesels — injector codes: each injector has its own correction code, which is entered into the module with the scan tool.
Updating the program to the current version, if the manufacturer has released one.
Clear the codes in all modules and check the car — that’s covered in the next lesson.
Why “just putting in a used one” doesn’t work
The immobilizer doesn’t recognize the keys: the engine won’t start or stalls after a second or two.
A program for a different engine, transmission or market: fault codes, poor running, limp mode.
No injector codes and adaptations: rough running, smoke, fault codes.
On some makes, a used module can’t be paired using the standard procedure — only a new one will do. Check this before buying.

We don’t pair modules and keys without documents for the car, and we don’t “disable the immobilizer so a used module will work”. The immobilizer is anti-theft protection, and jobs like that help car thieves. No documents — we don’t start the job.
Before replacing, make sure the module is faulty, and fix the cause in the wiring.
The module number, program, equipment and market must match.
After installation — immobilizer pairing at the dealer or following the manufacturer’s procedure, coding, adaptations, injector codes.
A used module often won’t work without setup; pairing — only with documents.
A used module from the same model was installed in the car: the starter cranks, the engine starts and immediately stalls. What is most likely?
The injectors are faulty
The module isn’t paired with this car’s immobilizer
A used module contains another car’s data, and it doesn’t recognize the keys. Pairing is done at the dealer or following the manufacturer’s procedure, with documents.
Where do you start before ordering a replacement module?
Make sure the old module is faulty and find out why it failed
Order the cheapest used module right away
Clear the codes and wait
Often a “dead” module is just short of power or ground. And if the old one burned out because of the wiring, the new one will burn out the same way.
The modules look the same from outside and the connector fits, but the software number is different. What does that mean?
Nothing, the connector is what matters
The software number only affects the label
The module just needs a reboot
The program may be for a different engine, transmission or market — without preparation, the module may not be compatible
Identical hardware doesn’t mean an identical program. The numbers, equipment and market have to match.
After a module replacement on a Common Rail diesel, the engine runs rough and smokes. What might have been forgotten?
Writing the VIN into the radio
Entering the injector codes and performing the adaptations
Each injector has its own correction code. The new module doesn’t know it until the code is entered with the scan tool.

A module repair isn’t finished when the soldering iron cools down. It’s finished by a bench test, a test in the car and a clear report for the customer. Better to catch an intermittent fault at your shop than a week later out on the highway.
Bench test
Current draw — the same as a good module of this type, with no jumps. How to evaluate it — in the lesson on connecting on the bench.
Communication with the scan tool and identification: the module and software numbers are the same as before the repair.
Memory: compare it with the backup. The data shouldn’t have changed unless you restored it.
Outputs — with a load simulator and an oscilloscope, as in the lesson on output stages.

Extended run: the module runs under power for a long time — for intermittent faults, hours, not minutes. After a repair for moisture or cracked solder joints, tap lightly on the housing and warm it up moderately: the fault shouldn’t come back.
Testing in the car
Installation: ignition off, battery negative disconnected, connector clean, seal in place, latch closed, module secured.
Turn on the ignition and read the codes in all modules. While the module was removed, other modules often log communication codes for it: write them down, clear them and check again.
Starting: the immobilizer allows the start, and the engine starts without long cranking.
Live data: temperature, rpm, throttle position and pressures are plausible; system voltage with the engine running is 13.5–14.5 V.
Load: turn on the headlights, fans and A/C, and check the outputs you repaired. Then a test drive — under the conditions in which the fault used to show up.
After the drive, read the codes in all modules once more.

If the module used to fail in the cold, a check in a warm service bay isn’t enough. Leave the car outside overnight and check the cold start in the morning: in winter this quickly shows whether everything is in order.

Don’t look at the scan tool while driving: the driver watches the road, and a helper watches the data or the scan tool records it. And don’t disconnect the battery with the engine running “to test the alternator” — the voltage spike can damage the module you’ve just repaired.
Customer report
The complaint in the customer’s words and what you found: what fault was on the board and which measurements confirmed it.
Photos of the board before and after: corrosion, a burnt-out driver, restored traces.
What was replaced and repaired.
The cause in the car and what was done about it: a short in the wiring, water through a seal, a clogged drain. If the customer declined to fix the cause, write that down.
Recommendations and warranty terms.
Warranty

You set the warranty period yourself and write it on the work order. It covers the repair performed and the parts installed. Agree in advance on what voids it: water getting in again, a cause in the wiring that the customer chose not to fix, the module being opened by other technicians, flashing or modifying the program by third parties, welding on the body without disconnecting the modules. Put your own mark on the housing — a sticker or a marking — so you can recognize your module.
What to record for yourself
The car, the VIN, the module and software numbers.
The complaint, what you found and where: the component reference designators — the labels on the board like R12 or C5 — what you replaced them with and where you bought it.
Current draw before and after the repair, test results.
Backup files — labeled, in two places.
Handover date and warranty period. After a year, this log will become your knowledge base on modules, as in the lesson on the profession.
On the bench: current, communication and numbers, memory compared with the backup, outputs, extended run.
In the car: codes in all modules, starting, live data, load and a test drive, codes once more.
Customer report — with photos of the board before and after, the cause in the car and the warranty terms.
For yourself — the numbers, what was replaced, the measurements, memory backups and the warranty date.

Reflash it just in case

Apply a second layer of coating to the board
Faults after moisture and cracked solder joints are often intermittent. They’re caught with a long run, light tapping and heating.

Replace the modules with the codes
Ignore them and hand the car over
While the module was disconnected, its neighbors logged that they couldn’t see it. If the codes don’t come back after clearing, everything is fine.

Only the amount due
The complaint, what was found, photos of the board before and after, what was replaced, the cause in the car and the warranty terms
The name of the software you used
Photos and a short explanation show what the customer is paying for and prevent disputes.
The customer declined to repair the wiring that caused the driver to burn out. What should you do?
Don’t write anything down

Record the customer’s refusal on the work order, and that in this case the warranty doesn’t cover this output

In the lesson on connecting a module on the bench, we wired the module up as a one-off. When modules come in every week, a test bench is more convenient — a permanent panel where the power, loads and diagnostic line are already assembled, labeled and checked. For a new module, only the adapter harness changes. Fewer wires on the bench means less chance of mixing up a pin.
Bench power
A bench power supply with current limiting, up to 30 V — enough for both 12 V passenger car modules and 24 V truck modules.

A fuse right after the power supply positive is a second line of protection: if you forget to set the current limit, the fuse blows, not a trace on the board. Its rating should be a little above the combined current of the module and the loads.

An ammeter in the common supply circuit. A power supply’s ammeter often shows the current only roughly, and a sleeping module draws just a few milliamps — you need an instrument that can read both milliamps and amps.
A “+30” switch — constant positive — and a “+15” switch — “ignition”: with it you wake the module up and put it to sleep without touching the wires.

The main relay sits in a socket so you can swap it to match the voltage: a 12 V relay will burn out on a 24 V system, and a 24 V relay may not switch on from 12 V. A “module / manual” switch: either the module itself switches the relay on, as in the lesson on connecting on the bench, or the relay comes on together with “+15” — for checking the bench.
Loads, communication and signals
Load simulators — in separate rows for 12 and 24 V: LEDs with a resistor of about 1 kΩ for 12 V and about 2.2 kΩ for 24 V, and small bulbs for each voltage, as in the lesson on output stages.

An OBD-II socket for the scan tool adapter — with CAN and K-line wired to it as in the lesson on connecting on the bench — and a 120 Ω resistor between CAN-H and CAN-L through a switch, in case the module doesn’t have its own. The adapter is powered from the bench: check its manual to see whether it can handle 24 V.

A crankshaft and camshaft signal simulator — a signal generator or a ready-made simulator. Without a rotation signal, many modules won’t switch the injectors and coils on. The signal type — inductive or Hall — and the number of teeth are set to match the engine, following the simulator’s manual.
An oscilloscope — connected to the module outputs and the simulator signal, with the ground clip on the bench’s common ground.
How to build it
Draw a diagram of the bench and keep it nearby. Make any change on the diagram first, then in the wiring.

The base is a panel made of an insulating material, such as phenolic laminate. Wires: positive — red, grounds — black, signal wires — other colors; power and grounds thicker, signals thinner. Connections — soldered or crimped with heat shrink, no twisted splices.

Bring all grounds to a single point at the power supply negative, together with the adapter and oscilloscope grounds. That way all the instruments share a common “zero”, and load current doesn’t flow through the signal ground.

Jacks — for banana plugs, each with a permanent label: “+30”, “+15”, “87”, “Relay control”, “Ground”, “CAN-H”, “CAN-L”, “Output 1” and so on. Label the relay voltage on its socket and the “12 V” and “24 V” load rows in large letters.
Adapter harnesses for different modules
The best one is a mating connector from a donor, from a salvage yard, with a piece of harness: the wires you need are brought out to plugs, each with a tag showing its function.
No connector — an adapter with thin clips sized to the pin, or a terminal block. A thick alligator clip will short adjacent pins, and a socket of the wrong size will spread the pin.
Connect only what’s needed: power feeds, grounds, the diagnostic line and the pins under test.

Store each adapter harness in its own bag or box compartment with a tag — the module and its number, 12 or 24 V, the pinout source, the date it was checked — and with a printout of the connection diagram. Inspect the wires and terminals before use.

A mistake in an adapter harness gets repeated on every module you connect to it. So check a new adapter harness for continuity wire by wire, compare it with the pinout, and make sure adjacent wires aren’t shorted to each other.
Checking the bench before the first module

The module and the scan tool adapter are not connected; the adapter harness is. Power supply set to 13.5 V and 0.5 A, switches off. Turn on the output: the current is almost zero, and if the panel has indicator LEDs, write down their current.

Switch on “+30”. Put the multimeter’s black probe on the “Ground” jack and, with a fine probe from the wire side, touch the red one to the terminals of the mating connector where the module pins will go. “+30” should read 13.5 V, “+15” and “87” — 0 V.
Switch on “+15”: “+15” reads 13.5 V. Set the relay switch to “manual”: the relay clicks, and “87” reads 13.5 V.
The ground, CAN, K-line, output and signal input terminals should read 0 V. If positive turns up on the wrong terminal, find the mistake and don’t connect the module.
Turn off the power and check continuity: adapter harness grounds to the power supply negative — almost 0 Ω; between CAN-H and CAN-L — about 120 Ω with the resistor switched in.
Check a truck adapter harness the same way at 24 V, with a 24 V relay and loads. Record the results in the bench log. The first module goes on with a current limit of 0.5–1 A.

Connect and disconnect an adapter harness to the module only with the power supply output turned off. Before a truck module, check that the relay and loads are for 24 V; before a passenger car module, check that the voltage is back at 13.5 V. Never bring 220 V mains into a homemade panel. Don’t connect direct injection and Common Rail injector outputs to the bench loads: they run at tens and hundreds of volts.
A test bench: a power supply with current limiting, a fuse, an ammeter, “+30” and “+15” switches, a main relay, labeled jacks, loads, a diagnostic line, a crankshaft simulator and an oscilloscope.
The relay and loads — separate for 12 and 24 V and labeled in large letters; all grounds to a single point.
Each module gets its own adapter harness, built to a verified pinout, with tags and a connection diagram.
Before the first module, the bench is checked without a module: voltages at the terminals, grounds, and 120 Ω between CAN-H and CAN-L.
Why does the bench need a fuse right after the power supply if there’s current limiting?
So the module wakes up faster
It’s a second line of protection: if you forget to set the limit, the fuse blows, not a trace on the board
The scan tool won’t work without a fuse
A person sets the current limit, and people make mistakes. The fuse protects the board against that mistake.
The bench has a 12 V main relay, and a 24 V truck module has come in. What should you do?
Supply 12 V so the relay doesn’t burn out
Nothing, all relays are the same
Remove the relay altogether
Fit a relay with a 24 V coil and connect 24 V loads
A 12 V relay will burn out on 24 V, and a truck module may not wake up on 12 V. The relay and loads are changed to match the module’s voltage.
How do you check a new bench before the first module?
Without a module: voltages at the adapter harness terminals, continuity of the grounds, and 120 Ω between CAN-H and CAN-L
Connect a module right away and see whether it wakes up
Raise the current limit to the maximum and switch everything on at once
A multimeter will reveal a mistake in the bench or an adapter harness in a few minutes. On a module, the same mistake can cost you the board.
Why is a thick alligator clip on a module connector pin dangerous?
It doesn’t hold the wire well
It heats up from the current
It can short adjacent pins and damage the pin
Connector pins sit close together. You need a thin clip sized to the pin, or a mating connector from a donor.

Finding a burnt-out part isn’t enough — you need to figure out what part it is, test it and find a replacement. SMD parts carry almost no markings, instruments read differently on the board than on a removed part, and there are plenty of counterfeits for sale. Let’s look at how to deal with this, and at a repair technician’s main technique — the comparison method.
SMD markings

Resistors. “103” is 10 kΩ, as in the lesson on soldering. Four digits are more precise: “1002” is 100 followed by two zeros — also 10 kΩ. The letter R is the decimal point: “4R7” is 4.7 Ω. Two digits and a letter are an EIA-96 code, read from a table: “01C” is 10 kΩ. “0” is a 0 Ω jumper.
Small resistors and ceramic capacitors are often unmarked, and capacitance can’t be measured accurately on the board: take the value from a good board of the same model.
Polarity: on a diode the stripe is the cathode, on an aluminum electrolytic the marking is negative, but on a tantalum capacitor the stripe is positive.

Transistors and diodes in small packages such as SOT-23 carry not a part name but a 2–4 character code, and different manufacturers sometimes use the same code for different parts. Look it up in an SMD code reference by code and package together, and check against the schematic and the same part on a good or donor board.
Datasheets and choosing an equivalent

A datasheet is the part manufacturer’s document — get it from the manufacturer’s website. The key points in it: maximum voltage and current, power dissipation — which depends heavily on the package — the package and the pin assignment: different parts in the same package can have different pinouts.

For a field-effect transistor, a MOSFET, it’s the channel on-resistance: the lower it is, the less it heats up. Check at what gate voltage it’s specified: if only at 10 V, and the module’s circuit provides 5 V, the transistor won’t turn fully on and will run hot.

Temperature — for a vehicle, from −40 °C, with margin at the top end. Automotive grade means AEC-Q qualification: AEC-Q100 for chips, AEC-Q101 for transistors and diodes, AEC-Q200 for resistors and capacitors.

An equivalent must be no worse in all the key parameters at once: the same package and pinout, voltage and current no lower, channel resistance no higher, the same turn-on threshold, a temperature range no narrower. “More powerful” isn’t always better: a high-power transistor has higher gate capacitance, and the module’s driver may switch it on less well.
How to test a part

Diode test mode: the meter passes a small current and shows the voltage drop across the junction. A good silicon diode reads about 0.5–0.7 V in one direction and OL, “infinity”, in the other; a Schottky diode — about 0.2–0.4 V. Almost 0 in both directions — shorted; OL in both — open.

A bipolar transistor tests like two diodes: base to emitter and base to collector. A MOSFET has a built-in diode between source and drain, and the gate doesn’t conduct to anything. The meter can charge the gate and partially turn the transistor on — short the gate to the source before measuring again.

On the board the readings are lower: other circuits are in parallel with the part, and on capacitors the readings “drift”. Consider a part on the board faulty only by comparison with a good board, or after desoldering at least one of its leads.

An electrolytic with a bulging top or a leak is replaced without measuring. With age its ESR — equivalent series resistance — rises, and it smooths ripple less well. ESR is measured with an ESR meter; many of them work right on the board.

A ceramic capacitor cracks from vibration and overheating and can short. A short or leakage — when the capacitor conducts direct current — shows up as a supply line that reads almost a dead short to ground, or noticeably lower than on a good board: check the capacitors on that line.

The regulator — powered up on the bench: a steady 5 V or 3.3 V at the output, as in the lesson on a module that won’t communicate. If the output is low, compare the output-to-ground resistance with a good board: if it’s much lower, the culprit isn’t the regulator but whatever is loading it.

The crystal — only with an oscilloscope on a running module, with an x10 probe, as in the same lesson. Replacement — a crystal of the same frequency, which is usually marked on the package, and in the same package.

This matters especially for measurements: intact probes and leads, a fresh battery in the meter. Otherwise the difference in the readings will come from the meter, not the part — and in the comparison method, the difference is exactly what counts.

The main technique when there’s no schematic for the module. Take two modules of the same model — with the same module number on the label: a good one and a suspect one. Inside they have identical circuits, so measurements on the same pins should match. Where the numbers differ noticeably, that’s where the damaged input circuit, driver, transceiver or broken trace is.
Both modules unpowered, nothing plugged into the connectors. Multimeter in diode test or resistance mode — the same meter for both modules.
Black probe on the module’s ground pin, red on each connector pin in turn. Record it in a table: pin, good, suspect.
Swap the probes and go through again: a fault often shows up in only one direction. On pins with capacitors, wait until the reading stops climbing.

Compare. A spread like 0.52 and 0.51 V is normal. A hypothetical example of a fault: 0.48 V on the good one, 0.02 V on the suspect one — the pin is almost shorted to ground: a protection component, the transceiver or the driver is shorted. OL where the good one shows a reading — a broken trace, via or resistor.
Found the pin? Follow the trace from it and keep comparing points on the boards relative to ground the same way until you find the part that differs.
Save the good module’s table in your log — next time the reference will be at hand even without a second module.
Where to get parts
Donor boards of the same model: the part is sure to fit, but it has also served its time. Take it from an undamaged area, remove it without overheating and test it.
New parts — from trusted suppliers: authorized distributors and stores that list the part’s manufacturer.

Beware of counterfeits: a remarked part with worse specs, or a different part altogether in the same package. Red flags: a price that’s too low, different markings within one batch, a package that doesn’t match the datasheet. Test a new part before soldering and compare it with the original — a counterfeit driver may burn out after the car is already back with the customer.
An SMD code is a hint, not a part name: search by code and package and check against the schematic and a good board.
An equivalent must be no worse in all the key parameters: package and pinout, voltage, current, channel resistance, threshold, temperature — preferably AEC-Q.
A good diode reads about 0.5–0.7 V in one direction and OL in the other; on the board the readings are lower because of parallel circuits.
The comparison method: two identical unpowered modules, one meter and one mode, every pin relative to ground — a difference points to the faulty circuit.
An SMD resistor is marked “4R7”. What is its value?
4.7 kΩ
The letter R stands in place of the decimal point: “4R7” is 4.7 Ω.
A desoldered diode in diode test mode reads almost 0 in both directions. What does that mean?
The diode is shorted
The diode is fine
The diode is open
The meter is showing current
A good diode conducts in one direction — about 0.5–0.7 V — and shows OL in reverse. Almost 0 in both directions means it’s shorted.
When replacing a MOSFET, why does it matter at what gate voltage the channel on-resistance is specified?
It determines the color of the package
It only matters for imported modules
To read the SMD code correctly
If the module’s circuit applies less to the gate, the transistor won’t turn fully on and will run hot
Channel resistance is specified for a particular gate voltage. At a lower voltage, the transistor isn’t fully on and overheats.
How does the comparison method work?
One module is measured twice and the results are compared
On two unpowered modules of the same model, the pins are measured relative to ground with one meter, looking for differences
The module is compared with any module from another car

Identical modules have identical circuits, so the readings match too. A noticeable difference on a pin points to a damaged circuit.

Modules in trucks, heavy equipment and farm machinery are built the same way as passenger car ones: power supply, processor, inputs, drivers, transceivers. But they have a harder life: 24 V, long harnesses along the frame, vibration, dust, washing and frost. Here, that mainly means Shacman, Howo, FAW and KAMAZ. And these modules end up on the bench more often not from old age but because of mistakes made while working on the vehicle.
The 24 V system and modules

As in the lesson on trucks and the 24 V system: two 12 V batteries are connected in series, the negative of the pair goes to the frame through the battery master switch, and the alternator holds about 28 V. The modules are designed for this system — a passenger car module or a 12 V device will burn out on it. The master switch is never turned off with the engine running: the voltage spike hits the modules. After the engine stops, wait the time given in the manual — the modules and the AdBlue system need to finish their work.
Why modules fail

Electric welding on the frame without preparation. The welding current looks for a path through the frame, the wiring and the module grounds, and voltage spikes punch through inputs, transceivers and drivers.
Overvoltage: a charger-starter in “start” mode, jump-starting from a vehicle with a different system voltage, mixing up 12 and 24 V. How to jump-start correctly — in the lesson on the 24 V system.
Reverse polarity — terminals mixed up when replacing a battery or jump-starting. Modules don’t always have protection against it, and what protection there is doesn’t cover everything.
Pressure washing: the jet forces water past the seals into the connectors and housings of the modules on the engine and frame. Never aim the jet at modules and connectors.

Vibration: cracked solder at heavy components and connector pins, as in the lesson on moisture and vibration, and a harness chafed through against the frame — which means shorts that burn out outputs.
Moisture and dust in connectors. Steppe and quarry dust mixed with water turns into mud that conducts current and corrodes the contacts. Seals and blanking plugs in unused cavities must be in place.

Frosts down to −30…−40 °C: connector plastic and seals harden and crack, during cranking with weak batteries the voltage sags and the module resets, and in a warm service bay condensation forms on a cold board.
Welding on the frame: by the book
Find the welding preparation procedure in the vehicle manufacturer’s documentation — it differs between makes — and follow exactly that. It usually includes the steps listed below.
Turn off the ignition and wait for the modules to go to sleep. Turn off the master switch and disconnect the batteries — which terminals and in what order is given in the instructions.
Unplug the connectors of the modules listed in the instructions — first of all, those closest to the welding spot.
Attach the welder’s ground clamp to the part being welded, as close to the weld as possible, on clean bare metal. The current must not flow through modules, bearings, leaf springs or harnesses.
Don’t lay the welding cables along harnesses, and shield harnesses and connectors near the weld from spatter and heat.
After welding — connectors back in until they click, then the batteries, the master switch and a code check in all modules.

A welder ground clamp at the other end of the frame or on a module housing is a common reason modules in several systems burn out at once. And welding near the fuel tank, fuel lines and wiring is also a fire risk: follow welding safety rules and keep a fire extinguisher nearby.
Types of modules

Engine ECU. On Common Rail diesels it controls the injectors and fuel pressure. On Weichai and Cummins engines it’s often mounted right on the engine — vibration, heat and washing, as in the lesson on a module that won’t communicate. Common Rail injector outputs operate at high voltage; they’re tested only with equipment designed for this.

Transmission module — on automated manual transmissions, often mounted right on the transmission. After a repair or replacement, the transmission may need a relearn following the manufacturer’s procedure.

ABS and EBS — braking system modules: ABS keeps the wheels from locking, EBS is electronic brake control. The modulators are mounted on the frame near the wheels and take water, salt and dirt. This is a safety system: after repair — a code check and a brake check following the manufacturer’s procedure.

AdBlue module — a dosing pump with its own control unit, sensors and heater. It gets repaired and restored to working order: power, grounds, connectors, heating, fluid quality. More in the “AdBlue” section.

We don’t touch the tachograph or the speed limiter: we don’t repair, reprogram or disable them. Only workshops authorized to do so work on them. AdBlue, EGR and the particulate filter — repair only: we don’t do removal, “emulators” or software disabling, as in the lesson on module memory. It’s a legal requirement and a matter of road safety, and the technician is responsible for such work.
Heavy equipment and farm machinery

Excavators, loaders, tractors and combines have, besides the engine ECU, hydraulics and transmission modules and a cab monitor — a display with fault codes, engine hours and settings. The modules communicate over a CAN bus, often using the same J1939 standard as trucks. If the monitor goes dark or communication with a module drops out, check power, grounds and the bus, as in the lesson on a module that won’t communicate. Pinouts and procedures — only from the equipment manufacturer’s documentation. Seasonal machinery sits for months in a field or under a shelter: before the season, inspect the connectors — you can find dust, water and signs of rodents there.

The bench’s main relay — with a 24 V coil, as in the lesson on the test bench.

Check the fuses first. On a truck, the engine, ABS and AdBlue modules have their own fuses and relays — check them and the battery master switch before you remove a module from the frame.
Truck modules are designed for 24 V; the master switch is never turned off with the engine running.

The scan tool is a diagnostician’s main instrument, but scan tools vary a lot. One reads only engine codes, another works with every module in the car, and a third can even change a module’s software. Let’s look at what each one can do and how to connect properly. We covered how the OBD-II connector and protocols work in the lesson on the scan tool and live data; here it’s about choosing equipment and the working procedure.
Three classes of equipment

An ELM327 adapter with an app. A small “dongle” that plugs into the OBD-II connector plus a program on a phone or laptop, connected via Bluetooth, Wi-Fi or a cable. It handles the generic OBD-II set: engine codes, freeze frame, readiness monitors, basic live data. Some apps know particular makes and read other modules, but only with a good-quality adapter.

A multi-brand scan tool, such as a Launch. It works with modules from many makes: engine, transmission, ABS, airbags, body, climate control. It shows factory parameters that aren’t in generic OBD-II, runs actuator tests, adaptations and service resets, and can do some coding. Exactly what’s available depends on the make, the model and the software updates.

Dealer software is the factory software for one make, such as Techstream for Toyota or GDS for Hyundai and Kia. It works through the original interface or one compatible with the J2534 (PassThru) standard. It can do everything the factory provided for: full coding, module software updates, learning new parts. You need a license, a suitable interface and sometimes online access to the manufacturer’s server.
Why an ELM327 “doesn’t see” some modules

The ELM327 is a translator chip between the car’s protocol and the program. The OBD-II standard requires the car to provide only emissions-related data under the common rules: the engine and sometimes the transmission. The other modules speak the manufacturer’s “language”: their own addresses, commands and decoding. The program has to know this language, and the adapter has to be able to pass it on. So modules “go missing” for several reasons:
The program doesn’t know the make. It reads generic OBD-II, but it doesn’t have the factory commands for ABS, airbags or the body.

The module is on a different line. On many cars, some modules sit on a separate CAN bus or on a K-line routed to other pins of the connector. A simple adapter is connected only to the main pins and can’t “reach” them.

A clone with stripped-down firmware. Genuine chips are expensive, so most cheap adapters are copies. Some commands and protocols don’t work on them or work with errors. The version number on the case guarantees nothing.
Weak hardware. A slow processor and poor power protection: the connection drops halfway through, and the adapter can burn out from a voltage spike.
Connecting step by step
Find the connector: 16 pins, trapezoid-shaped, usually under the dash on the driver’s side near the steering column, sometimes behind a cover.

Find out the system voltage. Passenger cars are 12 V. Trucks and heavy equipment — Shacman, Howo, FAW, KAMAZ — are 24 V. Connect only a scan tool or adapter rated for 24 V to them: a 12-volt one can burn out. Truck connectors vary — more on this in the lesson on trucks.
Switch the ignition on. For codes and most data you don’t need to start the engine; if the scan tool asks you to start the engine, start it.
Select the make, model, year and engine, or identify the car by VIN. A wrong selection is a common cause of “no communication” and incorrect parameters.

When you’re done, exit the program, switch the ignition off and only then unplug the adapter. Don’t leave a wireless adapter in the connector when the car is parked: pin 16 has constant positive, and the adapter slowly drains the battery.
Power during long sessions

With the ignition on and the engine off, the modules, the heater blower and the pumps draw current, and the battery runs down. While you’re reading codes, that’s no big deal. But adaptations, software updates and long diagnostics take tens of minutes. Connect a battery maintainer or a power supply that holds a steady voltage. A sagging battery causes false codes in many modules at once, and a voltage dip while software is being written can ruin the module. Hooking up jumper cables to another car is a poor substitute: the voltage jumps when the donor car revs, and there are spikes when the cables are connected and disconnected.

Don’t clear codes or run tests while driving. A test takes control of a component away from the module, and when codes are cleared the module resets some of its data — on the road this can end in a jerk, a stalled engine or a disabled system. All of this is done while parked, with the parking brake on, usually with the ignition on and the engine off — or under the conditions the scan tool specifies. Route the cable and adapter so they can’t get under the pedals.
ELM327 with an app — engine codes and data; a multi-brand scan tool — all modules, tests and adaptations; dealer software — everything for its own make.
A cheap ELM327 clone often doesn’t see the make-specific modules and drops the connection.
Passenger cars are 12 V, trucks and heavy equipment are 24 V: the adapter must be rated for 24 V.
Long sessions — with a battery maintainer; clear codes and run tests only while parked.

A multi-brand scan tool or dealer software

Generic OBD-II covers the engine and emissions. ABS and airbag modules and actuator tests are make-specific functions, provided by multi-brand scan tools and dealer software.

The ABS and body modules are faulty
You need to clear the engine codes first
Generic OBD-II covers only emissions, and other modules need the manufacturer’s protocols, which the clone and the app often don’t support
The adapter only works with the engine running
The other modules speak the manufacturer’s language, and often sit on other lines too. Both the program and the adapter have to support this.

That the scan tool or adapter is rated for 24 V

You have about an hour of adaptation work ahead with the ignition on. What should you do about power?
Nothing — the battery will last

Connect a battery maintainer or a power supply
A sagging battery causes false codes and is dangerous while software is being written. Jumping from a donor car causes voltage spikes; only a charger or a power supply holds a steady voltage.
The scan tool diagnostic procedure

A scan tool gives you a lot of information in a minute, and that’s the trap: you want to clear the codes right away and see what comes back. That’s how evidence gets lost. A diagnostician has a procedure, and it’s the same for an old Lada and a new Chinese crossover. We covered the general troubleshooting algorithm in the lesson on troubleshooting methods; here it’s about how to work with the scan tool within it.
Start with a conversation
Five minutes of talking saves an hour of work. The scan tool will show what the module saw, and the customer will tell you under what conditions it happens. Ask:
What exactly happens: a warning light is on, it jerks, won’t start, stalls, uses more fuel?
When: cold or hot, at idle, when accelerating, on the highway, in freezing weather, after rain or a car wash, after refueling?
How often: all the time, once a day, once a week? How to catch rare glitches is covered in the lesson on graphs and recording.
What has already been done: who cleared the codes and when, what was replaced, was an alarm, a tracker or LPG equipment installed?

Sometimes it’s clear from the conversation alone that the scan tool isn’t the first tool to reach for. “It clicks but won’t crank” means the battery, terminals, grounds and starter, as in the lesson on the starter. “Nothing switches on” means power and fuses.
Scanning all modules
Once connected, run a scan of all modules — scan tools call this an auto scan or quick test. Don’t limit yourself to the engine, even if the complaint is “about the engine”:
Modules exchange data. The transmission and the speedometer need wheel speed from the ABS, and a transmission fault can turn on the Check Engine light and limit engine power.
U communication codes in several modules at once point to the bus or the power supply, not to each module separately — more on this in the lesson on trouble codes.
A module that didn’t respond is also a result. Write it down; why this happens is covered in the “No communication with a module” lesson.
The list of modules with and without codes is the basis of the report for the customer.
Record before clearing
Save the scan tool report for all modules — as a file or to the cloud, if the scan tool can do that.
Open and save the freeze frame of every important code: rpm, temperature, load, speed at the moment of the fault.
No report function? Photograph the screen: the code, description, status, freeze frame.
Label it: date, license plate or VIN, mileage.
Only after that — live data, tests and looking for the cause.

Monitors are self-tests that the engine module runs on its own during normal driving: catalytic converter, oxygen sensors and their heaters, misfire, fuel system, evaporative emissions, comprehensive components, and on some cars EGR and other systems. “Ready” means the test has been run; if it had failed, a code would have appeared. “Not ready” means the test hasn’t been run yet since the codes were cleared or the battery was disconnected: the module needs its own conditions — warm-up, steady driving, cooling down after being parked. It’s not a fault, it’s an exam not yet taken. The misfire, fuel system and comprehensive component monitors run continuously and are usually “ready” right away.
Almost all monitors are “not ready” and there are no codes — the codes or the battery were reset recently. When buying a used car, that’s a reason to be wary: it’s sometimes how a fault is hidden.
“Not ready” after a repair is normal. Let the car be driven in different modes and check again; the drive cycle conditions are in the car’s manual.
“Not supported” — this car doesn’t have that monitor. It’s not a fault.
Clearing a code doesn’t mean fixing it

Clearing turns off the light and deletes the codes, freeze frames and monitor results, but the cause remains. A hard fault will come back immediately or on the very first drive; an intermittent one in a day or a week, when the customer is already sure the car is fine. So codes are cleared at the end: after the repair. Then the car is checked under the conditions in which the fault appeared, and all modules are scanned again.

Don’t clear airbag and ABS codes just to make the light go out: the light will go out, but the system may fail to work when it’s needed. Airbag faults are traced following the manufacturer’s procedure; never measure squib resistance with a multimeter.
Talk first: what, when, under what conditions and what has already been done.
Scan all modules; a module that didn’t respond is also a result.
Save codes and freeze frames before clearing; clear after the repair.
“Not ready” means the self-test hasn’t been completed yet; almost all “not ready” with no codes means the codes were cleared recently.
What does the readiness monitor status “not ready” mean?
The system is faulty and the catalytic converter needs replacing
The scan tool doesn’t support this car
The self-test hasn’t been run yet since the codes were cleared or the battery was disconnected
The module needs its own driving conditions to run the test. If it had failed, a code would have appeared.
Why scan all modules if the customer is complaining about the engine?
The cause may be in another module: ABS, transmission or communication codes affect how the engine runs
That way it’s faster to clear all the codes at once
Without it the scan tool won’t show live data
Modules exchange data. A transmission fault can limit the engine, and communication codes in several modules point to the bus or the power supply.
The code was cleared and the light went out. Why isn’t that a repair?
Clearing fixes only software glitches
The light would have gone out even without clearing
It is a repair if the light is off
The cause is still there, the code will come back, and the freeze frame is already lost
Clearing removes only the record of the fault. The cause has to be found and fixed, and then the car checked under the same conditions.
The scan tool shows two codes in the engine module. What’s the right step?
Clear the codes and see if they come back
Save the codes with their freeze frames and scan the other modules
Immediately replace the sensor named in the first code’s description
Disconnect the battery to reset the module
Evidence first: the codes and freeze frames from all modules. Clearing and disconnecting the battery destroy them, and a code points to a circuit, not to a part.

A code is a short message from the module: “in this circuit or system I saw this.” To understand it correctly, you need three things: the code’s status, the conditions under which it was stored, and its neighbors — what other codes are in this module and in the others.
Code statuses
Current, or active — the fault is present right now. Clear it and the code will come back as soon as the module checks that circuit again.
Stored, or confirmed — the fault occurred and was confirmed and is recorded in memory, but it may not be showing up right now. Typical of bad contacts and intermittent faults.

Pending — the module noticed a deviation once but hasn’t confirmed it yet. In many systems the code is confirmed if the deviation repeats on the next drive — then the light comes on. A pending code is an early hint: the light isn’t on yet, but the problem is already there.
Permanent — found on some cars. It can’t be cleared with a scan tool: the module deletes it by itself once the system passes its self-test.

Many scan tools also show a counter: how many times the fault has occurred or how many drives have passed since the last time. A stored code with a high counter means the fault comes back regularly, and you need to look for it seriously.
Freeze frame: conditions at the moment of the fault
