The freeze frame is the parameter values at the moment the code was stored. Usually these are rpm, coolant temperature, load, speed, fuel trims and intake pressure. Make-specific scan tools may have several snapshots with a larger set of parameters. The freeze frame answers the question “when?” and hints at how to reproduce the fault. For example, P0171 — system too lean, bank 1 — stored at 780 rpm, a coolant temperature of 90 °C, 20% load, 0 km/h and a long-term trim of +18%: that’s a warm idle, and the first thing to look for is an air leak.
The same P0171 stored on the highway under load is a different story: more often it’s a lack of fuel. More on this in the lesson on fuel trims.
The code was stored at a coolant temperature of −20 °C and a speed of 0 km/h — the fault shows up on a cold start. Check it in the morning on a cold car, not after it has warmed up.
The code was stored at 90 km/h and high rpm — you’ll have to check it on a drive, with recording, as in the lesson on graphs.
How a code is structured: a bit deeper
We covered the letters P, C, B, U and the digit right after the letter — generic or manufacturer code — in the lesson on OBD-II codes. In generic P codes, the next digit points to the system:
1 and 2 — mixture, air and fuel metering: air sensors, oxygen sensors, injectors.
3 — ignition and misfires.
4 — emission control systems: EGR, catalytic converter, evaporative emissions.
5 — vehicle speed, idle control, auxiliary inputs.
6 — the control module itself and its output circuits.
7 and 8 — transmission.

The last two digits are the specific fault. For example, P0420 — catalyst efficiency below threshold, bank 1. Many modern modules add two more characters after the code — the failure type: short to ground, open circuit, signal out of range. The scan tool usually spells them out in words — read the whole description, not just the number.
SPN and FMI on trucks

On trucks and heavy equipment on the J1939 bus, a code consists of two numbers. SPN is the parameter or component number: what is faulty. FMI is the failure mode, a number from 0 to 31: how it’s faulty. For example, SPN 110 is coolant temperature. FMI 3 — voltage above normal or shorted to positive, FMI 4 — voltage below normal or shorted to ground, FMI 5 — current below normal or open circuit, FMI 2 — erratic or incorrect signal. The same SPN with different FMIs means a different search: an open is traced differently from a short. Decoding is on the “Error codes” tab; truck specifics are in the lesson on trucks.
A pile of codes: what comes first

One failure often produces many codes in different modules. If you fix them down the list, you can end up replacing half the car. Look for the root-cause code — the one that explains the others. The order is:

Power: low or high voltage codes, a weak battery. A voltage dip during cranking causes codes in many modules at once — from the engine to the instrument cluster. Battery, alternator and grounds first.

Communication: U codes. If several modules report that they’ve lost communication with the same module, the problem is in that module — power, ground, connector — or on its section of the bus. If the codes are about different modules, check the whole bus, as in the lesson on digital buses.
Shared sensor circuits: a short in one sensor pulls down the 5 V reference, and the module logs codes for several sensors at once — as in the lesson on sensors.
Specific sensor and actuator circuits.
Consequential codes: misfires, lean or rich mixture, catalytic converter. P0420 with misfires is a consequence: fix the misfires first, or even a new catalytic converter will be ruined.
Check the fuses first. If several modules report that they’ve lost communication with the same module, start by looking at the fuses for its power supply.
A current code means the fault is present now, a stored one means it was there, and a pending one means it was noticed but not yet confirmed.
The freeze frame shows the conditions at the time of the fault and hints at how to reproduce it.
SPN — what is faulty, FMI — how: open, short, out of range.
In a pile of codes, start with power and communication; consequential codes come last.
A code has the status “pending”. What does that mean?
The module noticed a deviation but hasn’t confirmed it yet
The code has already been cleared and won’t appear again
The scan tool itself is faulty
A pending code is an early hint. If the deviation repeats, the code will be confirmed and the light will come on.
The code’s freeze frame shows a coolant temperature of −20 °C and a speed of 0 km/h. When is the best time to look for the fault?
Right after a long highway drive
In the morning, on a cold start, with the car fully cooled down
Any time — the conditions don’t matter
Only in summer, in a warm service bay
The freeze frame shows that the fault appeared with the engine cold. That’s the condition in which it needs to be reproduced.
A truck has the code SPN 110 FMI 4. How do you read it?
Engine speed above normal
Oil pressure — open circuit
Coolant temperature: voltage below normal or shorted to ground
SPN 110 is coolant temperature, FMI 4 is voltage below normal or shorted to ground.
After a start with a weak battery, there are codes in the engine, ABS and instrument cluster, plus low-voltage codes. Where do you start?
Replace the ABS module
Clear everything and never come back to it
Reflash the engine module
With power: save the codes, check the battery, alternator and grounds, then clear and see what comes back
Low voltage causes codes in many modules at once. Until the power problem is fixed, the other codes are consequences.

Live data is what the engine module sees and does right now. You don’t need to remember hundreds of specs: it matters more to look in the right order and under the right conditions. The values below are guidelines for a typical gasoline engine. Look up the exact values in your car’s data and on the “Sensors” tab.
Test conditions
The engine is warmed up to operating temperature: the radiator fan has come on at least once.
Idle, transmission in P or neutral, parking brake on.
Loads switched off: A/C, headlights, heaters. Otherwise the rpm and load will be different.
Pick the 8–10 parameters you need, not the whole list: the fewer parameters, the more often the numbers update.
Order: from simple to complex
Rpm. Steady, without dips or “hunting”. Higher on a cold engine, dropping to the car’s spec after warm-up.

Coolant temperature. On a warm engine usually about 90 °C, higher on some modern engines — per the car’s data. The key check is in the morning on a cold car: the coolant and intake air temperatures should be close to the outside temperature.
System voltage. With the engine running — 13.5–14.5 V, as in the lesson on the alternator. If it’s lower, look for a charging problem: low voltage interferes with the coils, injectors and modules.
Mass airflow (MAF), g/s or kg/h. Rises smoothly with rpm, without dips. The idle value depends on engine displacement — compare it with the car’s data or with an identical healthy car.

Intake manifold pressure (MAP). At warm idle — about 30–40 kPa. With the ignition on and the engine off — atmospheric, about 90–93 kPa in Almaty. If it’s noticeably higher at warm idle, check for an air leak, the sensor itself and the engine’s mechanical condition — more on this in the lesson on compression.

Throttle position and accelerator pedal position. The value at idle is small and differs from car to car. The key thing is that it rises smoothly with the pedal, without jumps, and returns to the same number when the pedal is released.
Load, %. Small at idle, rises as the throttle opens.

Ignition timing (spark advance) — in degrees before top dead center. At idle it’s usually a few degrees, and it “wanders” a little: that’s how the module keeps the idle steady. On a cold start the module may retard the timing a lot to warm up the catalytic converter faster.
Injection pulse width — a few milliseconds at idle, rising with load. The exact value depends on the engine and the injection system — per the car’s data.
Fuel system status. Closed loop — the module controls the mixture from the oxygen sensor; open loop — during warm-up, at full throttle and when there are faults. Trims are judged only in closed loop.

Oxygen sensors. The upstream narrowband sensor swings between 0.1 and 0.9 V, a wideband sensor shows lambda around 1.00; the downstream sensor, after a healthy catalytic converter, is steadier than the upstream one.
Fuel trims — short-term and long-term. A total within about ±10% is normal. How to read them and what to do with the oxygen sensors is covered in the next lesson.
Cross-check the parameters against each other

On a cold car the coolant and intake air temperatures are almost the same and close to the outside temperature. If at −25 °C the air reads −25 °C and the coolant +20 °C, the coolant sensor or its circuit is lying: the module thinks the engine is warm, gives too little fuel, and the car starts poorly.
Rpm, airflow, MAP and load rise together. If the rpm went up but the airflow barely changed, the sensor or its wiring is giving a wrong signal.
The throttle and the pedal move in sync.
The sensor shows “lean” — the trim goes positive: the module is honestly adding fuel. The sensor is “frozen” and the trim isn’t moving — the module is working without feedback.
A frozen “nice” number with a sensor fault may be a substitute: the module has switched to a default value instead of the signal. Cross-check with the codes.
Not just idle

Idle is just the beginning. Slowly raise the rpm to 2500–3000 and hold it: rpm, airflow and load should rise smoothly, the oxygen sensor should keep switching, and the trims should stay normal. A quick throttle blip checks the response: the throttle, MAF and MAP react immediately, without delays or dips. The car is checked under real load on a drive — more on this in the lesson on graphs and recording.

Check the fuses first. If a sensor parameter is “dead” — zero or a frozen number — and the sensor has its own power supply or heater, like a MAF sensor or an oxygen sensor, start with the fuses for those circuits.

A running engine in a closed garage means carbon monoxide: turn on the exhaust extraction or route the exhaust outside. The car must have the parking brake on and the transmission in P or neutral. Don’t hold high rpm for long on a stationary car, and keep your hands, clothing and the scan tool cables away from the belts and the fan.
Live data is checked at warm idle, with the loads off and a short list of parameters.
Order: rpm, temperature, voltage, air and throttle, ignition timing and injection, oxygen sensors and trims.
Guidelines: voltage 13.5–14.5 V, MAP at idle about 30–40 kPa, total trims within ±10% — more precisely, per your car.
Parameters are cross-checked: temperatures on a cold engine, rpm against airflow, throttle against pedal.
On a morning at −25 °C the scan tool shows: intake air −25 °C, coolant +20 °C. What is more likely?
Everything is normal: the coolant is always warmer than the air
The coolant temperature sensor or its circuit is lying — the module thinks the engine is warm
On a cold car both temperatures are close to the outside temperature. A false “warm” reading means too little fuel and hard starting in the cold.
MAP at warm idle is 34 kPa. How do you assess this?
Within the usual guideline of 30–40 kPa
Too low — the sensor is faulty
That’s atmospheric pressure; the engine is off
At warm idle there’s vacuum in the intake, and MAP is about 30–40 kPa. Atmospheric pressure in Almaty is about 90–93 kPa.
Why is it better to keep 8–10 parameters in the live data list rather than all of them?
Otherwise the codes will be cleared
The car manufacturer requires it
Otherwise the battery will run down
The fewer parameters, the more often the numbers update
The scan tool polls the parameters one at a time. A long list slows down the update of each one.
The rpm rose to 2500, but the MAF airflow barely changed. What does this tell you?
That’s normal engine operation
Fuel cut-off has kicked in
The mass airflow sensor or its wiring is giving a wrong signal
Clear the codes and check again
Rpm, airflow and load rise together. If one parameter “doesn’t move”, it and its circuit are the suspects.

The module keeps the mixture close to ideal — about 14.7 parts of air to 1 part of gasoline by mass. That’s λ = 1: the catalytic converter works best at it. The module can’t measure the mixture directly, so it looks at the oxygen in the exhaust through the oxygen sensor and adjusts the injection. The scan tool shows these adjustments as fuel trims. We covered the basics in the lesson on the scan tool and live data; here it’s about how to use the trims to find the cause.
Short-term and long-term
Short-term fuel trim (STFT) is a quick “here and now” correction. On a healthy warm engine it constantly swings around zero, following the oxygen sensor.

Long-term fuel trim (LTFT) is what the module has “learned”. If the short-term trim has to keep adding fuel for a long time, the module gradually transfers the correction into the long-term trim, and the short-term trim returns to zero. The long-term trim is stored in memory — on many cars separately for idle and for load.

Plus means the module is adding fuel: the sensor sees a lean mixture, excess oxygen. Minus means it’s taking fuel away: the mixture is rich. A trim isn’t a fault but the module’s reaction: it shows which way the module has to correct.
Judge the total STFT + LTFT on a warm engine in closed loop. The guideline is within about ±10%. On a V engine each bank of cylinders has its own trims: bank 1 is the one with cylinder 1.
Air leak or not enough fuel

Both problems cause a lean mixture and positive trims, and when the limit is exceeded — code P0171, or P0174 on the second bank of a V engine. A check in three modes helps tell them apart: warm idle, 2500 rpm with no load, and accelerating under load on a drive. In each mode, look at the total trim.

An air leak after the mass airflow sensor: a cracked intake duct, an intake gasket, a vacuum hose, the PCV valve. At idle little air passes through the engine, and the “unmetered” air is a noticeable share, so the trim is strongly positive. At higher rpm the total flow is many times greater, the leak’s share is small, and the trim drops. Example: idle +20%, 2500 rpm +4%, under load +3%.

Weak fuel supply: a worn fuel pump, a clogged filter or strainer, dirty injectors. At idle there’s enough fuel, but under load the demand rises, the pump can’t keep up, and the plus grows with the load. Example: idle +3%, 2500 rpm +4%, under load +20% or more. Over time a worn pump may stop altogether.

A mass airflow sensor that under-reads also causes a plus that grows with load. So the conclusion is verified: the air leak with a smoke machine and a visual inspection, the fuel supply with a pressure gauge, comparing the pressure with the manual, and the sensor against the spec or a known-good one.
If the fuel pump isn’t working, give the fuel tank a light tap from underneath. If the pump “wakes up”, it’s worn and due for replacement.
Rich mixture and LPG

A large minus means the mixture is rich on its own and the module has to take fuel away; when the limit is exceeded — P0172 or P0175. Common causes: leaking injectors, excessive fuel pressure, a temperature sensor that reads cold on a hot engine, a mass airflow sensor that over-reads. A car running on LPG: compare the trims on gasoline and on gas. If everything is normal on gasoline but on gas the trims are far into plus or minus, the problem is in the gas equipment setup, not in the engine.
Narrowband sensor
The signal ranges from 0.1 to 0.9 V: about 0.1 V is lean, about 0.9 V is rich, and the threshold is about 0.45 V. The sensor works like a “lean–rich” switch; it doesn’t give an exact mixture figure.

On a warm engine in closed loop, the upstream sensor constantly switches between these levels, and the short-term trim swings the opposite way: when the sensor shows “rich”, the module takes fuel away; when it shows “lean”, the module adds fuel.

Response check: on a sharp throttle blip the signal quickly goes to 0.9 V; when you let off the throttle from high rpm, the module cuts fuel and the signal drops almost to 0.1 V. A slow, “lazy” sensor responds with a noticeable delay — an oscilloscope will show the signal shape more precisely, as in the lesson on the oscilloscope.
The sensor is stuck at around 0.45 V or near zero — it’s cold (the heater isn’t working), there’s an open in the circuit, or the sensor is faulty.

False “lean”: an air leak in the exhaust ahead of the sensor. The sensor sees extra oxygen, the module richens the mixture, and the trim is positive even though the engine is fine. Check the manifold gasket and look for exhaust cracks before replacing the sensor.
Wideband sensor and the sensor after the catalytic converter

A wideband sensor measures the mixture accurately and over a wide range. The scan tool shows lambda (1.00 is the ideal mixture, higher is lean, lower is rich), the sensor current or a nominal voltage — exactly which depends on the make. It doesn’t switch like a narrowband sensor: at warm idle lambda stays around 1.00. Don’t apply the “0.45 V” rule to it.

The downstream sensor sits after the catalytic converter. A healthy catalytic converter stores and releases oxygen, so the downstream sensor’s signal is steadier and slower than the upstream one. If the downstream sensor starts copying the upstream sensor’s swings, the catalytic converter has stopped working — hence P0420.

The downstream sensor monitors the catalytic converter and fine-tunes the mixture a little. Cutting out the catalytic converter and fitting a “cheat device” in place of the downstream sensor isn’t a repair, it’s cheating the emissions monitoring system. We don’t do this.

Don’t look for air leaks by spraying cleaner or releasing gas near a hot running engine: it’s a fire hazard. A smoke machine is safer. Before working on the fuel system, relieve the pressure as the manual describes and keep a fire extinguisher nearby.
Plus — the module is adding fuel (lean), minus — taking it away (rich); a normal total STFT + LTFT is about ±10%.
A plus at idle that goes away at higher rpm — an air leak; a plus that grows under load — fuel supply or the MAF sensor.
A narrowband sensor switches between 0.1 and 0.9 V; a wideband sensor shows lambda around 1.00.
The downstream sensor after a healthy catalytic converter is steadier than the upstream one; if it copies the upstream one, the catalytic converter isn’t working.
At idle the total trim is +3%, when accelerating under load +20%, and the engine feels sluggish. What is more likely?
A rich mixture from leaking injectors
Not enough fuel — pump, filter, pressure — or the MAF sensor is under-reading
An air leak shows at idle and goes away at higher rpm. A plus that grows under load is a sign of a lack of fuel or under-reported airflow.
The upstream narrowband sensor on a warm engine sits at about 0.45 V and doesn’t change. What’s likely?
The sensor is cold because of a faulty heater, there’s an open in the circuit, or the sensor is faulty
The mixture is ideal, everything is fine
That’s normal wideband sensor operation
A healthy warm narrowband sensor constantly switches between 0.1 and 0.9 V. A frozen signal is a sign of a problem with the sensor or its heater.
The downstream sensor after the catalytic converter switches as often as the upstream one. What does that mean?
The downstream sensor works better than the upstream one
The mixture is too lean
You need to clear the codes
The catalytic converter has stopped storing oxygen
A healthy catalytic converter smooths out the swings, so the downstream signal is steadier. If it copies the upstream one, the catalytic converter isn’t working, hence P0420.
A car running on LPG: on gasoline the total trim is +2%, on gas +18%. Where should you look for the cause?
In the gas equipment setup
In the downstream oxygen sensor
On gasoline the engine is fine, so there’s no air leak and no sensor problem. A deviation only on gas points to the gas system setup.

Numbers on the screen change faster than the eye can follow. A graph shows what you can’t see in the numbers: a dip lasting a fraction of a second, a slow drift and, most importantly, which parameter changed first. And a recording lets you catch a fault that shows up once per drive and analyze it calmly once you’re parked.
Several parameters on one graph
Choose 3–6 related parameters for a specific question. The fewer parameters, the more often they update and the cleaner the graph.

Sample sets. Jerks and hesitation: rpm, throttle, MAF or MAP, load. Mixture: upstream oxygen sensor, short-term trim, rpm. Overheating: coolant temperature, rpm, fan. Engine stalls: rpm, speed, voltage, oxygen sensor, trim.

Each parameter has its own scale. Compare graphs by time, not by the height of the lines: what matters is what changes at the same moment and what changes earlier. It’s handy to place a cursor — a vertical line that shows the values of all parameters at the same second.

The scan tool polls the module one parameter at a time, and the data updates several times a second or less often. A pulse lasting milliseconds isn’t visible on a scan tool graph — for that you need an oscilloscope, as in the lesson on the oscilloscope.
Recording a drive

Preparation. Choose parameters for the complaint and check that the scan tool saves the recording to a file. Secure the cable so it doesn’t interfere with the pedals, and the scan tool so it can’t fall under your feet.
One person drives, another handles the scan tool. The driver watches the road and says “there, it’s started”; the helper places a marker if the scan tool can do that, or notes the time.
Repeat the conditions from the complaint and the freeze frame: cold start, warm-up, highway, bumps, uphill, A/C on.
Record with some margin — both before and after the glitch.
Save the file with a clear name: car, date, “before repair”.
Better to get a Launch scan tool — that’s proven equipment. Cheap ELM327 adapters sometimes “knock out” the car, and that’s the last thing you need on a drive.

The driver doesn’t look at the scan tool or press buttons while driving — that’s what the helper is for. Don’t clear anything or run tests during the drive. Checks at speed — only within the traffic rules, on a clear road.
How to find the moment of the glitch

Open the recording and find the marker or the glitch itself — an rpm drop, a jerk, the engine stalling. Now rewind a few seconds and ask yourself: which parameter changed first? The cause always comes before the effect. Example — a car sometimes stalls while driving:

The rpm dropped to zero in a single recording step, while the speed was still high and the oxygen sensor had been working normally — the module suddenly lost the rpm signal. The suspects are the crankshaft sensor, its wiring and its connector.

First the oxygen sensor went “lean”, to 0.1 V, the short-term trim went strongly positive, and only then did the rpm drop — the engine wasn’t getting enough fuel. Check the fuel pump, its relay and its wiring.
Before the glitch the voltage sagged or several parameters “blinked” at once — look at the module’s power and grounds and the main relay, as in the lesson on ECU power and grounds.
Comparing “before” and “after”

The recording before the repair is your baseline, as in the lesson on the scan tool and live data. After the repair, record the same set of parameters under the same conditions: the same warm-up, the same mode, the same stretch of road. Many scan tools can open two recordings side by side or overlay them. Example: an air leak — the total trim at warm idle was +20%, and after the cracked intake duct was replaced it’s about zero, within the normal ±10%. A comparison like that convinces both you and the customer better than any words.
Same conditions: warm-up, load, electrical loads switched on. Otherwise you’ll be comparing the weather, not the repair.
After a repair the module needs time to relearn: the long-term trim doesn’t change right away. Repeat the recording after a drive; resetting adaptations is covered in the lesson on adaptations.
Keep recordings for your customers’ cars: if they come back, you’ll have something to compare with.
On a graph — 3–6 related parameters: the fewer there are, the faster they update.
Recording on a drive: the driver watches the road, the helper watches the scan tool and places a marker at the moment of the glitch.
Look for which parameter changed first: the cause always comes before the effect.
“Before” and “after” are recorded under the same conditions; short pulses are caught with an oscilloscope.
Why is 3–6 parameters on a graph better than 30?
Otherwise the scan tool will clear the codes
The fewer parameters, the more often they update and the easier it is to see how they’re related
The scan tool polls the parameters one at a time. A short list updates more often, and on the graph it’s easier to see what changed first.
In the recording, the rpm dropped to zero in a single step at 60 km/h, and the oxygen sensor had been working normally before that. What is more likely?
The crankshaft sensor signal was lost: the sensor, wiring or connector
The car ran out of fuel
The downstream oxygen sensor is faulty
The engine overheated
An instant loss of rpm while driving with a normal mixture says the module lost the rpm signal. If fuel were short, the oxygen sensor would have gone “lean” first.
Who should watch the scan tool during a test drive?
The driver — from time to time
No one: no recording is needed
A helper in the passenger seat
The driver, at traffic lights, pressing buttons
The driver watches only the road. The scan tool, markers and buttons are the helper’s job.
You’re comparing trims before and after a repair. What is essential?
Record “after” right after clearing, on a cold engine
Delete the “before” recording so you don’t get confused
Make the recordings in different weather
The same conditions: warm-up, mode, electrical loads switched on
A comparison makes sense only if one thing changes — the repair. Different conditions give different numbers even without any repair.

An actuator test is a scan tool mode in which you ask the control module to switch on a specific component: the fuel pump, an injector, the fan, a valve. Different programs call it different things: “Tests”, “Activation”, “Component control”. The set of tests depends on the car and the scan tool: dealer software and a good multi-brand scan tool can do a lot, while a simple ELM327 adapter usually can’t run tests — more on this in the lesson on scan tools and connecting.

How is this better than the multimeter check from the lesson on actuators and PWM? The command takes the same path as in normal operation: from the module through its output switch — a transistor inside the module — through the wiring and connector to the actuator. If the actuator works, the whole circuit is good.
What tests give you

Separating two different faults: “the actuator doesn’t work” and “the module doesn’t switch it on”. The fan doesn’t come on with the engine hot, but runs in the test — so the circuit is good, and you need to look at what the module sees: the temperature sensor and live data, as in the lesson on live data.
Checking the whole circuit in a minute, without unplugging any connectors.
Finding the right valve on the engine: run the test — the one that clicks is it.
Verifying a repair: you replaced a relay or the fan — switch it on with a test and make sure everything works.
What you can usually switch on
Fuel pump: the module switches on the pump relay for a few seconds, and you can hear a hum near the tank or under the rear seat.
Injectors: one at a time, with short pulses — each one clicks.
Cooling fan: low and high speed, if it has them.

Valves: EGR (exhaust gas recirculation), EVAP canister purge (fuel vapor recovery), VVT (variable valve timing), boost control. The module controls them with PWM, as in the lesson on actuators and PWM.
On some cars — ignition coils, the A/C compressor clutch, relays and lamps.

Before a test, read the conditions on the scan tool screen and follow them exactly. Usually the ignition is on, the engine is off, the transmission is in P or neutral, and the parking brake is applied. The fan may come on at full speed right away: keep your hands, sleeves, scarf, long hair and the scan tool cable away from the fan blades and belts. When testing the pump and injectors, the fuel is under pressure: no open flames or smoking, and don’t take the fuel system apart at that time. If there’s pressure in the fuel rail, every injector actuation with the engine off sends fuel into the cylinder — keep the test short and don’t repeat it unnecessarily. Check a coil’s spark only with a spark tester. Don’t run tests while driving.
Not “by ear”, but with an instrument

A click means only that the valve armature moved. It won’t tell you whether the injector atomizes fuel, whether the EGR valve opens fully, or whether the pump delivers the right pressure. That’s why operation is confirmed with an instrument during the test.
A clamp meter on the fuel pump or fan wire: the current is steady and close to the spec in the manual or to an identical healthy car. Current with dips is a reason to suspect a worn pump motor.

A fuel pressure gauge during the pump test: the pressure quickly rises to the spec in the manual and doesn’t drop right after the pump switches off. If it drops quickly, there’s a leak: the pump check valve, the pressure regulator or an injector.
An oscilloscope on the injector or valve control wire: are there pulses from the module, and is their shape correct, as in the lesson on the oscilloscope.
Live data: for the EGR valve, the throttle body and the VVT system, compare the commanded value with the actual value from the sensor. What the module commanded, the sensor should show.
On some cars the VVT test is done at idle: if the mechanism works, the rpm drops noticeably or the engine starts running rough — that’s how it should be.
The actuator didn’t switch on
Check the test conditions and the battery voltage: at low voltage the module may refuse the test, and the actuator may not work.
Fuse and relay: the fuel pump and fan are usually powered through a relay.
Power at the actuator connector during the test — with a multimeter.
The control signal from the module — with an LED test light or an oscilloscope. If there’s a signal but the actuator is silent, the actuator or its connector is faulty.
No signal — check the wiring from the module to the actuator, and then the module’s own output.
If the fuel pump doesn’t hum during the test, I give the fuel tank a light tap from underneath. If the pump “wakes up”, it’s worn and due for replacement, even if it’s working now.
A test is a command to the module to switch on an actuator: if it works, the whole circuit is good, from the module output to the actuator.
Take the test conditions from the scan tool screen; usually the ignition is on and the engine is off. Keep hands and clothing away from the fan.
A click doesn’t prove it works: confirm with current, pressure, an oscilloscope or a position sensor.
Actuator silent — conditions and battery, fuse and relay, power, module signal, wiring.
The fan doesn’t come on with the engine hot, but runs at both speeds in the scan tool test. Where do you look?
Replace the fan motor
Replace the fan relay
Check what the module sees: the temperature sensor and live data
The test showed that the fan and its circuit are good. So the module isn’t getting a reason to switch it on — look at the sensor and the data.
Why isn’t an injector click during the test enough to call it good?
A click only says the armature moved; it says nothing about atomization and fuel delivery
Injectors click only while driving
Only faulty injectors click
The circuit’s operation is confirmed with an oscilloscope and current, while atomization and delivery are checked on a test bench.
What condition does a scan tool most often set for actuator tests?
A speed of at least 40 km/h
Ignition on, engine off
Battery disconnected
Engine at 3000 rpm
Most tests are done on a stationary car with the ignition on and the engine off. The exact conditions are on the scan tool screen.
During the fuel pump test the pressure rises to spec but drops quickly after the pump switches off. What does that tell you?
Everything is normal, that’s how it should be
A leak: the pump check valve, the pressure regulator or an injector
A healthy system holds pressure for a while after the pump switches off. A rapid drop is a sign of a leak.
Adaptations and resets

A control module adapts to the parts of a specific car and remembers this. These stored values are called adaptations, and the procedure for recording them is called learning, or a relearn. When a part is replaced or cleaned, the old values no longer fit it. Then the adaptation is reset and the module is taught again: with a scan tool in the “Special functions” or “Service” section, or on some cars by a manual procedure from the service manual. The order of work is the same for any of them.
Fix the cause first. An adaptation doesn’t repair anything: it only teaches the module to work with a good part.

The battery is charged, and a battery maintainer is connected for the duration of the procedure, as in the lesson on scan tools and connecting. A voltage dip in the middle of a relearn is a common cause of failure.
Meet the conditions on the scan tool screen: usually the engine is warmed up, the loads are off, and the pedals are not touched. Don’t guess — every car has its own.
Don’t interrupt the procedure: don’t switch off the ignition or disconnect the scan tool until it reports that it’s finished.
Check the result: live data, a test drive, codes in all modules.

An electronic throttle body is a motor and a position sensor in one housing. The module remembers its “closed” position and how much air is needed for idle. After the throttle body is cleaned or replaced, or the module is replaced, the idle speed is high or “hunts”, and the engine stalls when you let off the gas. A relearn helps — with a scan tool or by a manual procedure from the service manual, usually on a warm engine with the loads off. Then check the idle speed and the throttle position in live data. Don’t turn the throttle stop screw — it’s a factory setting.
Resetting fuel adaptations

As in the lesson on fuel trims: the long-term trim is what the module “learned” while the fault was present. After fixing an air leak or replacing the injectors, the MAF (mass airflow) sensor or an oxygen sensor, it’s reset, and the module relearns while driving. If after drives in different modes the trim stays around zero, the cause has been fixed. If it goes positive or negative again, the repair isn’t finished. On some cars the trims are also erased when the battery is disconnected, but other adaptations are lost along with them, so it’s better to reset them with a scan tool.
Automatic transmission

An automatic adapts the pressure and the clutch engagement timing to their wear. After a transmission repair, replacement of the valve body or the control module, and on some cars even after a fluid change, the adaptations are reset and a relearn is done per the manufacturer’s procedure. Often a certain fluid temperature is needed — you can see it in live data — and a drive during which the transmission goes through all the gears. Without a relearn there can be harsh or delayed shifts. Adaptations aren’t reset “just in case”: the transmission will have to relearn, and for a while the shifts may be harsher.
After battery replacement or disconnection

Power windows with an automatic mode lose their end positions: the window no longer goes up with “one touch”. The relearn is often done without a scan tool: lower the window all the way, raise it all the way and hold the switch for a few seconds — the exact procedure is in the manual.

The steering angle sensor is needed by the electronic stability control system (ESP). On some cars, after the battery is disconnected, and also after a wheel alignment, steering repairs or sensor replacement, it’s calibrated with a scan tool with the steering wheel and wheels pointing straight. Without calibration the ESP light stays on.
On cars with a battery monitoring system, a new battery is “registered” with a scan tool: you enter its capacity and type. Otherwise the module keeps charging it as if it were the old one.
Until the power window has been relearned, the anti-pinch protection may not work. Don’t test it with your hand or fingers, and warn the owner, especially if children ride in the car.
Check the fuses first. If after a battery replacement the power window doesn’t work at all, not just in automatic mode, that’s no longer an adaptation issue, and the first thing I check is its fuse.
Service interval

The maintenance reminder on the instrument cluster is reset with a scan tool or with the buttons on the cluster and steering wheel per the manual — and only after the service has actually been done. Otherwise the owner will miss an oil and filter change. It’s handy to log mileage and service dates on the app’s “Maintenance” tab.

“Disabling” EGR, the diesel particulate filter (DPF) and AdBlue/SCR — with software or an “emulator”. These systems reduce harmful emissions: without them the car doesn’t meet environmental requirements and may fail inspection, and tampering with them is prohibited by law.
Changing the mileage. It deceives the next buyer and also throws off the maintenance schedule: the owner doesn’t know when things are due to be replaced.

The tachograph and speed limiter on trucks and buses. The tachograph monitors the driver’s working and rest hours, and the speed limiter keeps a heavy vehicle from going faster than allowed. Tampering with them is prohibited by law, and only workshops authorized to do so may work on tachographs.
Immobilizer and keys without the car’s documents — the registration certificate and the owner’s ID or a power of attorney. Disabling or bypassing the immobilizer helps car thieves.

Such modifications break the law, and whoever made them is responsible for them. If the engine fails with a “disabled” system, if there’s an accident because of a tired driver, or if the car is stolen, the questions will be for the technician. Refuse directly and offer the legal option: find and fix the real cause of the EGR, DPF or AdBlue fault, perform a service regeneration of the particulate filter per the manufacturer’s procedure, program keys when the documents are provided. More in the “AdBlue” and “Immobilizer” sections.
An adaptation doesn’t repair anything: fix the cause first, then do the relearn — with a charged battery, following the scan tool’s conditions and without interruption.
After cleaning the throttle body — a relearn; after a fuel system repair — reset the fuel adaptations and check the trims on a drive.
After a battery replacement — relearn the power windows and, where needed, calibrate the steering angle sensor and register the battery; the service interval is reset only after maintenance.
“Disabling” EGR, DPF and AdBlue, mileage changes, tachographs, speed limiters and immobilizers without documents — we don’t do these.
After cleaning the throttle body, the idle speed “hunts”. What should you do?
Adjust the throttle stop screw
Perform a throttle relearn with the scan tool or by the hand procedure in the manual
Replace the MAF sensor
The module remembers the old “closed” position and the idle airflow. The relearn writes new values, and the stop screw is a factory setting.
You’ve fixed an air leak and reset the fuel adaptations. After a few drives, the long-term fuel trim is far into the positive again. What does this mean?
The reset failed — do it again
That’s how it should be after a reset
You need to disconnect the oxygen sensor
The cause hasn’t been fully fixed — keep looking
If the cause has been fixed, the trim stays near zero after a reset. Going back into the positive shows the mixture is still lean.
After the battery was replaced, the window stopped going up with “one touch”, but it works when you hold the switch. What is most likely needed?
Relearn the window’s end positions as described in the manual
Reflash the door module
Check the alternator belt
Without power, the module forgot the window’s end positions. The motor is fine — a relearn is needed.
A truck owner asks you to “disable AdBlue so the fault light stays off”. What’s the right answer?
Agree if the fault has been on for a long time
Fit an emulator — that’s not really disabling it
Refuse, since it’s prohibited by law, and offer to find and fix the cause of the fault
An emulator and software disabling are the same tampering with the exhaust aftertreatment system. The legal way is to find and fix the fault.

Many multi-brand and dealer scan tools can check the mechanicals and the cylinders without taking anything apart: compare compression, shut off cylinders one at a time, count misfires and monitor the timing. This quickly tells you which cylinder is “weak”. But it’s a hint, not a verdict: you confirm it with a compression gauge, which the next lesson covers, and with an oscilloscope.

When you crank the engine with the starter without letting it start, each cylinder slows the crankshaft down on its compression stroke. At that moment the starter current rises and the rpm dips slightly. The higher the compression, the bigger the current peak and the rpm dip. If the scan tool has this test, it compares the peaks between cylinders — using the starter current or the crankshaft sensor — and shows bars as a percentage of the best cylinder: for example, three cylinders at about 100% and one at about 70%.
Preparation — follow the scan tool’s instructions: it usually disables injection and ignition by itself for the cranking. The battery must be charged and the cranking even.
What it shows: which cylinder compresses worse than the others.
What it doesn’t show: the absolute pressure — if all cylinders are equally worn, the bars will be even. And it doesn’t name the cause: whether it’s the rings or the valves.
If the tool doesn’t know where cylinder 1 is (for example, a current clamp with no sync), the peaks come in firing order — for example, 1-3-4-2 — rather than by cylinder number.
Cylinder balance

At idle, the scan tool shuts off the injectors one at a time and watches how much the rpm drops. Healthy cylinders give about the same drop. If the rpm barely changed when a cylinder was shut off, that cylinder was already working poorly. The module tries to hold the idle speed, so the difference may be small — compare the cylinders with each other.

On Common Rail diesels, the module itself keeps the cylinders running evenly: based on how much each cylinder accelerates the crankshaft, it adds or takes away fuel. Many scan tools show these corrections cylinder by cylinder. If one cylinder’s correction is noticeably larger than the others and close to the limit, that’s a reason to check its injector and compression. Limits — see the manual.

Shut off the injectors, not the coils: with the spark cut, fuel keeps flowing and goes unburned into the catalytic converter, which overheats. Shut off each cylinder only briefly. While the engine is running, keep your hands and wires away from the belts and the fan; the parking brake is set and the transmission is in P or neutral. Don’t crank with the starter longer than the scan tool asks for, and let the starter cool down.

Many modules count misfires for each cylinder. The scan tool shows them in live data or in the on-board monitor test results — in OBD-II this is mode 06, which isn’t supported on every car. The counter doesn’t tell you the cause: it tells you where the crankshaft “stumbled”. Watch it under the conditions the customer complains about: at idle, under load, with a cold engine.
Rising in one cylinder — look in that cylinder: spark plug, coil, injector, compression. Swapping coils — as in the lesson on ignition and misfires.
Rising a little in all of them — a common cause: an air leak, fuel pressure, the MAF sensor, gasoline quality. Check the fuel trims, as in the lesson on fuel trims.
The module can mistake jolts from a rough road for misfires, so test on a smooth road.
Timing: camshaft and crankshaft

The module constantly compares the camshaft and crankshaft sensor signals. If their relative position goes out of tolerance, codes P0016–P0019 appear — crankshaft/camshaft position correlation. On engines with VVT, live data usually shows the desired and actual camshaft angle: at idle, when VVT isn’t active, the actual angle should be close to the base value, and when VVT is working, it should follow the desired angle. Some software also shows the timing deviation in degrees.
What it shows: the timing has “drifted” — a stretched chain, a belt that jumped teeth, timing marks set wrong after a repair, a faulty VVT phaser or its control valve.

What it doesn’t show is which of these causes it is. You find that with an oscilloscope — the crankshaft and camshaft signals on two channels, as in the lesson on the oscilloscope — and by the timing marks.

A correlation code can also come from the sensor itself, its wiring or a damaged reluctor wheel. But it’s worth starting with something simple — the oil level and condition: VVT phasers work on oil pressure.

I recommend getting a Launch scan tool — it’s proven equipment. Not every scan tool can do tests like relative compression and cylinder balance, and cheap ELM327 adapters usually can’t do them and sometimes even “knock out” the car.
Scan tool tests show which cylinder is worse, but not the cause and not the absolute compression.
Relative compression — from starter current peaks or rpm dips during cranking; balance — by shutting off the injectors, not the coils.
Misfire counter rising in one cylinder — look in that cylinder; in all of them — a common cause.
Codes P0016–P0019 — timing correlation: start with the oil, then the sensor signals and the timing marks.
The relative compression test showed even bars for all cylinders. What does this mean?
The compression is definitely within spec
The crankshaft sensor is faulty
The engine needs to go to an engine specialist
The cylinders compress equally, but the test doesn’t show the absolute pressure
The test compares the cylinders with each other. If they’re all equally worn, the bars will be even — only a compression gauge gives you the numbers.
Why do you shut off the injectors, not the coils, in the balance test?
Coils must not be disconnected at idle
Without a spark, the unburned fuel goes into the catalytic converter and overheats it
It makes the test faster
With the spark cut, the injector keeps delivering fuel, and it ends up burning in the catalytic converter.
Misfire counters are rising a little in all cylinders. Where should you look?
For a common cause: an air leak, fuel pressure, the MAF sensor, fuel trims
Replace all the coils
Replace the spark plugs in one cylinder
When all cylinders are affected, the cause is usually common to the whole engine, not one coil or spark plug.
The scan tool shows P0016 — crankshaft/camshaft correlation. Where is it sensible to start?
Replace the timing chain right away
Clear the code and keep driving
The oil level and condition, then the sensor signals with an oscilloscope, and the timing marks
Replace the ECU
The code says the timing doesn’t match, but it doesn’t name the cause. From simple to complex: oil, sensors, mechanicals.

An electrician shouldn’t try to fix what’s broken in the mechanicals. If a cylinder doesn’t hold compression — the pressure the piston builds on the compression stroke — no new coil or injector will bring it back to life. The scan tool tests from the previous lesson hint at which cylinder is weak, and a compression gauge confirms it and gives you the numbers.
Compression gauge
It’s a pressure gauge with a hose and a fitting for the spark plug hole. A threaded fitting is more reliable than a rubber one that you press in by hand: less leakage, and your hands are free.
Inside there’s a check valve: the needle stays at the maximum until you press the release button.
Scales come in bar, kgf/cm², MPa and psi: 1 bar is about 1 kgf/cm², 0.1 MPa or 14.5 psi.
A diesel needs its own compression gauge — with a higher scale and an adapter for the glow plug or injector hole. You don’t test a diesel with a gasoline gauge.
Measuring procedure
Warm the engine up to operating temperature: a cold engine gives lower readings.
Check the battery: it must be charged. Slow cranking lowers the readings.

Disable the fuel supply and ignition as the manual describes: the fuel pump fuse or relay, the injector and coil connectors. After reassembly, clear the codes that get stored because of the unplugged connectors.
Blow out the spark plug wells with compressed air so dirt doesn’t fall into the cylinders, and remove all the spark plugs — then the engine turns over easily and equally for every cylinder.
Thread the compression gauge fitting in by hand, without a wrench, so you don’t strip the threads.
Accelerator pedal to the floor: the throttle is fully open, and the cylinder fills with air.
Crank with the starter until the needle stops rising — usually a few seconds. Write down the reading, reset the gauge and move on to the next cylinder, cranking it for the same length of time.

Disable the fuel pump and ignition before cranking: gasoline vapor blows out of the open spark plug holes, and a spark can ignite it. The engine is hot — keep your hands away from the exhaust manifold and the radiator, and keep your hands and wires away from the belt and the fan. The parking brake is set and the transmission is in P or neutral. Remove spark plugs from a hot aluminum head smoothly and without cocking them. Don’t crank the starter for long stretches without a break — it overheats.

If the starter clicks instead of cranking during the test, I give the starter housing a few solid blows with a hammer. If it starts cranking, it’s time to check and repair the starter: the test readings depend on even cranking.
How to read the result

The absolute spec is in the engine’s manual: the numbers depend on the engine’s compression ratio and on the gauge. In Almaty and in the mountains, readings will be a little lower than the factory figures: at an altitude of about 800 m the air pressure is lower than at sea level, and the cylinder takes in less air. The main thing is to compare the cylinders with each other: the spread between them should be no more than about 10%.

Example: 12.0 — 12.2 — 11.8 — 9.5 bar. The limit in this example is about 11 bar, 10% below the best cylinder. The first three cylinders are above it, and the fourth is about 20% below the best — that’s the problem cylinder. All cylinders equally low — general wear or off timing. Two neighboring cylinders low — possibly a blown cylinder head gasket between them.
Oil test
Pour a little engine oil — about a tablespoon — into the weak cylinder through the spark plug hole and repeat the test. The oil will temporarily seal the gap between the rings and the cylinder wall.
Compression rose noticeably — the rings or the cylinder are to blame.
Barely changed — the valves (not seating properly or burnt) or the head gasket.
The oil test is usually not done on a diesel: the combustion chamber is small, and the oil can cause hydrolock.
When to send it to an engine specialist
Low compression in a cylinder has been confirmed by a repeat test.
Oil in the coolant or a milky emulsion in the oil, bubbles in the expansion tank, thick white exhaust smoke — signs of a blown head gasket.
The timing is off: correlation codes, as in the previous lesson, and wrong timing marks.
Unusual knocking, high oil consumption, blue smoke.

Your job as an electrician is to write down the measurements and tell the customer honestly that it’s a mechanical problem. Replacing spark plugs, coils and injectors when a cylinder has no compression is money thrown away. The engine specialist usually follows up with a leak-down test: feeding compressed air into the cylinder and listening for where it escapes — into the intake, the exhaust, the crankcase or the cooling system.
Compression is measured on a warm engine, with a charged battery, all spark plugs removed, the accelerator to the floor, and fuel and ignition disabled.
The key thing is the spread between cylinders: no more than about 10%; absolute specs are in the engine’s manual.
Oil test: compression rose — rings; didn’t change — valves or head gasket.
You don’t fix mechanical problems with electrics: once low compression is confirmed, the car goes to an engine specialist.
Why do you remove all the spark plugs for a compression test, not just one?
So the compression gauge doesn’t overheat
Only diesels require it
So the engine turns over easily and equally for every cylinder
The other cylinders don’t hold back the crankshaft, the cranking speed is even, and the cylinders can be compared fairly.
Compression by cylinder: 12.0 — 12.2 — 11.8 — 9.5 bar. Which is correct?
The fourth is about 20% below the best — that’s the problem cylinder
All cylinders are within spec
The compression gauge is faulty
First replace the coil on the fourth cylinder
A spread of more than about 10% is a sign of a fault. The coil doesn’t affect compression.
After a spoonful of oil, the compression in the weak cylinder barely changed. What’s the likely cause?
Worn rings
The valves or the head gasket
Oil only seals the rings. If it didn’t help, air is escaping past the valves or through the gasket.
A repeat test confirmed low compression in one cylinder. What does the electrician do?
Replaces the coil and spark plug
Writes down the measurements and sends the car to an engine specialist
Resets the adaptations
This is a mechanical fault. Replacing electrical parts won’t fix it.

“The scan tool can’t see the car” is one of the most common complaints. First answer two questions: is there no communication with any module, or only with one? And is the car to blame, or the scan tool itself? The answers tell you where to look. Keep the connector pinout at hand — it’s in the “OBD pinout” section of the app.
First rule out the scan tool
The correct make, model and year are selected in the software. For right-hand-drive Japanese domestic-market cars, select exactly those: generic OBD-II isn’t always supported on them.
The ignition is on: many modules “sleep” without it.
For a truck — a 24 V adapter, as in the lesson on scan tools and connecting them.
Check the scan tool on another car that’s known to be good. No communication there either — the problem is the scan tool, the cable or the adapter.
OBD connector power and grounds

By the standard, the OBD-II connector has: 16 — battery positive, present even with the ignition off; 4 — chassis ground; 5 — signal ground; 6 — CAN-H; 14 — CAN-L; 7 — K-line. On a particular car not every pin is used, and the manufacturer may use the free ones in its own way — check the wiring diagram.
Red multimeter lead into pin 16, black into pin 4: you should see battery voltage, 12.4–12.9 V at rest, for example 12.6 V.
Leave the red lead on 16 and move the black one to 5: the same voltage. Present on 4 but not on 5 — or the other way round — look for an open in that ground.
No positive on 16 — check the connector’s fuse and the wire to it. Which fuse it is — see the wiring diagram: it’s often shared with the cigarette lighter.
Voltage at the connector noticeably lower than at the battery terminals — a bad contact in the positive or in the ground.
Check the fuses first. When the scan tool won’t power up from the connector or can’t see the car, the first thing I check is the OBD connector power fuse.
CAN bus: 60 Ω between 6 and 14
As in the lesson on data buses: turn the ignition off, disconnect the battery negative and measure the resistance between pins 6 and 14.
About 60 Ω — both 120 Ω terminating resistors and the wires are intact.
About 120 Ω — an open in the bus or one resistor missing.
Near zero — a short between CAN-H and CAN-L. Then check 6 and 14 to ground: the resistance should be high.
With the ignition on — about 2.5 V on each wire.

On cars with a gateway — a separate module between the connector and the car’s buses — at the connector you’re only measuring the diagnostic line up to the gateway, and the numbers may differ. Check the wiring diagram.

This is pin 7, a single-wire diagnostic line found mostly on cars up to the late 2000s. With the ignition on and no traffic on the line, it sits at about battery voltage. Near zero — K-line shorted to ground: caused by a damaged wire or one of the modules on the line. Then the scan tool can’t communicate with any module on the K-line — disconnect them one at a time, following the wiring diagram.
Who “takes down” the bus

There’s no communication with any module, even though there’s power at the connector and the 60 Ω is fine. Then one node on the bus is often to blame: a faulty module — for example, after water got into it — or incorrectly connected aftermarket equipment: an alarm with remote start, a GPS tracker, a head unit with a CAN adapter. Such a node holds the bus down or floods it with messages, and the other modules can’t talk to each other.
Ask the owner: what’s been installed recently, any repairs, accidents, water in the cabin.
Disconnect the aftermarket equipment from the bus and check communication.

Didn’t help — disconnect the factory modules one at a time: pull their fuses or connectors according to the wiring diagram, and after each one check communication or look at the bus with an oscilloscope. If communication comes back, the last module you disconnected or its wiring is to blame.
Check the module you found: power, grounds, water in the connector. If needed — on the bench, as in the lesson on a module that won’t communicate.

Unplug and plug in module connectors only with the ignition off. During this kind of search, don’t touch the airbag module or the yellow airbag system connectors: they’re handled only according to the manual, with the battery disconnected and a waiting period. Don’t pierce bus wires with needles, and don’t apply voltage to CAN and K-line “to test them”.

Sometimes it’s the adapter itself that “takes down” the bus. I recommend getting a Launch scan tool — it’s proven equipment, while cheap ELM327 adapters sometimes “knock out” the car. If communication was lost while an adapter like that was plugged into the connector, unplug it first.
First rule out the scan tool: make and model in the software, ignition, 24 V for a truck, a check on another car.
OBD connector: 16 — positive, 4 and 5 — grounds; about 60 Ω between 6 and 14 with the car powered down; K-line (7) at rest — about battery voltage.
Power and 60 Ω are fine, but there’s no communication — look for the node that “takes down” the bus: aftermarket equipment first, then the modules one at a time.
Connectors — only with the ignition off; leave the airbag system alone during the search.
The scan tool won’t power up from the OBD connector. What should you check first?
CAN resistance between 6 and 14
The voltage between pins 16 and 4, and the connector’s power fuse
Replace the engine ECU
K-line on pin 7
The scan tool is powered from the connector: without positive on 16 and ground on 4, it won’t turn on. The bus is checked after that.
There’s power at the connector, the 60 Ω is fine, but there’s no communication with any module. An alarm with remote start was installed a week ago. Your first step?
Disconnect the alarm from the bus and check communication
Replace the engine module
Bridge CAN-H and CAN-L
Equipment recently connected to the bus is the first suspect. Disconnecting it is easier and faster than searching among the factory modules.
Between 16 and 4 there’s battery voltage, but between 16 and 5 — zero. What does this mean?
Normal for most cars
Faulty K-line
An open in the signal ground on pin 5
There’s positive on 16, so the ground on 5 is missing — look for an open in its wire.
When searching for a module that “takes down” the bus, why isn’t the airbag system handled the same way as the other modules?
Its connectors are too tight
It isn’t connected to the bus
Airbags are handled only according to the manual, with the battery disconnected and a waiting period
Mishandling the airbag system can make it deploy and cause injury.

The logic of diagnosing a truck is the same as for a passenger car: scan all modules, record the codes, look at live data. What’s different is the standard, the voltage, the connectors and the software. 24 V systems, two batteries and flash codes are covered in the lesson on trucks and the J1939 bus; here it’s about working with the scan tool.
J1939 for the diagnostician

J1939 is a standard for communication over the CAN bus for trucks, buses and heavy equipment. The speed is usually 250 kbit/s; newer vehicles may use 500 kbit/s. The bus physics is checked as on passenger cars: with the vehicle powered down, about 60 Ω between CAN-H and CAN-L.
The modules — engine, transmission, ABS, instrument cluster, AdBlue — often come from different manufacturers, and the scan tool polls each one.

The scan tool shows active faults separately from inactive ones recorded earlier: in J1939 these are the DM1 and DM2 messages. Inactive faults are evidence just like a freeze frame on a passenger car: record them before clearing.
A code is an SPN (what’s faulty), an FMI (how it’s faulty) and a counter of how many times the fault has occurred. Decoding is in the “Error codes” tab.
The FMI changes the whole plan of work. Here’s an example with the same parameter — SPN 100, engine oil pressure:
FMI 1 — the data is valid but below the normal operating range: the sensor is working and says the oil pressure really is low. Shut the engine off and check the pressure with a mechanical gauge.

FMI 4 — signal voltage below normal or shorted to ground: most likely the sensor circuit is faulty, not the engine. Look for a short in the wiring, but until the cause is found, check the oil pressure with a gauge anyway.
Connectors and adapter
A 9-pin round connector — on many trucks, buses and heavy equipment.

A 16-pin one — the same shape as OBD-II on passenger cars; found on Chinese trucks, among others. But the pin assignment may differ from passenger cars: a truck’s CAN may be on different pins. Check the documentation for the scan tool and the vehicle.
Adapter cables for each make and connector usually come with a truck scan tool. Homemade ones — only from a verified pinout.
The scan tool and adapter must be rated for 24 V: a 12 V passenger car adapter can burn out.
Chinese trucks and KAMAZ with Cummins

Shacman, Howo and FAW come with different engines — most often Weichai, sometimes Cummins and others — and with different transmissions and emission classes. The engine software is chosen by the engine and its control module, not just by the truck make: check the engine plate and the VIN.
Euro 4 and higher vehicles often have an AdBlue/SCR system with its own module — scan that too.

On a KAMAZ with Cummins, the engine is diagnosed with Cummins software and the other modules with KAMAZ software. Besides SPN/FMI, Cummins also shows its own fault codes — look for their descriptions in the Cummins documentation.
If the scan tool won’t communicate, check the bus and power, as in the lesson on lost communication; on the road, the flash codes from the “Self-diagnosis” section will help you out.
Russian localization and choosing software

Software for Chinese engines often comes in Chinese or English to begin with, and “amateur” Russian localization is often machine-translated: pressure and temperature mixed up, parameters named wrong. Go by the SPN and FMI numbers and check the description in the “Error codes” tab. Choose the scan tool manufacturer’s official software that supports the makes and engines you need and gets updates. Cracked software and dubious “builds” mean wrong descriptions, communication dropping out in the middle of a procedure, and a risk to the module.
I recommend getting a Launch scan tool — it’s proven equipment, and it has 24 V versions for trucks. Cheap ELM327 adapters sometimes “knock out” the car.
What we don’t touch

Tachograph and speed limiter: we don’t disable, reprogram or “adjust” them. The tachograph monitors the driver’s working and rest hours, and the limiter keeps a loaded vehicle from going faster than allowed. A tired driver or excess speed in a vehicle weighing many tons means serious crashes. Tampering is prohibited by law, and only workshops authorized to do so can work on tachographs.
AdBlue/SCR, EGR and the particulate filter — repair only. We don’t do “emulators”, removal or software disabling: it’s prohibited by law and sharply increases harmful emissions.

We don’t change the mileage — it deceives the next buyer. We don’t touch the immobilizer and keys without the vehicle’s documents — that’s helping car thieves. More in the lesson on adaptations and resets.

Whoever does such tampering is responsible for it. Offer the legal options: find the cause of the AdBlue fault — power, sensors, heating, fluid quality (more in the “AdBlue” section) — repair the EGR, do a service regeneration of the particulate filter following the manufacturer’s procedure. Run a parked regeneration only outdoors, away from dry grass and anything flammable, and don’t leave the vehicle unattended: the exhaust gets very hot.
A J1939 code is an SPN (what) and an FMI (how); record inactive faults before clearing. With FMI 1 the oil pressure really is low; with FMI 4, look at the wiring.
9- or 16-pin connector, pin assignment per the documentation; scan tool and adapter — 24 V only.
The engine software is chosen by the engine and its module; trust the SPN and FMI numbers, not machine translation.
Tachograph, speed limiter, “disabling” AdBlue, EGR and DPF, mileage, and the immobilizer without documents — we don’t touch.
The scan tool shows SPN 100 FMI 1. What does this mean?
The oil pressure really is below normal — shut the engine off and check with a gauge
The oil pressure sensor is shorted to ground
A communication fault with the instrument cluster
An AdBlue system fault
SPN 100 is oil pressure, FMI 1 is valid data below the normal operating range. The sensor isn’t lying: the engine is in danger.
What adapter do you need to diagnose a Shacman with a 24 V system?
Any ELM327
A 12 V passenger car one through a resistor
One rated for 24 V
A 12 V passenger car adapter can burn out on a 24 V system.
Why is the engine software for a Chinese truck chosen by the engine and not just by the make?
So the software loads faster
The same make is fitted with different engines and control modules
The make has no effect on diagnostics at all
So the Russian localization is better
A Shacman or Howo can come with a Weichai, Cummins or another engine, and each has its own module and its own software.
The owner asks you to “adjust” the speed limiter so the truck goes faster. Your answer?
Do it if it’s a privately owned vehicle
Do it temporarily, for one trip
Disable it with the scan tool
Refuse: tampering with the speed limiter is prohibited by law and dangerous
The speed limiter is a safety device. It isn’t disabled or “adjusted” at the owner’s request.

The engine is only part of the car. In manufacturer-specific mode, the scan tool also sees other modules: ABS and ESP — the brakes and the stability control system, SRS — the airbags, TPMS — tire pressure monitoring, climate control and the BCM — the body control module. Besides codes and live data, they have service functions — procedures the module carries out on the scan tool’s command: bleeding, calibration, relearning, entering codes. Scan tool menus differ, so here we cover what and why, not which button to press. General rules:
Codes and the cause come first. A service function doesn’t fix a fault: with a faulty sensor, the calibration won’t go through or the fault will come back.
Conditions — from the scan tool screen and the manual: ignition on or engine running, level ground, wheels straight. Read the prompts all the way through.
Stable power: on long procedures, connect a battery maintainer, as in the lesson on scan tools and adapters.

Don’t interrupt the procedure: don’t disconnect the adapter or turn off the ignition. You need a scan tool that supports the make and has a reliable connection — basic adapters usually can’t do service functions.
After the procedure — read the codes again and check that the system works.
ABS and ESP: wheels, bleeding, steering angle

ABS — the anti-lock braking system — monitors each wheel through a speed sensor. The easiest way to check the sensors is in live data: put all four wheel speeds on the screen and drive along a level, straight road. The speeds should match. If, say, at 40 km/h three wheels show about 40 and one shows 0 or jumps around, check that wheel: the sensor, its air gap and dirt on it, the tone ring — toothed or magnetic in the bearing — and the wiring, as in the lesson on sensors. A helper watches the scan tool, or the scan tool records a graph — the driver watches the road.

Bleeding with a scan tool. The ABS hydraulic unit has a pump, valves and its own passages. If air gets in there — for example, after the hydraulic unit is replaced or when the reservoir ran dry — ordinary pedal bleeding won’t get it out. If the manual calls for it, the scan tool cycles the pump and valves, a helper presses the pedal following the on-screen prompts, and you open and close the bleeder screws. Reservoir level — not below MIN; fluid — the type shown on the reservoir cap. If the procedure asks for a pause to let the pump cool down, wait it out. Brake fluid damages paint — wash off drips with water right away. The car goes back to the customer only with a firm pedal: check it on the spot, then at low speed in a safe area.

The steering angle sensor sits in the steering column. From it, ESP knows where the driver wants to go and compares that with how the car is actually turning. If the sensor’s zero point is off, ESP “sees” a skid: its light comes on, and the system may intervene when it shouldn’t. Calibration is needed after a wheel alignment if the tie rods were adjusted, and after replacing the sensor, the column or the steering rack; after a battery replacement — as in the lesson on adaptations and resets. The order: first the alignment is set and the steering wheel sits straight when driving straight ahead, then the wheels are pointed straight, the car is on level ground — and you calibrate with the scan tool. If the scan tool showed, for example, 10° with the wheels straight, it should read about 0° after calibration. Then turn the steering wheel both ways: the angle changes smoothly, with no jumps.
SRS means the airbags, seat belt pretensioners, crash sensors and the module. If the SRS light is on, the module has disabled the system or part of it, and it may not deploy in a crash.

Cause first, then reset. Typical trouble spots — connectors under the seats, the steering wheel clock spring, crash sensors, the seat belt buckle; you track them down by the code and live data. As long as the cause is there, the fault will come back — that’s how it should be.
Squibs aren’t measured with a multimeter — as in the lesson on safety. On many cars, the module itself shows the state of the airbag circuits in live data.
After the airbags have deployed, many modules store crash data, and such a code doesn’t go away when cleared: the deployed parts and the module are replaced following the manufacturer’s procedure.
We don’t fit “dummy” resistors in place of airbags: the light will go out, but the airbag won’t deploy in a crash.

Before working on airbag connectors, the steering wheel, the dashboard and the seats, turn off the ignition, disconnect the battery negative, insulate the terminal and wait for the time given in the manual: the module stores a reserve of energy, and an airbag can deploy. Place a removed airbag module with its cover facing up. When switching on for the first time after the work, don’t lean over the steering wheel and dashboard.
Tire pressure sensors (TPMS)

Indirect TPMS has no sensors of its own: it compares wheel speeds using the ABS sensors, and after the tires are inflated it’s reset with a button or in the car’s menu. Direct TPMS has a sensor in each wheel, usually on the valve stem: it transmits the pressure by radio, and each sensor has its own number — an ID. After a sensor is replaced, and on many cars after the set of wheels is changed, the module is taught the new IDs: with a scan tool, with a TPMS activation tool that “wakes up” the sensors, or by self-learning while driving — whatever the car calls for. Here wheels are changed twice a year, so it’s handy when both sets have sensors; on some cars the module remembers two sets of IDs. Before the relearn, set the pressure according to the placard on the door pillar. When the first frosts hit, the pressure drops and the light often comes on in the morning — check the pressure with a gauge first.
Diesel: injector codes and the particulate filter

Injector codes. Every Common Rail injector is tested at the factory, and its correction is written as a code on its body — for example, IMA; different manufacturers have their own names for it. After an injector is replaced, the code is entered into the ECU for that injector’s cylinder with a scan tool, and the module adjusts the delivery. If it isn’t entered or the cylinders are mixed up, the engine runs rough, smokes and knocks. Before installing, photograph each injector’s code and write down its cylinder.

Particulate filter regeneration. The particulate filter, DPF, traps soot, and on the highway the module burns it off by itself. In the city and on short trips, soot builds up and a light comes on. Forced regeneration with a scan tool is legal cleaning: the module raises the engine speed and exhaust temperature and burns off the soot. Conditions — per the manual: the engine is warm, there’s enough fuel, no differential pressure or temperature sensor faults, the vehicle is outdoors, away from dry grass and anything flammable. The exhaust gets very hot — don’t stand near it and don’t interrupt the procedure.

Regeneration doesn’t fix the cause. If the filter keeps clogging again and again, find out why: the differential pressure sensor and its tubes, the injectors, EGR, the turbocharger, oil consumption. Regeneration doesn’t burn off ash: a filter full of ash is washed out or replaced. We don’t do filter removal or software disabling — as in the lesson on adaptations and resets.
Climate and body

The scan tool reads the climate control module and the BCM — the body control module — the same way: codes, live data — temperatures, air flap positions, the state of buttons and switches — and actuator tests: air flaps, the blower fan, the compressor clutch, locks, windows, lights. How to work from the module to the actuator is covered in the lessons on body electrics and on climate control; tests follow the rules from the lesson on actuator tests, and nobody should be near the doors and windows during a test. Many body functions, such as speed-sensing auto door locking, are changed by coding. Save or photograph the previous settings first, and change only what the manufacturer provides for.
A service function doesn’t fix the cause: codes and the repair first, then the procedure under the scan tool’s conditions, without interruptions.
ABS: driving straight, the wheel speeds match; bleeding with the scan tool — if the car requires it; the pedal afterwards is firm.
The steering angle is calibrated after an alignment and steering parts replacement; an SRS code is cleared after the cause is fixed; connectors — with the battery negative disconnected.
TPMS is taught the new IDs, injector codes are entered after replacement, DPF regeneration is cleaning, not removal.

The steering angle sensor
That wheel’s speed sensor, air gap, tone ring and wiring
The airbag module

Replace the ESP module
Make sure the steering wheel sits straight when driving straight ahead, and calibrate the steering angle sensor with the scan tool
After the tie rods were adjusted, the sensor’s zero point shifted. Calibration restores it, and ESP stops seeing a “skid”.
The airbag light is on, and the code is an open in the seat airbag circuit. What’s the right way to handle it?
Find and fix the cause with the battery negative disconnected, then clear the code
Clear the code right away
Measure the squib resistance with a multimeter
Fit a resistor in place of the airbag

How does forced regeneration of the particulate filter differ from removing it?
No difference: both disable the filter
Regeneration is done only after removal
Regeneration is done on a cold engine
Regeneration burns off the soot in a filter that stays in place; we don’t do removal or disabling
